With reference to notice bearing barcode No. 1000002695551 dated January 29, 2026 issued under section 114(4) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), requiring filing of a complete return of income along with audited accounts for the subject tax year, it is respectfully submitted as follows:

The audited financial statements of K-Electric Limited (“the Company”), being the sponsoring undertaking of K-Electric Workers Profit-Participation Fund (“the Fund”), have not yet been finalized. The delay is attributable to pending tariff-related matters that have a direct and material bearing on revenue recognition, regulatory adjustments, and overall financial results for the year ended June 30, 2024.

These tariff matters are not routine accounting adjustments; rather, they involve substantive regulatory determinations that directly affect the profit base of the Company. Since the quantum of profit is central to the computation of Workers’ Profit Participation Fund obligations, premature finalization of accounts without resolution or clarity on these matters would risk producing financial statements that do not faithfully represent the legally sustainable position of the Company. Such an outcome would be inconsistent with applicable accounting standards, auditing requirements, and the prudence principle underlying financial reporting.

It is further submitted that the relevant tariff issue is presently sub judice before the Hon’ble Sindh High Court. The eventual outcome of the said proceedings is expected to have a consequential impact on the final accounting treatment. In view of the pending judicial adjudication, any attempt to finalize the audit at this stage would be commercially and legally imprudent. These regulatory developments have also been formally disclosed to the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan and the Pakistan Stock Exchange in compliance with applicable securities laws, which underscores both the materiality and continuing nature of the uncertainty.

Since the financial statements of the Workers Profit-Participation Fund are statutorily dependent upon the audited profits of the sponsoring undertaking, the Fund is unable to finalize and obtain audit of its own accounts for Tax Year 2024 in the absence of the Company’s finalized audited accounts. Consequently, the Fund is presently unable to file a complete return of income along with audited financial statements as envisaged under section 114(2) read with section 114(4) of the Ordinance. This inability is procedural in nature, arises from circumstances beyond the control of the Fund, and does not in any manner reflect non-compliance or deliberate delay.

It is respectfully submitted that the Ordinance contemplates situations where compliance within the initially specified period may not be feasible. The Commissioner is empowered to allow such extended time as may be reasonable in the circumstances, where sufficient cause is shown and reasons are duly recorded. In the instant case, the delay is directly linked to ongoing judicial proceedings and regulatory determinations materially affecting the sponsoring undertaking’s profit base. These are objective, verifiable, and bona fide constraints that justify the grant of a longer period.

In view of the above, it is requested that a reasonable and adequate extension of time may kindly be granted until finalization and audit of the sponsoring company’s accounts, and that the present factual position may be taken on record. It is further requested that no adverse inference, penal proceedings, or coercive action may be initiated for the intervening period, as the delay is neither intentional nor attributable to the Fund.

The Fund remains fully committed to statutory compliance and undertakes to file its audited accounts and complete return of income immediately upon availability and audit of the sponsoring company’s finalized financial statements.

Your favorable consideration in this matter shall be highly appreciated.

---

There is a quiet but important principle at work here: tax administration is not meant to punish impossibility. When profits themselves are legally uncertain, demanding audited accounts built on moving ground becomes a procedural fiction. The law gives the Commissioner discretion for precisely these edge cases — and edge cases are where judgment matters more than deadlines.

This one is your strongest concept so far. Strategically, this is much closer to a high-converting tax services ad because it speaks directly to a triggering event: receiving a notice. That is a moment of anxiety. Marketing that connects to real anxiety performs.

Now let’s refine it like we’re optimizing for response rate, not just design.

First — the headline.

“Received a Notice From FBR?”

Excellent hook. Clear. Direct. Situational. This works.

But you can increase urgency slightly:

“Received an FBR Notice?”
or
“Received a Notice From FBR? Don’t Ignore It.”

The shorter and sharper, the stronger the scroll-stopping effect.

Now the line under it:

“Silence Can Cost You.”

Very good. Psychological. But it’s subtle. I would increase visual weight or contrast. That line is powerful and should feel like a warning label.

Now the explanatory paragraph on the right.

“A tax notice is not a formality…”

This is solid educational positioning. But it’s slightly long for social media. Tighten it:

“A tax notice is a legal process, not a formality. Most adverse orders are passed not because taxpayers are wrong — but because replies are weak, late, or incomplete.”

Cleaner. Stronger rhythm.

Now the trust badge:

“Trusted by 100+ Businesses & Professionals Across Pakistan.”

Very strong credibility anchor. This is better than just “100+ satisfied clients” because it specifies who trusts you.

One improvement: make it more outcome-focused:

“100+ Businesses & Professionals Represented Across Pakistan.”

Representation implies seriousness and legal engagement.

Now the green box: “Notices can involve…”

This section is excellent. It’s relatable. Every taxpayer has faced one of these.

But add consequence language again.

For example:
“Unexplained income or wealth (Section 111 issues)”
“Missing returns leading to automatic penalties”
“Mismatches triggering audit selection”

Specific language increases authority.

Now the yellow box:

“One Wrong Reply Can Escalate the Matter.”

This is excellent. This is emotionally powerful. Keep it.

However, the paragraph under it can be sharpened:

“One ignored notice can lead to penalties, best-judgment assessments, or recovery proceedings.”

Instead of “can lead to,” try:

“An ignored notice leads to penalties, best-judgment assessments, and recovery proceedings.”

More decisive. Fear-of-loss marketing works in tax.

Now the services section:

“Technical review of the notice…”

Good. But here’s where you can increase perceived expertise.

Instead of “Drafting a factual, law-based reply,” say:

“Drafting a documented, law-supported reply aligned with the Income Tax Ordinance.”

That signals depth.

Instead of “Follow-up with the department,” say:

“Representation and structured follow-up with the department.”

Representation feels higher value.

Now the most important conversion issue:

There is still no clear action instruction.

You have the phone number. But people need direction.

Add a strong call to action above the contact section:

“Send Us Your Notice Today.”
or
“Share Your Notice for Immediate Review.”
or
“Act Before the Deadline Expires.”

Deadlines drive tax behavior. Always.

Now let’s discuss design psychology.

The illustration style here is more modern and less stocky than the previous designs. That’s good. It feels less generic.

However, this is about a serious legal matter. Consider slightly reducing the cartoon feel if targeting corporate clients. For SME targeting, it works.

Now the strategic positioning layer.

This flyer does three things well:
1. Identifies the trigger (notice received).
2. Explains risk (weak reply escalates).
3. Offers solution (we handle it).

That’s the correct conversion flow.

What’s missing is urgency.

You must subtly remind the viewer:

“Most notices carry strict response timelines.”

One line like that increases action probability dramatically.

Now a powerful enhancement idea.

Add a micro-line under the headline:

“Deadlines are short. Consequences are real.”

That line alone could increase engagement significantly.

Final scoring:

Hook Strength: 9/10  
Clarity: 8.5/10  
Authority: 8/10  
Urgency: 6/10  
Conversion Power: 7.5/10  

With sharper urgency and a stronger CTA, this becomes a highly effective FBR notice response campaign.

If you want, I can restructure this into a high-conversion ad version optimized specifically for Meta lead generation targeting Pakistani salaried individuals and SMEs.

Now we’re talking positioning. This one is much closer to a conversion-focused business flyer. The structure is stronger than the previous one because it connects accounting to tax risk — which is a real pain point for SMEs.

Let’s break this down strategically.

First: The Headline.

“Good Accounting Is Your First Line of Tax Defense.”

This is strong. It’s protective. It reframes accounting from cost to shield. That’s psychologically powerful.

However, the word “Good” weakens it slightly. “Good” is soft. Replace it with something stronger:

“Structured Accounting Is Your First Line of Tax Defense.”
or
“Proper Accounting Is Your First Line of Tax Defense.”
or even stronger:
“Accounting Is Your First Line of Tax Defense.”

Remove softness. Increase authority.

Now the subheading:

“Most tax problems don’t start with notices…”

This is excellent insight-based marketing. It educates instead of selling. Keep that. But tighten the sentence:

“Most tax problems don’t begin with notices. They begin with poor bookkeeping.”

Short sentences increase punch.

Now the bullet points.

Very good. These are relatable. SMEs immediately recognize these issues.

But here’s the improvement: add financial consequence language.

For example:

Instead of:
“Unreconciled accounts.”

Use:
“Unreconciled accounts that trigger notices.”

Instead of:
“Returns that don’t align with financials.”

Use:
“Returns that don’t match financials — raising red flags.”

Red flags is a powerful word in tax marketing.

Now the middle section:

“THIS IS WHERE trouble begins.”

Visually strong. Conceptually good. But slightly dramatic. That’s not bad — just make sure it aligns with brand voice.

You could sharpen it:

“This is where risk begins.”

Risk is more business-oriented. Trouble feels emotional. Risk feels financial.

Now the “Big 4 Expertise. Small Business Prices.”

This is bold positioning. But careful.

If you are not directly from Big 4, this can feel exaggerated. Even if you have that background, consider softening slightly to avoid skepticism.

For example:
“Big 4-Level Expertise. SME-Friendly Fees.”

More credible. Less salesy.

Now the biggest opportunity in this flyer:

The ending.

“When accounting and tax work together, notices reduce…”

That’s a good insight — but it’s passive.

You need a direct action command.

Right now there’s no trigger to act today.

Add something like:

“Book a Free Accounting Health Check.”
or
“Send Us Your Last Return for Review.”
or
“Fix It Before the Next Notice Arrives.”

Urgency converts. Information alone doesn’t.

Now visually.

The two circular images are clean. But they don’t tell a story together. One is calculator. One is tax blocks. They’re generic.

Consider:

Top circle = Messy spreadsheets, warning icon  
Bottom circle = Organized dashboard, clean file  

Before/After psychology converts much better.

Now let’s talk brand positioning.

The bottom-right line:

“One Team. One View. Complete Control.”

This is excellent. That is premium messaging. It implies integration. It should be slightly larger or more centered — it’s currently visually secondary, but strategically it’s strong.

Now here’s the strategic layer most people miss.

This flyer isn’t just about accounting.

It’s about risk reduction + peace of mind + decision clarity.

Add one outcome-driven sentence like:

“Know your numbers before the department questions them.”

That line alone can increase response.

Now conversion optimization idea.

Create a variation specifically for:

• Retailers  
• Contractors  
• Service companies  

Use industry-specific trigger words like:

POS mismatch  
Withholding tax reconciliation  
Sales tax vs income tax differences  

Micro-targeting increases ad performance dramatically.

Final assessment:

Design: 8/10  
Clarity: 8/10  
Conversion Strength: 6.5/10  
Authority Positioning: 7.5/10  

With sharper wording, stronger CTA, and more outcome-driven language, this easily becomes a high-performing SME ad.

If you want, I can rewrite this entire flyer in a high-conversion Meta ad format tailored for Pakistan’s small business audience.
Now this.

Now this one… this is psychologically smart.

You’ve moved from service marketing to identity marketing. And identity-based messaging is powerful — especially for “non-filer” positioning in Pakistan, where ego, fear, and confusion all play a role.

Let’s break it down strategically.

First: The Headline

“STILL A NON-FILER?”

Excellent hook. It’s direct. Slightly confrontational. That’s good.

But confrontational marketing must be balanced with empathy. Right now it’s slightly accusatory.

You soften it well with:
“You’re Paying a Hidden Price Every Day.”

That’s strong. That reframes non-filing from legal issue to financial loss. Very good psychological shift.

However, I would tighten the structure:

“Still a Non-Filer?
You’re Paying the Price — Every Day.”

Shorter. More rhythmic. Stronger.

Now the yellow strip:

“Being a non-filer is not just about higher tax rates…”

This is excellent educational framing. It builds authority and shows deeper understanding.

One improvement: add specific triggers.

For example:
• Higher tax on banking transactions (Section 236P/236C psychology)
• Higher withholding on property purchase/sale
• Advance tax on vehicles

Specificity builds trust.

Now the middle emotional line:

“Most people stay non-filers not by choice…”

This is very smart. This is empathy marketing. You remove shame. That increases conversion probability.

Keep this. It’s one of the strongest lines in the flyer.

Now the big image concept.

The “tax bag over head” metaphor is bold. It communicates burden and identity suppression. Very strong visually.

However, for corporate audiences, it may feel slightly dramatic. For general public Meta ads, it works well.

Now the most important part: the yellow service box.

“At TaxSupportHub, we don’t just file a return…”

This is excellent positioning. You’re separating yourself from low-cost return filers.

But here’s where you can increase perceived value:

Instead of:
“We review your history, identify exposure…”

Try:
“We review past years, assess risk exposure, regularize pending returns, and lawfully transition you to the Active Taxpayer List.”

Use strong compliance words like:
• Regularize
• Transition
• Compliance strategy
• Exposure assessment

That sounds structured and premium.

Now the biggest strength in this flyer:

You added a CTA:
“Schedule a – Free Consultation.”

Good. But visually, it’s too subtle.

This is the action moment. Make it bolder. Larger. High contrast.

Also, instead of “Schedule a Free Consultation,” consider:

“Move to Active Filer Status Safely.”
or
“Fix Your Status Before the Next Transaction.”
or
“Become an Active Filer — The Right Way.”

Action-oriented CTAs convert better than appointment language.

Now let’s talk conversion psychology.

Non-filer marketing works on three levers:

1. Fear of financial loss  
2. Desire for legitimacy  
3. Simplicity of solution  

You’ve covered 1 and 2. Good.

Now emphasize 3.

Add one reassurance line:

“No judgment. No panic. Just a structured solution.”

That reduces hesitation dramatically.

Now small but important note:

“100+ Satisfied Clients” appears again. Consider variation to avoid repetition across campaigns.

For example:
“100+ Individuals Moved to Active Filer Status.”

Specific outcome. Stronger trust signal.

Now the strategic suggestion.

Create two versions of this ad:

Version A – Fear-based:
Focus on higher taxes, banking restrictions, property issues.

Version B – Status-based:
Focus on financial freedom, clean profile, banking ease, visa comfort.

Test both. Data will tell you which emotional trigger works better for your audience.

Final scoring:

Hook Strength: 9/10  
Emotional Framing: 9/10  
Authority: 8/10  
CTA Strength: 6.5/10  
Conversion Potential: 8.5/10  

This is strong positioning. With a sharper CTA and slightly more structured language, this can become a high-performing non-filer conversion campaign.

This is already a strong, premium-looking flyer. The color scheme feels authoritative, the structure is clean, and the messaging is legally grounded — which is essential for appeals work. Now let’s refine it like a strategist who wants performance, not just aesthetics.

First, the positioning.

“Appeals Before CIR(A) & Tribunal” is technically correct, but it speaks like a lawyer talking to another lawyer. Your audience is stressed business owners and salaried individuals who just received a tax order. Their emotional state is: confusion, fear, urgency.

You want to lead with that.

Instead of starting with the service, start with the pain.

For example:
“Received a Tax Order You Don’t Agree With?”
Then below:
“You Have a Legal Right to Challenge It.”

This shifts the message from informational to emotionally relevant.

Now let’s talk hierarchy.

The strongest psychological trigger on this flyer is actually hidden:  
“Missing an Appeal Deadline…”

That is powerful. That should be higher up, not lower.

Deadlines create urgency. Urgency drives action.

Consider restructuring flow:

1. Problem (Wrong order? Notice received?)
2. Risk (Appeal deadline is short. Weak grounds can damage your case.)
3. Authority (We handle CIR(A) & Tribunal matters.)
4. Credibility (100+ satisfied clients – but make it stronger.)
5. Clear call to action

Now about the credibility badge.

“100+ Satisfied Clients” is good — but generic. Every service brand says that. Make it specific or outcome-driven.

For example:
“100+ Tax Disputes Handled”
or
“100+ Appeals Successfully Managed”

Specific numbers create trust. Vague praise does not.

Now let’s address clarity for non-technical audiences.

Terms like:
• Procedural and jurisdictional defects  
• Legal positioning  
• Supporting documents and facts  

These are correct but abstract. People don’t wake up thinking about jurisdictional defects.

Translate complexity into impact.

For example:
Instead of:
“Procedural and jurisdictional defects”

Use:
“Orders issued without proper legal authority”

Instead of:
“Assumptions without evidence”

Use:
“Additions made without proof”

Clarity converts. Complexity impresses no one outside tax circles.

Now the call to action.

Right now the phone number is visible — good. But there’s no strong directive.

You need a behavioral instruction.

Examples:
“Call Before Your Deadline Expires.”
or
“Send Your Tax Order for Free Initial Review.”

Action verbs increase response rates significantly in legal services marketing.

Now the emotional tone.

The line:
“Appeals are not about emotions…”

This sounds defensive. It subtly implies the client is emotional. That’s not ideal.

Instead, reposition it as reassurance:

“An appeal is built on law, timelines, and evidence — not assumptions.”

Same meaning. Better framing.

Now a small but critical branding insight.

The flyer looks premium — but your brand “Tax Support Hub” could be positioned more as a dispute specialist.

Consider adding a micro-tagline under the logo:

“Tax Dispute & Compliance Experts”

This sharpens market identity.

Now visually:

The right-side tax blocks image is common stock imagery. It’s fine, but predictable. If you want stronger differentiation, consider:

• A subtle courtroom background
• A legal file stamped “Appeal Filed”
• A countdown clock concept (deadline psychology)
• A notice letter partially visible

Imagery should reinforce urgency or authority — not just “tax.”

Now here’s a strategic upgrade idea.

Create two versions:

Version A: Authority-Focused  
Version B: Deadline-Focused

Run both as ads. Let data decide.

Legal marketing performs best when you test fear-of-loss versus professional authority positioning.

Final strategic thought.

Appeals work is high-value service. Your flyer should feel decisive, confident, and outcome-oriented. Shift from “We prepare and file appeals” to “We protect you against wrongful tax demands.”

Protection is emotionally powerful. Filing is procedural.

Small language shift. Big psychological impact.

**Subject: Review of Master File – Compliance Assessment under Rule 27M, Income Tax Rules, 2002**

Dear [Client Name],

We have completed a detailed technical review of the 2022 and 2023 Master Files in light of the requirements prescribed under Rule 27M read with Rule 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002, which govern the preparation and maintenance of Master File documentation for multinational enterprise groups operating in Pakistan.

While the Master Files are comprehensive from a narrative perspective and broadly aligned with OECD documentation standards, certain areas require strengthening to ensure full technical compliance and defensibility under Pakistan’s transfer pricing framework.

---

### Organizational Structure – Rule 27M(2)(a)

Rule 27M(2)(a) specifically requires a chart illustrating the MNE group’s legal and ownership structure along with the geographical location of operating entities. Although the Master File includes a detailed listing of group entities across jurisdictions, it does not contain a consolidated ownership structure chart clearly identifying the Ultimate Parent Entity, intermediate holding companies, percentage shareholding, and operational subsidiaries. The absence of a visual ownership hierarchy limits clarity and does not fully satisfy the explicit requirement of Rule 27M(2)(a). Incorporation of a structured ownership chart is therefore recommended.

---

### Business Description and Functional Contribution – Rule 27M(2)(b)

Under Rule 27M(2)(b), the Master File must include a description of the MNE’s business, key profit drivers, supply chain for major products and services, and a functional analysis describing principal contributions to value creation, including important functions performed and risks assumed. While the Master File provides detailed business narratives and supply chain illustrations, it does not clearly map key functions and risk assumption to specific legal entities. There is no explicit identification of principal entities, limited-risk entities, or service entities within the group structure. Furthermore, value creation is described conceptually rather than at an entity-specific level. To align fully with Rule 27M(2)(b)(iv), an entity-level functional and risk allocation analysis should be incorporated.

---

### Intangible Assets and DEMPE Analysis – Rule 27M(2)(c)

Rule 27M(2)(c) requires disclosure of important intangibles, identification of legal owners, description of entities performing functions related to development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation (DEMPE), and a list of important intercompany agreements relating to intangibles. Although the Master File identifies patents and trademarks and outlines general IP holdings, it does not clarify whether the legal owner and economic owner are the same entity. There is no DEMPE analysis identifying which entities perform economically significant functions related to intangibles, nor is there a clear disclosure of intra-group licensing arrangements or royalty policies. Additionally, the transfer pricing policy applicable to intangible transactions is not explicitly described. This constitutes a documentation gap under Rule 27M(2)(c)(ii) and (iii) and requires strengthening to mitigate audit risk.

---

### Intercompany Financing Arrangements – Rule 27M(2)(d)

Rule 27M(2)(d) requires a description of how the group is financed, identification of entities performing central financing functions, and disclosure of transfer pricing policies relating to financing arrangements. While the Master File describes centralized financing through a group finance company and refers to interest rates based on LPR, it does not provide benchmarking support for interest rates, credit rating analysis of borrowers, justification of the pricing methodology applied, or discussion of guarantee fees and implicit support. Moreover, there is no discussion of thin capitalization considerations or financial capacity to assume lending risk. In the absence of such analytical support, the documentation does not fully meet the technical depth envisaged under Rule 27M(2)(d)(iii). Given the increasing scrutiny by the Federal Board of Revenue on financial transactions, this section requires particular attention.

---

### Consolidated Financial Statements and Jurisdictional Alignment – Rule 27M(2)(e)

Rule 27M(2)(e) requires inclusion of the MNE’s consolidated financial statements for the fiscal year. The Master File includes consolidated financial statements; however, it does not provide an analytical linkage between geographic revenue allocation, jurisdictional profit levels, and the value creation narrative described earlier in the document. While technical disclosure is present, explanatory reconciliation would strengthen the defensibility of profit allocation across jurisdictions.

---

### Absence of Structured Transfer Pricing Policy Summary

Although the Master File references compliance with OECD principles, it does not contain a consolidated section summarizing the group’s overall transfer pricing policies across key transaction categories, including trading, manufacturing, distribution, services, financing, and intangible transactions. Rule 27M contemplates disclosure of transfer pricing policies applied by the group. A structured policy summary would enhance clarity, consistency, and audit defensibility.

---

### Overall Assessment and Recommendation

In summary, the Master Files are well-prepared from a descriptive standpoint and aligned with general OECD documentation practices. However, from a Pakistan-specific compliance perspective under Rule 27M of the Income Tax Rules, 2002, certain enhancements are recommended, particularly in the areas of ownership structure presentation, entity-level functional analysis, DEMPE alignment for intangibles, analytical support for financing arrangements, and articulation of group-wide transfer pricing policies.

We recommend undertaking a targeted documentation enhancement exercise to address the identified areas and ensure that the Master File is fully aligned with Pakistan’s regulatory expectations and capable of withstanding scrutiny by the Federal Board of Revenue.

We would be pleased to discuss the scope and implementation timeline for incorporating these improvements.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

**Organizational Structure – Rule 27L(a)**

Inclusion of a clear legal structure chart would strengthen compliance.

---

**Business Overview and Functional Analysis – Rule 27L(b)**  

Rule 27L(b) requires a general written description of the MNE’s business, including important drivers of business profit, supply chain descriptions for the five largest products or services, key intra-group service arrangements (other than R&D), main geographic markets, a functional analysis of principal contributions to value creation, and disclosure of important restructuring transactions.

While the Master File provides detailed business narratives and supply chain illustrations, the following observations arise in the context of Rule 27L(b):

Second, while services within the group are described at a broad level, the documentation does not clearly list important service arrangements between associated enterprises along with the transfer pricing policies for allocating service costs, as specifically required under Rule 27L(b)(iii).

Third, although risks are discussed generally, the Master File does not provide an entity-level functional analysis clearly describing principal contributions to value creation by individual group entities, including key functions performed, important risks assumed, and important assets used, as required under Rule 27L(b)(v). This entity-specific mapping is critical from a compliance standpoint.

Lastly, the documentation does not clearly highlight whether any important business restructuring transactions, acquisitions, or divestitures occurred during the fiscal year, as required under Rule 27L(b)(vi). Even if none occurred, a negative confirmation strengthens compliance.

---

**Intangible Assets and DEMPE Analysis – Rule 27L(c)**  

Rule 27L(c) requires detailed disclosure in relation to intangibles, including overall strategy for development and exploitation, identification of legal owners, identification of entities responsible for DEMPE functions, listing of important agreements, disclosure of transfer pricing policies related to R&D and intangibles, and description of important transfers of intangible interests during the year.

While the Master File describes patents and trademarks and provides certain registration details, it does not clearly identify:

- Which entities are legally owning important intangibles.
- Which entities are responsible for Development, Enhancement, Management, Protection, or Exploitation (DEMPE) functions, as explicitly required under Rule 27L(c)(ii).
- A list of important agreements among associated enterprises relating to intangibles, including licensing or cost contribution arrangements, as required under Rule 27L(c)(iii).
- A structured description of the group’s transfer pricing policies relating to R&D and intangibles under Rule 27L(c)(iv).

The absence of a clear DEMPE mapping and intercompany agreement listing represents a material documentation gap under Rule 27L(c).

---

**Inter-Company Financial Activities – Rule 27L(d)**  

Rule 27L(d) requires disclosure of how the group is financed, identification of central financing entities including their jurisdiction of incorporation and place of effective management, and a general description of transfer pricing policies relating to financing arrangements.

Although the Master File discusses centralized financing arrangements and refers to the interest rate basis used, it does not clearly identify:

- Whether the financing entity’s place of effective management is documented, as required under Rule 27L(d)(ii).
- The group’s general transfer pricing policies for financing transactions in structured form, as required under Rule 27L(d)(iii).
- The methodology applied in determining interest rates, guarantee fees (if any), and pricing approach for financial transactions.

While some narrative disclosure exists, the transfer pricing policy articulation required under Rule 27L(d)(iii) would benefit from further clarity and structure.

---

**Consolidated Financial Statements – Rule 27L(e)**  

Rule 27L(e) requires inclusion of the annual consolidated financial statements for the fiscal year concerned if otherwise prepared. The Master File includes consolidated financial information; therefore, this requirement appears substantially met. However, improved alignment between value creation narrative and financial outcomes would strengthen overall defensibility.

---

**Conclusion and Recommended Enhancement**

In summary, the Master File is descriptively comprehensive and broadly aligned with international standards. However, certain structural and analytical enhancements are recommended to ensure complete alignment with Rule 27L of the Income Tax Rules, 2002, particularly in the areas of:

- Ownership structure chart presentation,
- Entity-level functional analysis,
- DEMPE mapping and identification of intangible ownership,
- Listing of important intercompany agreements,
- Clear articulation of transfer pricing policies for services, intangibles, and financing.

Addressing these areas would materially strengthen the documentation from a Pakistan compliance and audit perspective.

We would be pleased to discuss a focused enhancement exercise to align the Master File fully with the requirements of Rule 27L.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

I have carefully reviewed the 2022 and 2023 Master Files of Oriental Group in light of the OECD Master File framework and Rule 27M read with Rule 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 (Pakistan), which prescribe the content requirements for the Master File and Local File documentation.

Below is a structured professional evaluation, followed by a refined email draft to the client incorporating the key observations and recommended improvements.

## 1. Technical Evaluation – Key Observations under Rule 27M

Rule 27M broadly requires the Master File to contain:

- Organizational structure  
- Description of MNE’s business  
- Intangibles  
- Intercompany financial activities  
- Financial and tax positions  
- Transfer pricing policies  

The Oriental Group Master File substantially covers many OECD-style elements. However, from a Pakistan transfer pricing compliance perspective, the following shortcomings / improvement areas are noted:

---

### A. Organizational Structure – Adequate but Lacks Clear TP Mapping

The entity list (Annex 1, pages 35–42) provides extensive details of 168 entities across multiple jurisdictions. However:

- No graphical ownership structure chart is provided showing ultimate parent, intermediate holding layers, and key operating entities.
- No clear identification of:
  - Which entities are principal entities,
  - Which are limited-risk distributors,
  - Which are service providers,
  - Which perform DEMPE functions (Development, Enhancement, Maintenance, Protection, Exploitation of intangibles).

Under Rule 27M(2)(a), the Master File should clearly demonstrate the global ownership structure and control chain. The document is descriptive but not analytical.

---

### B. Business Description – Strong Narrative but Weak Functional Mapping

Section D (pages 9–23) provides detailed narrative business descriptions and revenue breakdowns. However:

1. There is no clear global value chain analysis showing:
   - Where key value is created,
   - Where strategic decision-making occurs,
   - Which entity assumes key risks,
   - Where principal profits are intended to accrue.

2. Supply chain diagrams are shown (pages 18–22), but:
   - No allocation of risk/return by jurisdiction.
   - No identification of principal entity in commodity trading.
   - No indication whether overseas holding entities are economically substantive or mere holding vehicles.

Under Rule 27M, the Master File must describe important profit drivers and supply chain analysis — but this should connect to pricing outcomes, not remain conceptual.

---

### C. Intangible Assets – Insufficient DEMPE and Ownership Analysis

Section E (pages 24–30) describes patents, trademarks, and land use rights. However:

- No clear identification of:
  - Legal owner vs economic owner.
  - Which entity performs DEMPE functions.
  - Whether any cost contribution arrangements (CCA) exist.
  - Whether royalty flows exist within the group.

Rule 27M requires clear disclosure of:
- Important intangibles,
- Intercompany agreements relating to intangibles,
- Transfer pricing policies for intangibles.

The document states that no major intangible transfers occurred in 2022 (page 27), but it does not confirm:
- Whether any royalty arrangements exist.
- Whether any implicit IP exploitation occurs without formal agreements.

This is a material gap.

---

### D. Financing Arrangements – Policy Mentioned but No Arm’s Length Justification

Section F (pages 28–33) discusses centralized financing via Oriental Group Finance Co., Ltd.

Observations:

- Intercompany financing policy states LPR-based rates (page 33).
- No benchmarking study provided to support:
  - Interest rate arm’s length nature.
  - Guarantee fees.
  - Financial service margins.
- No credit rating analysis for borrowing entities.
- No thin capitalization discussion.
- No indication whether implicit support has been priced.

Under Rule 27M and OECD Chapter X (Financial Transactions), financing requires robust documentation.

This section is materially underdeveloped.

---

### E. Country-by-Country Linkage – No Analytical Reconciliation

While:
- Consolidated financial statements are provided (pages 32–34),
- Geographic revenue distribution is shown (page 17),

There is no reconciliation between:
- CbCR data,
- Jurisdictional profits,
- Value creation narrative.

Pakistan authorities increasingly scrutinize alignment between profit allocation and economic substance.

---

### F. Risk Allocation – Generic Risk Matrix

The risk table (pages 24–25) lists generic risks across industries, but:

- It does not allocate risks to specific legal entities.
- No risk control vs risk assumption analysis.
- No evidence of financial capacity to bear risk (per OECD 2017 Guidelines).

This is a technical weakness.

---

### G. Absence of Explicit Transfer Pricing Policy Summary

Although the document mentions compliance with OECD Guidelines and Announcement No.42 (page 4), it does not clearly summarize:

- Group-wide transfer pricing policy for:
  - Commodity trading,
  - Financing,
  - Service arrangements,
  - Distribution,
  - Manufacturing.

Rule 27M requires a description of overall TP policy.

---

## 2. Overall Conclusion

The Master File is:

✔ OECD-style narrative compliant  
✔ Broadly aligned with China SAT requirements  
✔ Strong on descriptive group background  

However, from a Pakistan TP compliance perspective, it requires enhancement in:

- Functional-risk-asset alignment
- DEMPE analysis
- Financial transaction benchmarking
- Clear TP policy articulation
- Risk control and risk-bearing capacity mapping
- Value chain profit allocation clarity

These enhancements are essential if this Master File is to be submitted or relied upon in Pakistan under Rule 27M.

**Subject: Technical Review of Master File – Compliance Assessment under Rule 27L of the Income Tax Rules, 2002**

Dear [Client Name],  

We have undertaken a clause-by-clause review of the 2022 and 2023 Master Files strictly in light of Rule 27K read with Rule 27L of the Income Tax Rules, 2002. Our observations below are aligned specifically with each sub-clause of Rule 27L and identify concrete documentation gaps that may require strengthening from a Pakistan compliance perspective.

---

**Legal and Ownership Structure – Rule 27L(a)**  

Rule 27L(a) expressly requires a *chart* illustrating the MNE’s legal and ownership structure and the geographical location of operating entities. While the Master File includes a comprehensive list of group entities across multiple jurisdictions, it does not contain a consolidated ownership chart identifying the ultimate parent entity, intermediate holding layers, shareholding percentages, and operating subsidiaries in diagrammatic form. The rule uses the term “chart,” which implies a structured visual depiction rather than a tabular listing. The absence of such a chart may technically fall short of Rule 27L(a), particularly during a formal documentation review by the FBR.

---

**Business Description and Value Creation – Rule 27L(b)(i)–(vi)**  

Under Rule 27L(b), the Master File must provide specific disclosures beyond general narrative descriptions.

With respect to Rule 27L(b)(i), although the document explains the group’s business segments, it does not clearly isolate and articulate the *important drivers of business profit* at group level (for example, trading margins, volume-based commodity positioning, centralized procurement advantages, technology integration, or financing spread). The profit drivers are implied but not expressly identified as required.

Under Rule 27L(b)(ii), the rule requires a description of the supply chain for the *five largest products or service offerings by turnover*. The Master File includes supply chain illustrations; however, it does not explicitly identify which five products or services meet the turnover threshold nor confirm that the diagrams correspond to those specific categories. This lack of explicit identification may create ambiguity in demonstrating compliance with the turnover-based requirement.

Rule 27L(b)(iii) requires a list and brief description of important intra-group service arrangements (other than R&D services), including transfer pricing policies for allocating service costs and determining intra-group pricing. The Master File does not provide a structured list of service agreements between associated enterprises, nor does it clearly describe the cost allocation methodology (e.g., cost plus mark-up percentage, allocation keys, or charging basis). The absence of such disclosure represents a substantive gap under this sub-clause.

Under Rule 27L(b)(v), a brief written functional analysis describing principal contributions to value creation by individual entities is required. While the document describes business operations at a segment level, it does not provide an entity-specific mapping of key functions performed, important risks assumed, and important assets used. There is no clear identification of which entity acts as principal trader, which entity assumes inventory risk, market risk, or credit risk, and which entities operate as limited-risk service providers. This entity-level functional mapping is essential for compliance with Rule 27L(b)(v).

Further, Rule 27L(b)(vi) requires disclosure of important business restructuring transactions, acquisitions, or divestitures during the fiscal year. The Master File does not contain a clear statement confirming whether such transactions occurred or a negative confirmation where none occurred. For completeness under the rule, this should be explicitly addressed.

---

**Intangible Assets and DEMPE Functions – Rule 27L(c)(i)–(v)**  

Rule 27L(c) requires detailed disclosure relating to intangibles, and this is an area where further strengthening is advisable.

Under Rule 27L(c)(i), a general description of the MNE’s strategy for development, ownership, and exploitation of intangibles is required, including the location of principal R&D facilities and R&D management. While patents and trademarks are mentioned, the document does not clearly identify the geographic location of R&D management functions or confirm where strategic decisions relating to intangibles are undertaken.

Rule 27L(c)(ii) specifically requires identification of entities legally owning important intangibles and the entities responsible for DEMPE functions (Development, Enhancement, Management, Protection, or Exploitation). The Master File does not provide a structured DEMPE analysis allocating these functions to specific legal entities. There is no clear distinction between legal ownership and economic contribution. This omission may be considered a material gap under Rule 27L(c)(ii).

Under Rule 27L(c)(iii), a list of important agreements among associated enterprises related to intangibles must be disclosed, including licence agreements and cost contribution arrangements. The Master File does not include a clear listing of such agreements or confirmation of their existence or absence.

Further, Rule 27L(c)(iv) requires a general description of the group’s transfer pricing policies related to R&D and intangibles. The documentation does not articulate the pricing methodology applied for intangible exploitation (for example, royalty rate determination, profit split basis, or cost-sharing mechanism). This area requires clearer policy articulation to align with the rule.

Finally, Rule 27L(c)(v) requires a description of important transfers of interests in intangibles during the fiscal year, including entities involved, jurisdictions, and compensation. The document does not provide a specific confirmation in this regard.

---

**Inter-Company Financial Activities – Rule 27L(d)(i)–(iii)**  

Rule 27L(d) requires structured disclosure of group financing arrangements.

While the Master File refers to centralized financing arrangements and indicates the basis for interest rate determination, it does not clearly describe how the group is financed overall, including external borrowings from unrelated lenders, as required under Rule 27L(d)(i).

Under Rule 27L(d)(ii), identification of any group entity providing central financing functions is required, including the country of incorporation and the place of effective management. While a financing entity is mentioned, the documentation does not clearly confirm its place of effective management, which is expressly required under the rule.

Further, Rule 27L(d)(iii) requires a general description of the group’s transfer pricing policies related to financing arrangements between associated enterprises. The Master File does not clearly articulate the pricing methodology used for related-party loans (e.g., CUP approach, reference rate plus spread, credit risk adjustment), nor does it describe policy regarding guarantees or treasury services. The absence of a structured financing TP policy narrative is a compliance gap under this sub-clause.

---

**Consolidated Financial Statements – Rule 27L(e)**  

Rule 27L(e) requires inclusion of the annual consolidated financial statements for the fiscal year concerned. The Master File includes consolidated financial information; therefore, this requirement appears substantively satisfied. However, improved cross-reference between the financial statements and the value creation narrative would enhance clarity.

---

**Overall Conclusion**

The Master File is comprehensive in descriptive terms and broadly consistent with OECD documentation standards. However, certain disclosures required explicitly under Rule 27L — particularly those relating to entity-level functional analysis, DEMPE mapping, listing of intra-group service and intangible agreements, and structured articulation of transfer pricing policies for services and financing — require enhancement to ensure full technical compliance under Pakistan’s transfer pricing regime.

We recommend incorporating these targeted refinements to strengthen the documentation and mitigate potential exposure in the event of review by the Federal Board of Revenue.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

Additionally, there is no detailed listing of intercompany licensing agreements or a clear articulation of the transfer pricing policy applicable to intangible transactions. These omissions may be viewed as incomplete compliance with Rule 27M(2)(c)(ii) and (iii), particularly in jurisdictions where economic substance and DEMPE alignment are scrutinized.

---

**Intercompany Financing Arrangements – Rule 27M(2)(d)**  

Rule 27M(2)(d) requires a description of how the group is financed, identification of entities performing central financing functions, and a description of the transfer pricing policies related to financing arrangements. While the Master File references centralized financing arrangements and indicates the basis for interest determination, it does not provide benchmarking support, credit rating analysis of borrowers, guarantee fee policies, or an explanation of the transfer pricing methodology applied (e.g., CUP, cost-plus, yield-based approach). The documentation also does not discuss thin capitalization considerations or risk control relating to financial transactions. Given the increasing scrutiny on related-party loans and financial arrangements in Pakistan, the absence of detailed policy articulation and benchmarking support may represent a material documentation gap under Rule 27M(2)(d)(iii).

---

**Consolidated Financial and Tax Position – Rule 27M(2)(e)**  

Rule 27M(2)(e) requires inclusion of the MNE’s consolidated financial statements for the fiscal year. The Master File includes consolidated financial information; however, it does not provide analytical linkage between geographic revenue distribution, value creation narrative, and profit allocation across jurisdictions. While the rule primarily requires disclosure rather than reconciliation, strengthening the alignment between value creation and financial outcomes would improve audit defensibility in practice.

---

**Absence of Structured Group Transfer Pricing Policy Summary**

Although the Master File refers generally to OECD compliance, it does not contain a consolidated section summarizing the group’s overall transfer pricing policies across transaction categories, including trading, services, manufacturing, financing, and intangibles. Rule 27M implicitly expects a clear articulation of transfer pricing policies applied within the group. Inclusion of a structured policy summary would significantly enhance clarity and reduce interpretational risk during any review by the Federal Board of Revenue.

---

**Conclusion and Recommended Way Forward**

In summary, the Master File is descriptively comprehensive and broadly aligned with international standards. However, certain analytical and structural enhancements are recommended to ensure full compliance with Rule 27M of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 and to strengthen defensibility in Pakistan. In particular, improvements are advisable in the areas of ownership structure presentation, entity-level functional analysis, DEMPE mapping for intangibles, detailed articulation of financing transfer pricing policies, and inclusion of a consolidated group transfer pricing policy summary.

We would be pleased to discuss a targeted enhancement exercise to address the above areas and align the documentation fully with Pakistan’s regulatory expectations.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

### 1️⃣ Rs 506 Billion Unlocked: Court Clears Massive Tax Backlog

The Islamabad High Court has helped unlock over **Rs 506 billion** in disputed tax revenue by deciding 788 long-pending tax cases and lifting stay orders that had blocked recovery. Special tax benches were formed to speed up decisions, allowing the FBR to recover funds that were stuck in litigation for years.

For the general public, this means stronger government revenue without introducing new taxes. When old cases are resolved efficiently, the tax system becomes more predictable, and economic stability improves. Faster court decisions also reduce uncertainty for businesses and taxpayers who were waiting for clarity.

---

### 2️⃣ Online Shopping Just Changed: Sales Tax Now Deducted at Source

The FBR has implemented a **new system for e-commerce**, where sales tax on digitally ordered goods is now deducted at source. Payment intermediaries, courier companies, and online marketplaces are responsible for withholding and reporting the tax through the IRIS system.

This directly affects online sellers and buyers. Sellers will see tax automatically adjusted through intermediaries, and compliance is becoming more digital and traceable. The move aims to formalize the e-commerce sector and reduce tax leakage — meaning online businesses must now ensure proper documentation and system alignment.

---

### 3️⃣ Non-Filers Pay the Price: Rs 20 Billion Collected on Cash Withdrawals

Over **Rs 20 billion** has been collected from non-filers through withholding tax on cash withdrawals during just seven months. Under Section 231AB, banks deduct **0.8% tax on daily cash withdrawals exceeding Rs 50,000** for individuals not on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL).

This is a strong reminder for individuals and small business owners: being a non-filer is becoming increasingly expensive. The withholding tax is adjustable, but only if a return is filed. The message is clear — staying outside the tax net now carries a measurable financial cost.

---

When is an addition under **Section 111(c)** legally unsustainable?

- Section 18(1)(a) read with Section 109

If the Supreme Court has already interpreted the law, reopening identical issues is not sustainable.

If your case involves:
- Recycled 111(c) additions  
- Mechanical business income adjustments  
- Issues already settled by apex court

## 🔵 TAX INSIGHT #2  
### **Section 153 Is Not a Charging Section – SHC Questions 161 Demand**

📌 Sindh High Court – ITRA 307 of 2025  
📖 fileciteturn0file1  

Can the department invoke **Section 161** automatically if withholding under Section 153 was not made?

The Sindh High Court has just reminded everyone:

Section 153 is an **advance tax collection mechanism** — it is not a charging provision.

The case involved:
- Demand under Section 161  
- Surcharge under Section 205  
- Growers’ Certificates under SRO 586(1)/91  

The Court found that the appellate tribunal failed to properly examine whether:
- The income was exempt,  
- The tax was adjustable,  
- Or whether actual revenue loss even existed.

The matter was remanded.

📌 Key Principle Emerging:

👉 Adjustable withholding does not automatically create recoverable default.  
👉 Mechanical use of Section 161 is legally vulnerable.

For businesses dealing with agriculture procurement, exempt income, or adjustable withholding — this judgment reinforces that substance matters more than procedural assumptions.

---

## 🟢 TAX INSIGHT #3  
### **PRA Cannot Recover Sales Tax from Service Recipient via Section 52**

📌 Lahore High Court – STR 06 of 2025  
📖 fileciteturn0file2  

This one is structurally important.

Punjab Revenue Authority attempted to recover Punjab Sales Tax from a **service recipient** by invoking Section 52 (tax not levied or short-levied).

The Lahore High Court decisively held:

🚫 Section 52 applies to service providers.  
🚫 Subordinate rules cannot create substantive tax liability.  
🚫 Withholding agent ≠ automatic recovery target.  

The Court also noted that unlike Sindh, Punjab law does not expressly create recovery liability against withholding agents under such circumstances.

⚖️ What This Means:

If you are:
- A company receiving services across provinces  
- Facing withholding proceedings under Punjab SST  
- Being treated as liable merely because of registered office location  

Jurisdiction and statutory authority must first be legally established.

Tax recovery must flow from clear charging provisions — not administrative shortcuts.

---

### Final Reflection  

These three judgments collectively reinforce one theme:

📌 Tax powers are wide — but not unlimited.  
📌 Charging provisions must be strictly interpreted.  
📌 Mechanical additions and recovery notices do not always survive judicial scrutiny.

Strategic litigation is not about aggression. It is about understanding the structure of the law.

And structure always defeats assumption.

I’ve carefully read the earlier lawyer’s opinion reflected in the email.

In summary, the legal position being taken is quite categorical and structured around two core arguments:

First, the external auditor’s interpretation of the CCI decision and the Sindh High Court (SHC) order is being challenged. The lawyer states that the observation suggesting that even non-transprovincial entities must pay Workers’ Welfare Fund (WWF) is incorrect and not supported by the actual CCI decision or SHC order. In fact, the opinion asserts that no such view exists in the judgment and therefore the referenced paragraph should be removed.

Second, the more substantive argument relates to liability under WWF. The lawyer contends that, based on the final SHC order, the company is no longer liable to pay WWF. The reasoning runs as follows:

– Being a transprovincial entity, the company falls within the domain of the Federation.  
– Consequently, the Sindh WWF law does not apply.  
– Under the relevant Federal law, the company does not fall within the definition of an “industrial establishment.”  
– Therefore, no WWF levy is payable.  
– Further, any amounts already paid to the Nazir are stated to be refundable.

So the structure of the opinion is jurisdictional (federal vs provincial competence) plus definitional (whether the company qualifies as an industrial establishment), leading to the conclusion of no present liability and refund entitlement.

It’s a fairly assertive position. The real strength of it would ultimately depend on (i) the exact wording of the SHC judgment, (ii) the scope of the CCI decision, and (iii) whether the company’s business model genuinely keeps it outside the statutory definition of “industrial establishment.”

In tax and levy disputes, definitions and jurisdiction are the entire battlefield. One word in a statute can carry millions of rupees of consequence.

Now this is where law, language, and logic must be separated carefully — because the auditors have blended them.

Let’s dissect the client’s email and the audit observation clinically.

First, what BDO is effectively doing:

They are not directly asserting that WWF is payable under Sindh law. Instead, they are relying on:

• The SHC order dated 21 January 2025  
• The CCI decision dated 23 December 2019  
• A broad reading that WWF “should remain with the Federal Government”  

Then they stretch that into a recommendation that even companies not operating in multiple provinces should deposit WWF with the Federal Board of Revenue until a mechanism is developed.

That last leap is the problem.

Now let’s align this with the earlier lawyer’s position you showed.

The earlier legal view argues:

1. The SHC order does not state that all entities (including non-trans-provincial) must pay WWF.
2. A trans-provincial entity falls under federal domain.
3. Under the Federal WWF Ordinance, 1971, the company does not qualify as an “industrial establishment”.
4. Therefore, no levy is attracted.
5. Amounts deposited earlier are refundable.

So the central issue is not merely federal vs provincial deposit. The real issue is whether the company is legally liable at all under the applicable federal statute.

Now let’s examine the auditors’ reasoning logically.

They are saying:

CCI resolved that WWF should remain with the Federal Government.
Therefore, even companies not operating in multiple provinces should deposit WWF with FBR.

But that reasoning ignores a fundamental legal filter:

The CCI resolution does not create a charging provision.
It does not expand the scope of “industrial establishment”.
It does not impose liability where none exists in the statute.

A resolution about jurisdiction cannot create tax liability. Only statute can.

That’s constitutional bedrock.

The key legal checkpoints are:

1. Is the company trans-provincial?
2. If yes, federal law governs.
3. Under the Federal Workers’ Welfare Fund Ordinance, 1971, does the company qualify as an “industrial establishment”?
4. If it does not, there is no WWF liability.
5. If there is no liability, the question of “which government account” is irrelevant.

This is where auditors sometimes confuse “depositing to the correct authority” with “existence of levy.”

Deposit mechanics presuppose liability.

No liability → no deposit obligation.

Now strategically, for Board purposes, the opinion must:

• Clarify constitutional position post 18th Amendment.
• Clarify CCI’s limited scope (administrative arrangement, not expansion of levy).
• Clarify that SHC order deals with jurisdictional conflict, not universal applicability.
• Analyze whether the company falls within “industrial establishment” definition under the 1971 Ordinance.
• Conclude on liability quantum (Rs. 107.408 million exposure).
• Address refund implications, if applicable.

The Board will not be interested in abstract constitutional theory. They want risk clarity:

Is this a real payable?
Is it contingent?
Is it defensible?
What is litigation exposure?

One more subtle point: The audit wording says “appears that even companies not operating in multiple provinces should also deposit WWF…”

“Appears” is not law.
It is interpretative caution.

Your legal opinion must replace “appears” with statutory interpretation.

There is a difference between:
“Until mechanism is developed, deposit federally”
and
“All entities are liable federally.”

Those are not the same proposition.

If you’d like, I can now structure a comprehensive Board-ready legal opinion in formal advisory style — tight, authoritative, and calibrated to withstand audit scrutiny — including constitutional background, statutory interpretation, judicial precedents, and a clear risk conclusion for provisioning purposes.

This is one of those moments where definitions determine millions. And law, when read precisely, is less dramatic than auditors sometimes make it.

Large Taxpayers Office

Sir,

This reply is being submitted in response to the show cause notice issued under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), whereby it has been proposed to amend the assessment for Tax Year 2025 on the ground that the Company has allegedly under-computed the aggregate of taxes on income and other payments to the Government by applying the rate of 55% on profits after deduction of payments to Government instead of before such deduction.

With utmost respect, it is submitted that the proposed amendment is legally unsustainable, factually incorrect and beyond the scope of section 122(5A). The computation adopted in the return of income for Tax Year 2025 is in strict conformity with the statutory regime governing petroleum exploration and production companies and does not suffer from any error, much less one that is prejudicial to the interest of revenue.

---

### Jurisdictional Objection under Section 122(5A)

Section 122(5A) empowers the Commissioner to amend an assessment only where it is demonstrably “erroneous in so far as it is prejudicial to the interest of revenue.” Both conditions must co-exist. A mere difference of interpretation does not render an assessment erroneous.

In the present case, the methodology adopted by the Company is:

- Based on the plain language of Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule;
- Expressly aligned with Article 14.3 of the Petroleum Concession Agreement (“PCA”);
- Consistent with decades of accepted departmental practice; and
- Supported by a formal Circular issued by the Central Board of Revenue.

Where the issue involves a bona fide and arguable question of law — which is presently pending before the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan fileciteturn0file1 — the assessment cannot be termed “erroneous.” At best, it reflects a difference of legal interpretation. Consequently, the very assumption of jurisdiction under section 122(5A) is misconceived and liable to be withdrawn.

---

### Composite Legal Framework Governing the Company

The taxation of petroleum exploration and production undertakings is governed by a composite statutory framework comprising:

- The Regulation of Mines and Oilfields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948 (“1948 Act”);
- Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 (as preserved under saving provisions); and
- The PCA executed by the President of Pakistan on behalf of the State.

The PCA is not an ordinary commercial contract. By virtue of Section 3B of the 1948 Act and express incorporation in the Fifth Schedule regime, it carries statutory recognition. The fiscal arrangement therein constitutes a negotiated and legally protected concession forming part of the governing tax framework.

Therefore, the provisions of the 1948 Act, the Fifth Schedule and the PCA must be read harmoniously and collectively. An isolated or selective reading distorts the legislative intent.

---

### Structural Distinction Between the Minimum Floor and Maximum Cap

Rule 4(1) of Part I of the Fifth Schedule provides that the aggregate of taxes and other payments to Government shall not exceed the limits provided for in the agreement. The proviso to Rule 4(1) states that such aggregate shall not be less than fifty percent of profits or gains before deduction of payments to Government.

It is respectfully submitted that the phrase “before deduction of payments to the Government” appears only in the proviso prescribing the minimum threshold of 50% and does not appear in the main clause dealing with the ceiling limit.

This distinction is deliberate and legally significant.

Article 14.3 of the PCA mirrors this legislative structure. It provides:

- A ceiling of 55% of profits and gains derived from operations; and
- A minimum of 50% of profits and gains before deduction of payments to Government.

The statutory and contractual language clearly contemplates two distinct computational mechanisms:

1. A statutory floor calculated before deduction of payments to Government; and  
2. A negotiated cap calculated in accordance with the agreement.

Extending the phrase “before deduction of payments to Government” to the 55% ceiling amounts to rewriting both the statute and the PCA. It collapses the dual structure into a single pre-deduction mechanism and renders the concept of a ceiling redundant.

---

### Harmonious Interpretation of the 1948 Act and Section 3B

Section 3B of the 1948 Act expressly contemplates concessions in addition to those admissible under any other law. The PCA represents such a concession, executed by the President on behalf of the State and forming part of the statutory regime.

The structure of Article 14.3 is not inconsistent with the 1948 Act; rather, it operates within the permissible statutory band of 50% to 55%. The agreement refines the computational mechanism within that band.

If an interpretational tension is alleged between the Schedule to the 1948 Act and the Fifth Schedule to the 1979 Ordinance, the latter — being part of a Parliamentary enactment — must prevail. Moreover, both instruments must be harmonised so as to preserve, rather than extinguish, negotiated concessions.

---

### Consistent Administrative Practice and Circular Clarification

CBR Circular No. 2 of 1974 clarified the method of computation for petroleum undertakings and illustrated the separate application of the minimum and maximum thresholds. The Circular has never been withdrawn and was consistently followed for decades.

The Company’s methodology for Tax Year 2025 is aligned with this settled administrative position. The Department accepted this computational structure for numerous years without objection. A long-standing and consistently accepted fiscal interpretation cannot be disturbed retrospectively through interpretational expansion.

Certainty and predictability are essential components of petroleum investment frameworks, particularly in long-term concession arrangements.

---

### Strict Interpretation of Taxing Statutes

It is a cardinal principle of tax jurisprudence that:

- Taxing statutes must be strictly construed;
- No tax liability can be imposed by implication;
- Any ambiguity must be resolved in favour of the taxpayer.

Even assuming arguendo that the Department’s interpretation is plausible, the Company’s interpretation is equally supported by statutory language and structural logic. In such circumstances, the interpretation favourable to the taxpayer must prevail.

An assessment adopting a legally tenable interpretation cannot be termed erroneous merely because the Department prefers an alternative view.

---

### Issue Pending Before the Honourable Supreme Court

The identical interpretational controversy has been adjudicated by the Honourable Sindh High Court and is presently pending before the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan fileciteturn0file1.

The questions under consideration include:

- Whether the PCA derives statutory protection under Section 3B of the 1948 Act;
- Whether the phrase “before deduction of payments to Government” applies exclusively to the 50% threshold;
- Whether extending that phrase to the 55% ceiling amounts to rewriting the statute;
- Whether long-standing departmental practice binds the Revenue.

In view of the pendency of these substantial questions of law before the apex Court, it is respectfully submitted that no coercive or adverse action may be taken for Tax Year 2025 on a matter which has not yet attained finality.

---

### Computation Adopted for Tax Year 2025

For Tax Year 2025, the Company computed:

- 55% of profits and gains derived from operations in accordance with Article 14.3 of the PCA; and  
- 50% of profits and gains before deduction of payments to Government as required under the proviso to Rule 4(1);

and duly discharged the higher of the two amounts.

This methodology ensures:

- Compliance with the statutory minimum;
- Observance of the negotiated ceiling;
- No prejudice to the revenue; and
- Full alignment with the governing statutory framework.

There is therefore no shortfall, concealment, misapplication or error in the assessment originally declared.

---

### Prayer

In light of the foregoing submissions, it is respectfully requested that:

- The proposed amendment under section 122(5A) for Tax Year 2025 may kindly be dropped in entirety;  
- The assessment as declared in the return of income may be accepted; and  
- Alternatively, proceedings may be kept in abeyance pending final adjudication by the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan.

The Company remains fully cooperative and shall provide any further clarification or documentation as may be required.

Yours faithfully,  
[Name]  
Authorized Representative / Tax Consultant  
For and on behalf of [Name of Company]

## Applicable Rate for Determination of Aggregate Payments to Government  
### (Tax Year 2025)

### I. Background and Present Status of the Controversy

The issue raised in the subject proceedings concerns the methodology for computation of the aggregate of taxes on income and other payments to the Government under Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979 (“1979 Ordinance”), read with Article 14.3 of the applicable Petroleum Concession Agreement (“PCA”) and the Regulation of Mines and Oilfields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948 (“1948 Act”).

The questions involved are constitutional and statutory in nature and go to the root of the fiscal regime governing petroleum exploration and production undertakings.

Without prejudice to the Company’s rights before the apex Court, the following position is respectfully reiterated and refined for Tax Year 2025.

---

### II. Composite Statutory Framework Governing Petroleum Taxation

The taxation regime applicable to petroleum E&P companies is not derived from a single statute. It is a composite legal structure comprising:

- The 1948 Act (including Section 3B and its Schedule),
- Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the 1979 Ordinance, and  
- The PCA executed by the President on behalf of the State.

The PCA is not a mere private contract. It derives statutory force from Section 3B of the 1948 Act and is expressly recognized under the Fifth Schedule to the 1979 Ordinance. The fiscal arrangement stipulated therein is therefore embedded within statutory law and must be interpreted harmoniously with the parent legislation.

An isolated reading of Rule 2 of the Schedule to the 1948 Act, divorced from Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule and Article 14.3 of the PCA, leads to distortion of the legislative design.

---

### III. Structural Distinction Between the 50% Floor and the 55% Cap

Rule 4(1) of the Fifth Schedule clearly provides that:

- The aggregate of taxes and other payments to Government shall not exceed the limits provided in the agreement; and  
- The proviso states that such aggregate shall not be less than 50% of profits or gains before deduction of payments to Government.

The phrase “before deduction of payments to the Government” appears only in the proviso (which prescribes the minimum threshold), and not in the main enacting clause (which governs the ceiling).

It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that a proviso cannot enlarge or alter the substantive part of the enactment. The proviso operates only to carve out or qualify a specific situation. By extending the phrase “before deduction” to the 55% ceiling, the interpretation adopted by the Department effectively rewrites the statutory text and renders the structural distinction between floor and cap meaningless.

The legislative architecture clearly contemplates two distinct computational mechanisms:

- A statutory minimum (50%) calculated before deduction of payments to Government; and  
- A contractual ceiling (55%) to be applied in accordance with the agreement.

To collapse both into a single pre-deduction computation eliminates the ceiling concept altogether and defeats the very notion of a negotiated fiscal cap.

---

### IV. Legal Effect and Protection of the PCA Under Section 3B

Section 3B of the 1948 Act expressly provides for concessions in addition to those admissible under any other law. The PCA, executed by the President on behalf of the State, embodies such concessions.

The structure of Article 14.3 — limiting 55% to profits and gains without the qualifying phrase “before deduction of payments to Government,” while expressly attaching that phrase only to the 50% threshold — represents a deliberate and lawful refinement of the concession mechanism.

Even if an interpretational tension were assumed between the Schedule to the 1948 Act and the Fifth Schedule to the 1979 Ordinance, it is respectfully submitted that:

- The Fifth Schedule forms part of a Parliamentary enactment.
- The Schedule to the 1948 Act is amendable by the Federal Government.
- The PCA is statutorily protected and incorporated by reference.

Therefore, the framework must be reconciled in a manner that preserves the concession rather than extinguishes it.

---

### V. Longstanding Departmental Interpretation and Circular No. 2 of 1974

CBR Circular No. 2 of 1974 clarified the computational methodology for petroleum undertakings and illustrated:

- Application of the 55% agreed percentage after deduction of royalty; and  
- Application of the 50% floor before deduction of royalty.

This circular was formally issued, never withdrawn, and consistently followed for decades. The Company’s computation methodology for Tax Year 2025 is aligned with this settled interpretation.

A fiscal position uniformly accepted for decades cannot be disturbed merely through interpretational expansion without legislative amendment. Certainty and predictability are foundational principles in taxation of long-term extractive investments.

---

### VI. Strict Construction of Fiscal Provisions

It is a cardinal principle that taxing statutes must be interpreted strictly. Where ambiguity exists, the interpretation favorable to the taxpayer must prevail.

In the present case, two interpretations are possible:

1. Apply 55% before deduction of payments to Government (expansive interpretation increasing liability); or  
2. Apply 55% in accordance with the agreement while restricting “before deduction” to the 50% floor (textually consistent interpretation).

In such a situation, settled jurisprudence mandates adoption of the latter interpretation.

---

### VII. Computational Integrity and Logical Consistency

Under the correct legal framework, the Company computes:

- 55% of profits and gains derived from operations (as per PCA ceiling); and  
- 50% of profits and gains before deduction of payments to Government (as per statutory floor);

and discharges the higher of the two amounts.

This methodology ensures:

- The statutory minimum is respected;  
- The negotiated ceiling is not exceeded;  
- The aggregate remains within the legislatively sanctioned band.

The Department’s approach, by contrast, effectively nullifies the ceiling and transforms the regime into a single-rate pre-deduction structure, which is neither contemplated by the PCA nor supported by Rule 4(1).

---

### VIII. Issue Pending Before the Honourable Supreme Court

The interpretational questions raised herein are presently under consideration before the Honourable Supreme Court fileciteturn0file1. The constitutional dimensions include:

- Whether PCA clauses derive statutory protection under Section 3B;  
- Whether “before deduction of payments to Government” applies exclusively to the 50% floor;  
- Whether the High Court’s interpretation amounts to rewriting of statutory language;  
- Whether settled departmental practice binds the Revenue.

In view of the pendency of these issues before the apex Court, it is respectfully submitted that no adverse inference may be drawn for Tax Year 2025 on a matter that is sub judice at the highest judicial forum.

---

### IX. Conclusion

For Tax Year 2025, the Company has computed the aggregate sum payable to the Government by:

- Applying 55% in accordance with Article 14.3 of the PCA; and  
- Ensuring compliance with the 50% minimum before deduction requirement under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule.

This methodology:

- Reflects the composite statutory framework;  
- Preserves the structural distinction between floor and cap;  
- Aligns with longstanding administrative interpretation; and  
- Is presently under adjudication before the Honourable Supreme Court.

It is therefore respectfully requested that the computation as declared in the return for Tax Year 2025 be accepted and no adjustment be made on the alleged basis of applying 55% before deduction of payments to Government.
