Zuhair, I’ve reviewed the Local File titled **“Transfer Pricing Local File – United Energy Pakistan – Tax Year 2023”** fileciteturn0file0 very carefully from a Rule 27M compliance lens.

Technically, the document is strong from an OECD narrative perspective. However, if we test it strictly against **Rule 27M of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 (as amended through SRO 1179(I)/2021)**, there are certain structural and documentary gaps that could create exposure during audit or TP proceedings.

Let me walk you through this like a tax authority would.

---

### 1️⃣ Rule 27M Compliance – Structural Gap

Rule 27M does not merely require an economic analysis. It requires **specific disclosures in a prescribed structure**.

Your Local File is narrative-heavy and technically sound, but it is not structured exactly in the Rule 27M format.

Under Rule 27M, the Local File must contain:

• Detailed description of the local entity  
• Management structure  
• Detailed description of business strategy  
• Details of controlled transactions (with value, counterparties, agreements)  
• FAR analysis (Functions, Assets, Risks)  
• Transfer pricing method selection and justification  
• Comparable analysis (including selection/rejection criteria)  
• Financial information and reconciliation with audited accounts  

Your file addresses many of these conceptually — but not always in the form expected under Rule 27M.

---

### 2️⃣ Missing / Weak Areas That Need Strengthening

#### A. Detailed Management Structure of UEP (Rule 27M(2)(b))

The file mentions group structure but does not provide:

• Organizational chart of UEP Pakistan branch  
• Reporting lines  
• Key decision-makers for financing  
• Board oversight or treasury control  

This is specifically required. FBR increasingly questions who controls financial risk — especially post OECD 2020 financial transaction guidance.

Recommendation:
Add a management structure section with a reporting diagram and identify who:
• negotiates loan terms  
• monitors repayment  
• manages currency risk  

---

#### B. Clear Reconciliation to Audited Financial Statements

Rule 27M requires:

> Reconciliation of financial data used in TP analysis with statutory financial statements.

Your benchmarking discusses interest rates but does not:

• Reconcile interest expense to audited accounts  
• Provide note reference numbers  
• Show ledger extract summary  
• Confirm that interest expense tested = interest expense booked  

This is a common audit trigger.

Recommendation:
Add a reconciliation table:

| Description | Amount (USD) | Amount (PKR) | FS Note Reference |
|-------------|--------------|--------------|-------------------|

---

#### C. Explicit Quantification of Controlled Transactions

Rule 27M expects value disclosure of transactions during the year — not just outstanding principal.

You need:

• Total interest expense paid in 2022  
• Accrued vs paid  
• Any FX gain/loss interaction  

Right now, only principal balances are discussed in detail.

Add:

| Loan Type | Principal | Interest Charged 2022 | Interest Paid | Closing Balance |

---

#### D. Search Strategy Documentation (Critical)

Your CUP benchmarking relies heavily on macro indicators:
• LIBOR movement  
• KIBOR  
• Sovereign spreads  

But Rule 27M requires:

• Description of search methodology  
• Databases used (Bloomberg? Refinitiv? LoanConnector?)  
• Screening criteria  
• Comparable rejection criteria  

Currently, it reads as analytical justification — not as a documented comparable search process.

This is risky.

Recommendation:
Add a dedicated section titled:

**“Comparable Search Methodology”**

Include:
• Search date  
• Geographic filters  
• Industry filter (E&P / emerging markets)  
• Credit rating filters  
• Loan tenure filter  
• Currency filter  

Without this, FBR can argue that no proper CUP benchmarking was performed.

---

#### E. Explicit Credit Rating Analysis of UEP

OECD Chapter X requires borrower credit rating analysis.

Your file discusses country risk — but does not:

• Determine standalone credit rating of UEP  
• Assess group uplift  
• Explain how 5.3% spread corresponds to rating  

FBR increasingly applies synthetic credit rating testing.

Recommendation:
Add:

• Synthetic credit rating calculation (EBITDA/interest, leverage ratios)
• Comparison of spread to rating-based market spreads

This strengthens defensibility.

---

#### F. Debt vs Equity Delineation Risk

There is a silent vulnerability here.

The acquisition loan:

• No maturity  
• Subordinated  
• Long outstanding  
• Partially repaid  

This could be challenged as quasi-equity.

Your file acknowledges quasi-equity characteristics but does not robustly defend debt characterization under:

• Section 108  
• Thin capitalization concepts  
• Substance-over-form principles  

I strongly recommend adding a subsection:

**“Accurate Delineation – Debt Characterization Analysis”**

Address:
• Intention to repay  
• Actual repayment history  
• Interest actually paid  
• Enforceability  
• Commercial rationale  

Otherwise, recharacterization risk exists.

---

#### G. Rule 27M Cross-Reference Table (Highly Recommended)

Add a compliance matrix:

| Rule 27M Requirement | Section of Local File |
|----------------------|-----------------------|

This makes the file audit-proof.

---

### 3️⃣ Technical Strength – What Is Done Well

Let’s be fair.

The file is excellent in:

• Macroeconomic contextualization  
• Country risk explanation  
• LIBOR movement analysis  
• Cost-of-funds cross-check  
• OECD Chapter X referencing  

From an OECD defense perspective, it is strong.

From a Pakistan procedural compliance perspective, it needs structural tightening.

---

### 4️⃣ Risk Rating (Professional Assessment)

If filed as-is:

• OECD defensibility: Strong  
• Procedural compliance under Rule 27M: Moderate  
• Audit robustness against FBR TP Wing: Needs strengthening  

---

### 5️⃣ Immediate Improvement Roadmap

I would suggest adding:

1. Rule 27M compliance matrix  
2. Detailed management structure  
3. Reconciliation to audited FS  
4. Controlled transaction value summary  
5. Documented comparable search methodology  
6. Synthetic credit rating analysis  
7. Debt characterization defense  

Once these are added, the Local File will move from narrative-compliant to audit-ready.

---

Transfer pricing documentation is like engineering a bridge. It’s not enough that it looks strong — it must withstand stress testing from someone trying to break it. Rule 27M is the stress test.

If you want, I can now restructure this into a revised Local File outline aligned strictly to Rule 27M so it becomes fully litigation-ready for UEP.

parts:
Zuhair, let’s dissect this like a tax surgeon with a steady scalpel and a copy of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 open beside us.

I have reviewed the Local File (fileciteturn0file0), and technically speaking, it is well-written from an OECD perspective. The economic narrative is strong, the benchmarking discussion is thoughtful, and the functional analysis is reasonably articulated. However, when we evaluate it strictly against Pakistan’s Income Tax Rules, 2002 — especially Rule 27L (Master File) read with Rule 27M (Local File) — there are some structural and compliance gaps that should be addressed to make it bullet-proof before any FBR scrutiny.

Let’s go step by step.

First — Structural Issue: Mixing Master File and Local File Content

Rule 27L deals specifically with Master File requirements. Your current document is titled as a “Local File”, but it includes certain group-level descriptions (ownership structure, UEG background, shareholder information, etc.) that belong in the Master File.

However, what is missing is far more important:

Rule 27L requires standardized group-wide disclosures, including:

– Legal and ownership structure chart with geographical location of operating entities  
– Description of supply chain for the group’s five largest products/services  
– List and description of important service arrangements between group members  
– Description of intangibles and R&D policy  
– Intercompany financial activities (central financing arrangements)  
– Consolidated financial statements of the MNE group  
– List of unilateral APAs and rulings  

Your document includes a basic group description, but it does not comprehensively address Rule 27L(a) to (f) requirements in structured format.

Recommendation:

Prepare a separate Master File document strictly aligned with Rule 27L headings. The Local File should only focus on Pakistan-specific controlled transactions.

If you intend to merge, then add a separate section clearly titled:

“Compliance with Rule 27L – Master File Requirements”

And systematically address each clause of Rule 27L.

Right now, if the FBR officer checks Rule 27L checklist, they will mark multiple boxes as missing.

Second — Rule 27M Local File Content Gaps

Now coming to Rule 27M (Local File). This is where precision matters.

Your Local File covers:

– Transaction description  
– Functional analysis  
– Economic analysis  
– Method selection  
– Benchmarking rationale  

That’s good.

But under Rule 27M, the following must also be explicitly included:

1. Detailed Description of Management Structure of Local Entity  
Currently missing. You have not described reporting lines within Pakistan branch or how treasury decisions are made.

Add:
– Organizational chart of UEP Pakistan Branch  
– Reporting relationship with GTI/UEG  
– Who negotiates financing terms  

2. Detailed FAR Analysis with Risk Allocation Matrix  
Your functional analysis is narrative-based. It should be structured.

Improve by adding a table:

Functions | UEP | GTI  
Assets | UEP | GTI  
Risks | UEP | GTI  

FBR prefers tabulated risk allocation. Narrative explanation alone is risky.

3. Copy of Intercompany Agreements  
You summarized extracts. Rule 27M requires actual agreements to be referenced and annexed.

Add:
“Certified copy of loan agreements attached as Annexure X”

4. Financial Information Used in Applying TP Method  
You have benchmarking logic but no quantitative arm’s length range.

Critical issue:
There is no statistical range.

You say “within arm’s length range” — but you have not computed any range.

Under Rule 27M, you must provide:

– Comparable set  
– Screening criteria  
– Arm’s length range (interquartile range if multiple comparables)  
– Positioning of tested transaction within range  

Right now, your benchmarking relies heavily on macroeconomic discussion (KIBOR, sovereign yields, CDS spreads). That is academically sound but procedurally weak under Pakistani TP audits.

You need:

– External database search (e.g., Bloomberg, Refinitiv, LoanConnector)  
– Comparable USD loans to emerging market oil & gas companies  
– Credit rating based spread analysis  
– Interquartile computation  

Otherwise, FBR may argue the analysis is not sufficiently data-driven.

Third — Missing Credit Rating Analysis

OECD Chapter X requires borrower credit rating assessment.

Your document mentions implicit support but does not:

– Compute standalone credit rating  
– Estimate group-adjusted credit rating  
– Map rating to spread  

This is a vulnerability.

You should add:

Step 1: Determine UEP standalone rating using financial ratios  
Step 2: Adjust for implicit support  
Step 3: Compare spreads for similar rated borrowers  

Without this, the CUP application lacks scientific grounding.

Fourth — Thin Capitalization / Section 106 Exposure

Your Local File focuses purely on Section 108. However, for financing transactions, FBR often examines:

– Debt-to-equity ratio  
– Whether loan is quasi-equity  
– Whether no maturity makes it capital in substance  

You briefly mention quasi-equity characteristics but do not defend debt characterization.

Add a section:

“Debt vs Equity Characterization Analysis”

Cover:
– Legal enforceability  
– Interest payment history  
– Subordination analysis  
– No conversion rights  
– Actual repayment history  

Otherwise, officer may invoke recharacterization.

Fifth — No Reconciliation with Tax Computation

Rule 27M requires financial information used in applying TP method.

You have not:

– Reconciled interest expense per books  
– Reconciled interest claimed in tax return  
– Confirmed no secondary adjustment  

Add a reconciliation table:

Interest per books  
Interest per tax return  
Adjustment (if any)  

This is critical for audit defensibility.

Sixth — Country-by-Country Reporting Cross Reference

If UEG exceeds threshold, CbCR filing obligation arises.

Local File should state:

– Whether CbCR filed  
– Filing jurisdiction  
– Notification submitted in Pakistan  

Currently absent.

Seventh — Inconsistency in Year

Document mentions:

– Tax Year 2023  
– Accounting year 2022  

Make explicit:

“Accounting period 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2022 corresponds to Tax Year 2023 under Pakistani law.”

FBR officers notice these inconsistencies instantly.

Eighth — Missing Declaration and Contemporaneous Documentation Statement

Local File should include:

– Preparation date  
– Statement confirming contemporaneous documentation  
– Responsible signatory  

Add certification section.

Ninth — Risk of Excessive Narrative Macroeconomic Justification

Your macro discussion is strong but may backfire.

Why?

Because FBR may say:
“If country risk was so high, why did group charge only 9%?”

When narrative is too strong, it can contradict pricing logic.

Tone it down and rely more on empirical comparable spreads.

Tenth — Specific Rule 27L Observations

If Master File to be prepared, ensure inclusion of:

– Group intangibles strategy  
– List of APAs  
– Consolidated financial statements  
– Group financing policy  
– Central treasury description  

Your current document does not satisfy Rule 27L(b)(iii) and 27L(e) requirements fully.

Final Strategic Recommendation

Technically, your Local File is conceptually robust and professionally drafted. However, for Pakistan audit defence, it needs:

1. Formal Rule 27L compliance section (or separate Master File)
2. Quantitative benchmarking with arm’s length range
3. Credit rating analysis
4. Debt vs equity defence
5. Financial reconciliation tables
6. Structured FAR matrix
7. Annexures properly referenced

Right now, it is OECD-aligned but not fully FBR-proof.

And in Pakistan, surviving an audit requires procedural perfection as much as economic logic.

If you want, I can now:

– Redraft the Local File structure strictly aligned to Rule 27M headings, or  
– Prepare a separate Rule 27L-compliant Master File template tailored for UEG group.

Transfer pricing in Pakistan is no longer theoretical compliance. It’s a documentation engineering exercise. The stronger the structure, the shorter the litigation cycle.

Now let’s make these posts more punchy, interactive, and engaging — the kind that stops the scroll and starts conversation.

---

**“Infrastructure Cess Almost Gone — Is Sindh Finally Listening to Industry?”**

After years of litigation, pressure, and industry complaints, the Sindh Assembly has amended the Infrastructure Cess regime — reducing the rate to below 1% and abolishing it entirely on exports fileciteturn1file0. Previously standing at 1.8%, the cess had become a cost burden and a reason many factories quietly shifted operations to other provinces. With more than 500 cases pending in courts, the government has now requested traders to withdraw litigation under the revised framework. This move signals something important: when tax policy starts hurting competitiveness instead of generating meaningful benefit, it eventually gets corrected. For exporters especially, this directly improves margins and pricing flexibility in global markets.

---

**“Super Tax on the Way Out? Structural Reform or Strategic Messaging?”**

The Director General of the Tax Policy Office has confirmed that options are being considered to gradually reduce or eliminate super tax fileciteturn1file0. At the same time, a new trader scheme is under design and simplification of income tax, sales tax, and federal excise laws is being discussed. More interestingly, policymaking is now formally separated from tax collection through the Tax Policy Office. That institutional separation matters — because enforcement mindset and policy mindset are not the same species. If consultations genuinely take place before budget, we may see a more predictable fiscal environment. The real question now is not whether reform is discussed — but whether it is implemented consistently.

---

**“Seven Years. Endless Adjournments. Court Says: Enough.”**

In a customs appeal pending since 2019, the Sindh High Court dismissed the case and openly criticized mechanical revenue litigation fileciteturn0file0. The Court emphasized that filing appeals on issues already settled by higher courts clogs the judiciary and undermines constitutional discipline. It even reproduced Supreme Court observations warning government departments against repetitive litigation. This is a serious institutional message: revenue authorities must litigate responsibly. For businesses, this strengthens legal certainty. Once an issue is settled, it should not haunt taxpayers for years through recycled appeals.

---

**“Changed HS Code = Automatic Penalty? High Court Says Not So Fast.”**

In another customs ruling, the High Court upheld that a classification dispute does not automatically amount to misdeclaration fileciteturn0file2. The goods description was correct, declared value was even higher than the valuation ruling, and the dispute arose after laboratory testing. The Court made it clear that classification involves interpretation and legal judgment. Penalty requires intent — not merely disagreement. This reinforces a powerful principle: every technical dispute is not fraud. For importers navigating complex tariff schedules, this judgment provides important judicial balance.

---

Step back and connect the dots.

Provincial tax reduction. Possible super tax rationalization. Judicial discipline on revenue litigation. Clarification on penal overreach.

These are not isolated events. They reflect pressure on the fiscal system to become more predictable, competitive, and legally disciplined.

Tax policy, like gravity, always pulls on business behavior. When the pull becomes too heavy, systems adjust. And right now, adjustment seems underway.

Four major developments. One clear theme: the tax and fiscal landscape is being recalibrated — structurally, legally, and politically.

Here are sharp, public-facing social media posts you can use.

---

**Post 1: Sindh Infrastructure Cess Slashed – Exports Fully Exempted**

Big relief for traders and exporters.

The Sindh Assembly has approved amendments reducing Infrastructure Cess to below 1% and abolishing it entirely on exports fileciteturn1file0.

Earlier, the rate stood at 1.8%, and businesses had long argued that the levy:
• Increased cost of doing business  
• Encouraged relocation to Punjab  
• Led to 500+ pending court cases  

Now:
• Export sector fully exempt  
• Traders’ rate reduced below Punjab’s level  
• Government urging withdrawal of litigation  

This is more than a rate cut. It’s a policy correction driven by economic reality and sustained business pressure.

For exporters, this improves cost competitiveness immediately.

---

**Post 2: Super Tax May Be Phased Out – Government Signals Structural Reform**

At a meeting with the business community, the DG of the Tax Policy Office confirmed that options are being explored to gradually reduce or eliminate super tax fileciteturn1file0.

Key points:
• A new trader scheme under design  
• Simplification of income tax, sales tax and FED laws  
• Separation of policy-making from tax collection  
• Stakeholder consultation before budget  

The creation of the Tax Policy Office signals a structural shift: policymaking separated from enforcement.

If implemented properly, this could reduce unpredictability in fiscal decisions and restore some confidence in the system.

Super tax reform will be closely watched by large corporates.

---

**Post 3: High Court Slams Mechanical Revenue Appeals**

In a customs case pending for 7 years, the Sindh High Court dismissed the appeal and warned against repetitive, unmerited litigation by government departments fileciteturn0file0.

The Court cited a recent Supreme Court judgment emphasizing:
• Courts are being clogged with repetitive revenue litigation  
• Settled law must be respected  
• Costs and accountability may follow  

This is a strong judicial message: litigation should not be filed as a reflex.

For taxpayers, this strengthens the doctrine of finality and certainty in fiscal matters.

---

**Post 4: Classification Dispute Is Not Always Misdeclaration**

In another decision, the High Court held that change of HS Code alone does not automatically justify penalty fileciteturn0file2.

The Court observed:
• Description was correct  
• Value declared was higher than valuation ruling  
• Classification is often interpretational  
• Penalty requires intent (mens rea)  

Important takeaway: Every classification difference is not fraud.

This is critical for importers facing aggressive penal action in customs matters.

---

Zooming out.

We are witnessing:
• Policy simplification signals from the executive  
• Judicial restraint enforcement against excessive litigation  
• Provincial tax rationalization to retain industry  

The fiscal system appears to be adjusting under economic pressure and judicial discipline.

The next budget cycle will be pivotal.

Three fresh judicial developments. Three signals from the fiscal universe. And each one quietly tells Revenue: “Litigation is not a reflex. It’s a responsibility.”

Let’s distill them for public-facing tax insight content.

---

**1. Seven Years of Adjournments? High Court Says Enough is Enough**

In *High Court Appeal 03 of 2019*, decided on 13.02.2026, the Sindh High Court dismissed a customs appeal that had been pending for over seven years without meaningful prosecution fileciteturn0file0.

The case concerned entitlement to exemption under SRO 1125(1)/2011 for import of raw material at the spinning stage. The earlier judgment (aligned with *Searle Solutions* 2019 PTD 347) had already settled the issue in favour of the taxpayer. Yet the department kept seeking adjournments, even suggesting the matter be kept pending due to a review petition in another case.

The Court refused. It emphasized:
- Filing a review petition elsewhere does not justify freezing litigation.
- Government departments must respect settled law.
- Repeated appeals clog dockets and undermine Article 189 (binding nature of Supreme Court judgments).

Most significantly, the Court reproduced paragraphs from a recent Supreme Court judgment criticizing mechanical appeals by Revenue and even suggested internal FBR accountability mechanisms.

The appeal was dismissed outright.

This is not just a dismissal. It’s a judicial warning shot against habitual, non-meritorious fiscal litigation.

---

**2. Classification Dispute ≠ Automatic Penalty: Mens Rea Still Matters**

In *SCRA 273 of 2013*, order dated 13.02.2026, the Sindh High Court upheld the Tribunal’s decision removing penalty in a customs classification dispute fileciteturn0file2.

The department had changed the HS Code after laboratory testing and imposed penalty alleging misdeclaration. However:

- Description of goods was correct.
- Declared value was higher than the valuation ruling.
- Dispute was essentially about tariff classification.

The Court held that not every change in HS Code amounts to misdeclaration. Classification is a matter of legal interpretation and factual determination. Penal consequences require intent (mens rea). Where there is no fraudulent intent and no revenue loss manipulation, harsh penalty is not justified.

The reference was dismissed in limine.

For businesses, this reinforces a principle: disagreement in classification is not synonymous with fraud. Context matters. Intention matters.

---

**3. FBR (Amendment) Bill, 2026 – Structural Shift in Appointment Powers**

The Federal Board of Revenue (Amendment) Bill, 2026, introduced on 13.02.2026 fileciteturn0file1, proposes significant structural changes:

- Section 6 (Policy Board) is proposed to be omitted.
- The Secretary, Revenue Division, is to be empowered to appoint FBR Members (BS-21 and above) through transfer/posting.
- A validation clause is introduced to retrospectively validate past appointments and actions.

The Statement of Objects and Reasons clarifies that the amendment aims to address legal ambiguity following Supreme Court interpretation of “Federal Government” in *Mustafa Impex*, and to ensure administrative continuity.

Translation: governance structure is being recalibrated. The balance between policy formulation and revenue administration is being redefined. And past appointments are being legally insulated.

For tax professionals, this is not cosmetic. It affects institutional independence, administrative decision-making, and possibly litigation strategy going forward.

---

Zoom out and you see a pattern.

The judiciary is insisting on discipline in fiscal litigation.
The courts are drawing boundaries around penal overreach.
The legislature is reshaping FBR’s internal structure.

Tax law is not just about rates and exemptions. It’s about institutional behavior, administrative restraint, and the architecture of accountability.

The fiscal ecosystem evolves in layers. And right now, those layers are shifting in interesting ways.

**Subject:** SMTA Agreement – Clause-wise Tax Review and Suggested Amendments  

Dear Mr. Musani,  

Further to your email and our earlier advice on the tax characterization of the relocation arrangement fileciteturn0file0, we have now carried out a detailed clause-by-clause review of the updated draft Agreement dated 31 January 2026 fileciteturn1file0.

Overall, the commercial framework is sound. However, certain clauses—if left as presently drafted—may expose KE to characterization risk under:  

- Section 153(1)(c) (execution of contract) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001; and  
- Provincial sales tax on construction/engineering services under CPC-based classification.  

Below we have pinpointed the relevant clauses and suggested precise refinements to mitigate such risk while preserving commercial intent.

---

## 1. RECITALS – Risk of “Works Contract” Characterization  

**Relevant portion:**  
Recital stating:  
> “SMTA has requested KE to execute the scope of work… for which KE has consented…”

### Risk  
The language suggests KE is executing defined works *for SMTA*, which is the classical formulation of a works contract. Tax authorities could rely on this phrasing to argue that the arrangement falls within “execution of contract” under section 153(1)(c).

### Recommended Amendment  
Insert an additional recital immediately after the fourth recital:

> “The Parties expressly acknowledge that the relocation/replacement activities are undertaken by KE solely in respect of its own transmission infrastructure forming part of its Common Distribution System, and such activities are necessitated exclusively due to the alignment of SMTA’s Yellow Line Project. SMTA is funding the relocation as reimbursement of costs incurred by KE and not as consideration for provision of works, services, or supply of goods to SMTA.”

This clarification directly supports the cost-recovery position.

---

## 2. ARTICLE IV – Scope of Work  

**Relevant Clause:** Article IV (Scope of Work)

### Risk  
The current wording mirrors an EPC contract (survey, engineering, construction, commissioning). In isolation, it reads like a construction services contract rendered to SMTA.

### Recommended Amendment  

Insert a clarificatory paragraph at the end of Article IV:

> “For avoidance of doubt, the activities described in this Article IV relate exclusively to KE’s own Assets and shall not be construed as construction, engineering, consulting, or other services rendered by KE to SMTA. The relocated Assets shall at all times remain owned, operated and controlled by KE and shall continue to form part of KE’s regulated transmission and distribution network.”

This neutralizes the service characterization argument.

---

## 3. ARTICLE V – Project Cost and Payment Structure  

### (a) Nature of Payments  

**Relevant Clause:** Article V – introductory paragraph and milestone payments.

### Risk  
Milestone-based advance payments combined with defined scope resemble consideration under a works contract.

### Recommended Amendment  

Insert a new sub-clause under Article V (e.g., 5.1A):

> “The Parties agree that all amounts payable by SMTA to KE under this Agreement constitute reimbursement of actual costs incurred by KE for relocation of its own infrastructure and do not represent consideration for sale of goods, rendering of services, or execution of works for SMTA.”

This clause becomes central in defending non-applicability of section 153.

---

### (b) Section 5.8 – Tax Deduction at Source  

**Relevant Clause:** Section 5.8 (withholding mechanism)

### Risk  
The current clause contemplates deduction “if required under law.” This weakens the non-withholding position because it assumes possible applicability.

### Recommended Amendment  

Revise Section 5.8 to read:

> “The Parties acknowledge and agree that payments under this Agreement are in the nature of cost reimbursement and are not subject to withholding under section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. In the event any withholding is required by a tax authority, SMTA shall gross-up the payment such that KE receives the full Project Cost in net terms.”

This preserves KE’s economic neutrality and strengthens interpretative defense.

---

## 4. PROJECT COST DEFINITION – Taxes Component  

**Relevant Clause:** Definition of “Project Cost” (Article I)

### Risk  
Although Taxes are included, it does not explicitly address non-adjustable input sales tax.

If the receipt is treated as non-taxable, KE may be unable to claim input tax adjustment under section 8 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

### Recommended Amendment  

Amend the definition of “Project Cost” to add:

> “Project Cost shall include all federal and provincial taxes, duties, levies, and any non-adjustable input sales tax incurred by KE in connection with the Project.”

This ensures SMTA bears the full tax burden.

---

## 5. ANNEXURE A – Transfer Agreement  

### Risk  
The term “Transfer Agreement” raises red flags. If Annexure A implies transfer of assets to SMTA, it may:

- Trigger sales tax on supply of goods;
- Fall under section 153(1)(a);
- Alter capital vs revenue analysis.

### Recommendation  

Confirm that Annexure A does **not** provide for transfer of ownership or beneficial interest in relocated Assets to SMTA.

If required, insert a clarification in Article IV:

> “Nothing in this Agreement or any annexure shall be construed as transfer, assignment, lease, license, or creation of any proprietary or beneficial interest in the Assets in favor of SMTA.”

---

## 6. ARTICLE VI – Implementation  

**Relevant Clause:** Article VI (SMTA involvement and Steering Committee)

### Risk  
Excessive operational involvement of SMTA may support argument that KE is executing a project “for” SMTA.

### Suggested Clarification  

Add:

> “SMTA’s involvement shall be limited to monitoring and funding oversight and shall not alter the nature of the Project as relocation of KE’s own infrastructure.”

---

## 7. Accounting Alignment (Internal Recommendation)

Though not necessarily contractual, we strongly recommend that:

- Receipts be accounted for as capital reimbursement;  
- No revenue be recognized under IFRS 15;  
- Documentation reflects restoration of capital structure.

Tax characterization and accounting treatment must not contradict each other.

---

# Overall Risk Position

With current drafting: **Moderate exposure** under section 153(1)(c) and provincial sales tax.

With recommended amendments: **Significantly mitigated exposure**, defensible as:

- Non-taxable reimbursement;  
- Capital receipt;  
- Outside section 153;  
- Outside scope of sales tax supply.

The difference lies not in economics, but in wording. Tax disputes are often won or lost on one sentence.

---

I have carefully read the attached advice regarding tax implications on payments from SMTA to K-Electric in respect of the Yellow Line relocation project fileciteturn0file0.

Now let me step back and analyze it like a slightly obsessive tax philosopher who doesn’t trust surface classifications until they survive a stress test.

At a structural level, the advice builds on three pillars:

First, commercial substance.  
The memo strongly positions the arrangement as a compelled relocation due to a public infrastructure project, not a voluntary commercial service by KE. That is the backbone of the entire tax position. If that characterization collapses, the rest becomes fragile.

Second, sales tax non-taxability.  
The argument is that KE is not supplying goods, nor rendering services to SMTA. The payment is framed as pure cost recovery for business disruption, not consideration for a taxable supply under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 or the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011.

Third, withholding tax exclusion under section 153.  
The advice takes the view that the payment does not fall within sale of goods, services, or execution of contract. It is characterized as a capital receipt / reimbursement outside the scope of withholding.

Now, let’s pressure-test this from a technical perspective.

On commercial substance  
The logic is coherent: KE retains ownership; no asset or right is transferred; no enduring benefit is granted to SMTA. That part is well-articulated. The stronger the agreement reflects that KE is acting for itself and not “for and on behalf of SMTA,” the safer the position.

However, here is where tax authorities typically get aggressive:  
If KE is contractually responsible for executing defined relocation works and receiving payment against milestones, authorities may argue that KE is executing a works contract — regardless of ownership retention. Substance over form cuts both ways.

If the agreement reads like:
– SMTA appoints KE to relocate infrastructure  
– KE undertakes defined scope  
– Payment linked to completion  

Then the department may argue this is execution of contract under section 153(1)(c).

So the legal drafting becomes critical. If it looks like a works contract, it will be treated like one.

On sales tax  
The advice states KE is not rendering a service. That argument rests on this idea: KE is merely adjusting its own network to avoid interference.

That’s intellectually elegant. But here’s the counterpoint a revenue officer might raise:

SMTA requires KE to perform relocation.  
KE undertakes engineering, construction, commissioning.  
SMTA pays KE.

Authorities may argue this resembles construction / infrastructure service falling under CPC-based classification under SSTSA.

The defense then becomes: who is the beneficiary?

If KE remains the sole beneficiary of the relocated infrastructure and SMTA gets no service output, that strengthens the non-taxability stance.

But if the contract language implies KE is “providing relocation services to SMTA,” the risk increases.

On capital vs revenue receipt  
The capital receipt argument is interesting but delicate. Not every reimbursement automatically becomes capital. The real test is: does this receipt relate to the profit-earning structure or day-to-day operations?

If relocation results in replacement of capital assets and the receipt merely compensates for structural alteration, capital characterization is defensible.

However, if treated as revenue in books, the tax position weakens significantly. The memo correctly emphasizes accounting alignment. That is not cosmetic — it is strategic.

On input tax  
The advice takes a conservative approach: if receipt is non-taxable, input tax cannot be adjusted.

That is technically aligned with the “taxable supply nexus” principle. But this becomes economically inefficient unless the agreement clearly states SMTA reimburses gross cost including taxes.

This is where contract drafting and tax economics meet.

Now, zooming out.

The advice is conceptually strong. It is coherent. It is defensible. But its survival depends almost entirely on documentation language and accounting treatment.

Tax law often behaves like quantum mechanics — the classification changes when observed under audit conditions.

If you want, I can next:

– Redraft key contractual clauses to strengthen non-taxable positioning  
– Prepare a risk matrix (low / medium / high exposure areas)  
– Develop an alternative position in case FBR treats it as contract execution  
– Or analyze implications under section 113 minimum tax and section 4C super tax impact if treated as revenue  

The intellectual puzzle here is fascinating: when does compelled infrastructure relocation become a taxable service? That boundary is thin — and that thin line is where serious tax advisory lives.

**Subject:** Review of Draft Agreement with SMTA – Tax Alignment Comments  

Dear Mr. Musani,  

We refer to your email below and have reviewed the updated draft Agreement titled *“Agreement for Relocation/Replacement of Extra High Tension Oil Filled Transmission Line Network – Karachi Mobility Project (BRT Yellow Line Corridor)”* fileciteturn1file0 in light of our earlier tax advice shared with you fileciteturn0file0.  

At the outset, the draft is generally aligned with the commercial framework earlier discussed. However, from a tax risk containment perspective—particularly concerning sales tax characterization and withholding exposure under section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001—certain refinements are advisable to strengthen the intended treatment of the arrangement as *cost recovery* rather than a *taxable works or services contract*.  

Below are our detailed observations and suggested amendments.

---

### 1. Recitals – Characterization Risk

The current Recitals state that SMTA “has requested KE to execute the scope of work” and that KE has consented to execute such scope. While commercially understandable, this language may create interpretational risk that KE is executing a works contract *for SMTA*, thereby strengthening a withholding and sales tax argument.

**Suggested refinement:**  
The Recitals should clearly state that:  

- The relocation arises solely due to SMTA’s Yellow Line alignment;  
- KE is undertaking relocation of its *own* infrastructure to preserve network continuity;  
- SMTA is funding the relocation as compensation for disturbance/displacement of KE’s pre-existing assets; and  
- KE is not acting as contractor or service provider to SMTA.  

A clarificatory recital may be inserted along the following lines:

> “The Parties acknowledge that the relocation is necessitated solely due to the Yellow Line Project and is undertaken by KE to maintain and restore its own transmission network. SMTA is funding such relocation as reimbursement of the cost incurred by KE and not as consideration for provision of any works or services to SMTA.”

This language is critical to defend non-applicability of sales tax and section 153 withholding.

---

### 2. Article IV – Scope of Work

The scope is presently drafted in conventional EPC terminology (survey, design, engineering, supply, construction, installation, etc.). While operationally accurate, the phrasing resembles a classic works contract.

To mitigate characterization risk:

- Insert a clarification that the scope represents activities undertaken by KE in respect of its own assets;
- State expressly that SMTA shall not acquire ownership, possessory rights, operational control, leasehold, or any beneficial interest in the relocated Assets;
- Clarify that the Project does not constitute provision of construction, engineering, consulting, or other taxable service to SMTA.

---

### 3. Article V – Project Cost and Payment

This Article is central to the tax position.

Currently, “Project Cost” is defined broadly and payments are milestone-based. While the mechanics are appropriate, the drafting should clearly state:

- Payments represent reimbursement of actual cost incurred by KE;
- KE shall not earn any margin, mark-up, or service fee (other than regulatory design/supervision charges, if these are separately defensible under NEPRA framework);
- Payments are not consideration for supply of goods or services.

We recommend insertion of a specific clause under Article V stating:

> “The Parties acknowledge that all amounts payable by SMTA to KE under this Agreement constitute reimbursement of costs incurred by KE in relocating its own infrastructure and do not represent consideration for sale of goods, provision of services, or execution of works for SMTA.”

---

### 4. Tax Clause – Section 5.8 (Critical)

Section 5.8 currently allows deduction of withholding if required under law, with recovery rights if KE cannot adjust.

From a tax defense standpoint, it would be preferable to include a specific acknowledgment that:

- The Parties agree that payments are not subject to deduction under section 153;  
- If any tax authority requires deduction, SMTA shall gross-up the amount to ensure KE receives full Project Cost.

Otherwise, if SMTA deducts under section 153(c) (execution of contract), it may weaken the “non-contractual” position before tax authorities.

We recommend strengthening the clause to include an explicit gross-up mechanism.

---

### 5. Input Sales Tax Implications

The draft does not explicitly address the economic treatment of input sales tax suffered by KE on contractor invoices.

In line with our earlier advice:

- A clause should clarify that Project Cost includes all federal and provincial taxes, including non-adjustable input sales tax suffered by KE;
- SMTA shall fund the gross cost including such taxes;
- KE shall not be obligated to claim or pass through any input tax adjustment.

This prevents future disputes and aligns accounting treatment with tax characterization.

---

### 6. Transfer Agreement (Annexure A)

Given that Annexure A is titled “Transfer Agreement,” this requires careful review. Any language implying transfer of assets or rights to SMTA may materially contradict the tax position.

If the Transfer Agreement contemplates eventual transfer to SMTA, that would fundamentally alter the characterization and may trigger:

- Sales tax exposure (supply of goods);
- Withholding under section 153(1)(a);
- Possible capital gains implications.

We recommend reviewing Annexure A separately to ensure no asset transfer occurs.

---

### 7. Accounting Treatment Alignment

Although accounting is not expressly addressed in the draft, we strongly recommend internal documentation clarifying:

- The receipt will be treated as capital receipt / cost reimbursement;
- No revenue recognition under IFRS 15;
- Corresponding asset treatment and capitalization adjustments.

This alignment significantly strengthens defensibility during audit proceedings.

---

### 8. Dispute Clause – Payment Continuity

The clause stating that SMTA shall not stop payments during dispute is commercially beneficial and also consistent with tax defensibility (i.e., reinforces cost recovery mechanism).

However, care should be taken that such clauses do not appear as contractor-like protections typical in EPC agreements.

---

### Overall Risk Assessment

With current drafting, there remains moderate risk that tax authorities may characterize the arrangement as:

- Execution of contract under section 153(1)(c);  
- Engineering/construction service under provincial sales tax;  
- Possibly a works contract in substance.

With the refinements suggested above—particularly strengthening the reimbursement narrative and eliminating “service provider” overtones—the tax position becomes substantially more defensible.

---

### Concluding Remarks

In summary, the draft is commercially robust but requires targeted tax-sensitive refinements to align fully with the non-taxable characterization previously advised fileciteturn0file0.

We would be pleased to share mark-ups reflecting the suggested language for incorporation into the draft.

Please let us know a convenient time if you would like to discuss the proposed refinements with the legal team to ensure contractual language remains commercially balanced while minimizing tax exposure.

Kind regards,  

Zuhair  
Partner – Tax Advisory

### 1. Recitals – Risk of “Execution of Contract” Characterization  

**Existing wording (Recitals):**  
> “SMTA has requested KE to execute the scope of work… for which KE has consented…”

**Risk Identified:**  
The phrase “execute the scope of work” may be interpreted as KE executing a works contract for SMTA. This language may be relied upon to invoke section 153(1)(c) (execution of contract).

Such relocation is necessitated exclusively due to the alignment of SMTA’s Yellow Line Project. SMTA is funding the relocation as reimbursement of costs incurred by KE and not as consideration for provision of works, services, or supply of goods to SMTA.”

This wording anchors the commercial substance and protects against re-characterization.

---

### 2. Article IV – Scope of Work  

**Existing wording (Article IV):**  
> “The scope of the Project tender includes survey, design, engineering, supply, construction, installation, erection, testing, commissioning and energization…”

**Risk Identified:**  
The drafting mirrors an EPC construction contract and may support characterization as engineering/construction services rendered to SMTA.

**Recommended insertion at the end of Article IV:**

> “For avoidance of doubt, the activities described in this Article IV relate exclusively to KE’s own Assets and shall not be construed as construction, engineering, consulting, or other services rendered by KE to SMTA. The relocated Assets shall at all times remain owned, operated and controlled by KE and shall continue to form part of KE’s regulated transmission and distribution network.”

This clarification directly mitigates sales tax and withholding exposure.

---

### 3. Article V – Nature of Payments  

**Existing wording (Article V – introductory paragraph):**  
> “SMTA hereby agrees to pay the complete Project Cost to KE.”

**Risk Identified:**  
Milestone-based advance payments, without clarification, may resemble contractual consideration.

**Recommended insertion as new Clause 5.1A:**

> “The Parties agree that all amounts payable by SMTA to KE under this Agreement constitute reimbursement of actual costs incurred by KE in relocating its own infrastructure and do not represent consideration for sale of goods, rendering of services, or execution of works for SMTA.”

This clause becomes critical in defending against section 153.

---

### 4. Definition of “Project Cost” – Article I  

**Existing wording:**  
> “Project Cost shall mean the total amount that will be incurred by KE… including… custom duties, Taxes, fees…”

**Risk Identified:**  
The definition does not explicitly address non-adjustable input sales tax suffered by KE.

**Recommended amendment (add at end of definition):**

> “For clarity, Project Cost shall include all federal and provincial taxes, duties, levies, and any non-adjustable or non-creditable input sales tax incurred by KE in connection with the Project.”

This ensures KE is not economically exposed if input tax cannot be adjusted.

---

### 5. Section 5.8 – Withholding Tax  

**Existing wording (Section 5.8):**  
> “All payments… shall be made free and clear… unless SMTA is required to make a tax deduction…”

**Risk Identified:**  
This implicitly accepts possible applicability of withholding under section 153.

**Recommended replacement wording for Section 5.8:**

> “The Parties acknowledge and agree that payments under this Agreement are in the nature of reimbursement of costs incurred by KE and do not constitute consideration for sale of goods, rendering of services, or execution of a contract within the meaning of section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Accordingly, no withholding shall apply. In the event any deduction is required by a competent tax authority, SMTA shall gross-up the payment so that KE receives the full Project Cost in net terms.”

This protects both tax position and cash flow.

---

### 6. Annexure A – Transfer Agreement  

**Risk Identified:**  
The title “Transfer Agreement” creates concern. Any transfer of ownership may trigger supply of goods and withholding under section 153(1)(a).

**Recommended insertion in Article IV or Article V:**

> “Nothing contained in this Agreement or any annexure, including Annexure A, shall be construed as transferring, assigning, leasing, licensing, or otherwise creating any proprietary or beneficial interest in the Assets in favor of SMTA. Ownership of all relocated Assets shall at all times vest in KE.”

This eliminates transfer-based exposure.

---

### 7. Article VI – Implementation and SMTA Oversight  

**Risk Identified:**  
Extensive operational involvement of SMTA may support argument that KE is acting on behalf of SMTA.

**Recommended insertion at end of Article VI (first paragraph):**

> “SMTA’s involvement under this Article VI shall be limited to funding oversight and coordination and shall not alter the nature of the Project as relocation of KE’s own infrastructure.”

---

### Overall Tax Risk Position  

In its current wording, the Agreement carries moderate exposure to characterization as:

- Execution of contract under section 153(1)(c);  
- Construction/engineering service under provincial sales tax laws.

With the above refinements incorporated, the Agreement will more clearly support the position that:

- Payments represent reimbursement of capital cost;  
- No taxable supply is made to SMTA;  
- Section 153 withholding does not apply;  
- No sales tax is chargeable on the receipt.

The tax exposure here is not about economics — it is about drafting precision. A few sentences determine whether the transaction is seen as public infrastructure disturbance compensation or as a taxable works contract.

**Subject:** Clause-wise Tax Review and Recommended Amendments – SMTA Relocation Agreement  

Dear Mr. Musani,  

Further to your email and our earlier tax advice regarding the proposed relocation arrangement fileciteturn0file0, we have undertaken a detailed review of the updated draft Agreement dated 31 January 2026 fileciteturn1file0.  

While the commercial structure of the Agreement is generally consistent with the intended framework, certain clauses, if left unrefined, may create interpretational exposure under section 153(1)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (execution of contract) and under provincial sales tax laws relating to construction or engineering services.  

Our clause-specific observations and recommended refinements are set out below.

---

### 1. Recitals – Clarification of Commercial Substance  

The Recitals currently state that SMTA has requested KE to execute the scope of work and that KE has consented to execute the same. Although commercially accurate, this language may be construed as KE undertaking a works contract for SMTA. Such phrasing could be relied upon by tax authorities to argue that the arrangement constitutes execution of a contract for consideration, thereby attracting withholding tax under section 153 and possibly provincial sales tax.  

To mitigate this risk, an additional recital should be inserted expressly clarifying that the relocation is necessitated solely due to the Yellow Line alignment, that KE is undertaking relocation of its own infrastructure forming part of its Common Distribution System, and that SMTA’s payments represent reimbursement of costs incurred by KE rather than consideration for provision of works or services.  

An appropriate recital would state that the relocation is undertaken by KE to preserve its own regulated network and that no goods, services, or works are being supplied to SMTA.

---

### 2. Article IV – Scope of Work and Service Characterization Risk  

Article IV describes the Project in conventional EPC terminology (survey, engineering, construction, installation, commissioning, etc.). While operationally correct, this structure resembles a construction services contract. In isolation, it may support the view that KE is rendering engineering or construction services to SMTA.  

To align the Agreement with the intended tax characterization, a clarificatory paragraph should be added at the end of Article IV stating that the activities described therein relate exclusively to KE’s own assets and shall not be construed as construction, consulting, engineering, or other taxable services rendered to SMTA. It should also expressly confirm that the relocated assets shall at all times remain owned, operated, and controlled by KE and continue forming part of KE’s regulated transmission and distribution network.  

This clarification is essential to support the non-taxable reimbursement position.

---

### 3. Article V – Nature of Payments and Cost Reimbursement  

Article V currently provides for milestone-based advance payments and defines Project Cost broadly. Although commercially appropriate, milestone payments tied to defined scope may resemble consideration under a works contract.  

To mitigate this exposure, a specific clause should be inserted within Article V clarifying that all amounts payable by SMTA constitute reimbursement of actual costs incurred by KE in relocating its own infrastructure and do not represent consideration for sale of goods, rendering of services, or execution of works for SMTA.  

This explicit acknowledgment materially strengthens the defense against section 153 withholding and sales tax exposure.

---

### 4. Section 5.8 – Withholding Tax Provisions  

Section 5.8 presently allows deduction of withholding tax if required under applicable law, subject to recovery rights. While commercially pragmatic, this formulation weakens the interpretational position that section 153 does not apply in the first place.  

To reinforce the intended tax position, Section 5.8 should be refined to expressly state that payments under the Agreement are in the nature of cost reimbursement and are not subject to withholding under section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Additionally, a gross-up mechanism should be included to ensure that, in the event any deduction is imposed by a tax authority, KE receives the full Project Cost in net terms.  

Such drafting preserves economic neutrality and prevents downstream disputes.

---

### 5. Definition of “Project Cost” – Inclusion of Non-Adjustable Taxes  

Although the definition of Project Cost includes Taxes, it does not expressly address non-adjustable input sales tax incurred by KE on contractor invoices. Given that the receipts from SMTA are intended to be non-taxable, KE may not be able to adjust such input tax under the normal input-output mechanism.  

To avoid KE being economically out-of-pocket, the definition of Project Cost should be amended to expressly include all federal and provincial taxes, including non-adjustable input sales tax incurred by KE in connection with the Project. This ensures that the entire tax burden is funded by SMTA as part of the relocation cost.

---

### 6. Annexure A – Transfer Agreement  

The reference to a “Transfer Agreement” in Annexure A requires careful review. Any provision implying transfer of ownership, leasehold rights, or beneficial interest in the relocated assets to SMTA could fundamentally alter the tax characterization. Such transfer could potentially trigger sales tax on supply of goods and withholding under section 153(1)(a).  

It is therefore critical to ensure that Annexure A does not provide for transfer of ownership or proprietary rights in favor of SMTA. For additional protection, a clarification may be inserted within Article IV stating that nothing in the Agreement or its annexures shall be construed as transferring ownership or creating any proprietary or beneficial interest in the assets in favor of SMTA.

---

### 7. Article VI – Implementation and SMTA Involvement  

Article VI provides for Steering Committee oversight and SMTA involvement. While governance oversight is reasonable, excessive operational characterization may inadvertently support the argument that KE is executing a project for SMTA.  

A clarificatory statement may therefore be inserted specifying that SMTA’s role is limited to funding oversight and coordination, and does not alter the nature of the Project as relocation of KE’s own infrastructure.

---

### Overall Risk Position  

In its current form, the Agreement carries moderate exposure to characterization as a works contract under section 153(1)(c) and potentially as a taxable service under provincial sales tax laws.  

With the targeted refinements outlined above—particularly strengthening the reimbursement narrative, clarifying ownership retention, and refining the withholding clause—the Agreement can be more robustly defended as:  

- A cost recovery arrangement;  
- A capital reimbursement rather than revenue receipt;  
- Outside the scope of section 153; and  
- Outside the definition of taxable supply under applicable sales tax regimes.  

We would be pleased to provide a consolidated mark-up incorporating the above refinements for circulation with the legal team.  

Please let us know a suitable time for discussion.  

Kind regards,  

Zuhair  
Partner – Tax Advisory

Based on the attached material fileciteturn0file0, here are four more interactive and eye-catching social media headlines with engaging explanations:

---

### 🚨 “Pay Tax Twice?” Businesses Stuck Between Pakistan & AJK Tax Authorities

Imagine paying your tax properly… and then receiving another demand for the same transaction from a different authority.

That’s exactly what businesses dealing between Pakistan and AJK are facing. FBR has now clarified that it cannot intervene because AJK’s tax authority operates independently. The result? Jurisdictional confusion, double withholding demands, and compliance stress for genuine taxpayers. Until a coordinated solution is introduced, cross-border trade within our own territory remains legally uncertain.

---

### ⚖️ FTO Speaks Clearly: “We Don’t Decide Your Tax Bill”

Many taxpayers believe the Federal Tax Ombudsman can cancel or reduce their tax liability. The FTO has now clarified — it is not a court and cannot determine tax payable.

In a case related to net metering taxation, the FTO stated its role is limited to addressing maladministration, not rewriting tax laws or revising assessments. For the general public, this is crucial: disputes about tax amount must go through appeals, not Ombudsman complaints.

Understanding the right forum can save both time and frustration.

---

### 🏠 Property Buyers Get Relief — But FBR Revenue Drops 29%

Advance tax on property purchases has been reduced, and the impact is visible: FBR collection under this head has fallen by 29% in seven months.

For buyers on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL), this means lower upfront cost when purchasing property. However, non-filers still face very high rates. The government is clearly trying to stimulate the real estate market — but the big question remains: can revenue targets survive long term if rates continue to fall?

This is a classic balance between relief and revenue.

---

### 🔍 Green Channel Under Watch After Rs 14 Million Customs Fraud

**Technical Note**  
**E&P Companies Opting for 40% Rate under Paragraph (4A) of Fifth Schedule – Position on Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C**

This note examines the tax position of petroleum exploration and production (E&P) companies that exercised the option under paragraph (4A) of the Fifth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, to pay tax at the rate of forty percent of profits and gains, net of royalty, from Tax Year 2012 onward, and the implications of levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C in light of the recent Supreme Court judgment dated 27 January 2026.

1. Legal Framework of Paragraph (4A) – Forty Percent Regime  

Paragraph (4A) of the Fifth Schedule introduced a one-time irrevocable option whereby an E&P undertaking could elect, from Tax Year 2012 onward, to pay tax at 40% of profits and gains, net of royalty. The option was conditional upon withdrawal of pending litigation relating to tax rate disputes and payment of outstanding liabilities up to Tax Year 2011 by 30 June 2012. Once exercised, the option became irrevocable.

This provision effectively settled historical disputes regarding applicable tax rates under various Petroleum Concession Agreements (PCAs) and established a fixed statutory rate regime for those opting companies. The 40% regime therefore became the governing income tax rate for such E&P companies, read with the Fifth Schedule framework.

2. Nature of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C  

Section 4B (introduced through Finance Act 2015) imposed Super Tax as an additional tax on income. Section 4C (introduced via Finance Act 2022) imposed Super Tax on high earning persons and companies, subsequently amended to enhance rates.

The Supreme Court has now held both Sections 4B and 4C to be constitutionally valid and enforceable. Importantly, it has clarified that Section 4C is a standalone levy on income, independent of Section 4 of the Ordinance. Therefore, as a matter of general principle, Super Tax is an additional charge over and above normal income tax.

3. Crucial Qualification for E&P Companies under Fifth Schedule  

While upholding the vires of Sections 4B and 4C, the Supreme Court made a critical distinction in respect of E&P companies governed by the Fifth Schedule and PCAs. The Court held that Sections 4B and 4C shall apply to E&P companies only to the extent that their application does not result in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes provided in the Fifth Schedule and respective PCAs.

Further, it was expressly held that Super Tax cannot be imposed where its application would cause taxation to exceed the threshold stipulated in Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule. The Court recognized that the Fifth Schedule establishes a sector-specific fiscal regime reflecting the contractual and legislative understanding applicable to petroleum operations. That safeguard cannot be overridden absent clear legislative intent.

4. Position of Companies Opting for 40% under Paragraph (4A)  

For E&P companies that exercised the option under paragraph (4A), the 40% rate represents a negotiated and statutorily entrenched tax rate governing profits and gains net of royalty. Since the option was irrevocable and conditional upon withdrawal of litigation, it constituted a binding fiscal settlement under the Fifth Schedule regime.

The key issue therefore is whether levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C, when added to the 40% rate, results in exceeding the aggregate tax ceiling envisaged under the Fifth Schedule read with the relevant PCA and the Regulation of Mines & Minerals (Government Control) Act, 1948.

In light of the Supreme Court’s findings, the following principles emerge:

• Super Tax is generally valid and applicable.  
• However, in the case of E&P companies governed by the Fifth Schedule, it cannot operate so as to increase the aggregate tax burden beyond the permissible ceiling.  
• The determination must be undertaken in a PCA-specific manner, examining the contractual tax cap and statutory framework.  

Therefore, for companies that opted for the 40% regime, if the 40% rate already represents the aggregate tax ceiling contemplated under their PCA and Fifth Schedule framework, imposition of Super Tax would result in exceeding the permissible threshold. In such circumstances, Super Tax would not be enforceable to the extent of such excess.

5. Practical Interpretation  

If an E&P company under paragraph (4A):

– is already paying 40% of profits and gains net of royalty; and  
– that 40% represents the maximum aggregate tax incidence permissible under its PCA and Fifth Schedule framework;  

then Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C cannot legally increase the overall tax burden beyond that ceiling.

However, where the 40% rate does not exhaust the aggregate tax cap (for example, depending on the specific PCA wording or whether the cap refers only to “income tax” and not “additional tax”), a detailed contractual and statutory analysis would be required.

6. Conclusion  

The Supreme Court judgment has closed the constitutional debate but preserved the Fifth Schedule ceiling for E&P companies. For those who opted for the 40% regime under paragraph (4A), Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C is not automatically payable. Its enforceability depends on whether the aggregate tax burden, after including Super Tax, exceeds the permissible ceiling under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule read with the applicable PCA and governing mining legislation.

Accordingly, the position of each opting E&P company must be evaluated on a contract-specific basis. Where the 40% rate already represents the maximum aggregate tax incidence, Super Tax cannot legally be imposed in addition thereto.

The decisive question is no longer whether Super Tax is valid in abstract, but whether its application breaches the sector-specific fiscal ceiling that the Legislature itself has chosen to preserve.

Dear [Name],  

We have carefully reviewed the short order dated 27 January 2026 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 1243 of 2020 and connected matters concerning the levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Since United Energy Pakistan Limited operates as an E&P company under the Fifth Schedule and its respective Petroleum Concession Agreements (PCAs), the judgment is particularly relevant to your tax position.

Any challenge to the legislative competence or constitutional vires of Section 4B now stands settled against taxpayers. Consequently, the levy of Super Tax under Section 4B is legally sustained, subject only to proper computation under the applicable statutory framework.  

With respect to Section 4C, the Court has similarly declared the provision to be intra vires and applicable from Tax Year 2022 onwards at the prescribed rates fileciteturn1file9L46-L54. The earlier view of certain High Courts that Section 4C was not applicable to Tax Year 2022 has been expressly set aside fileciteturn1file4L17-L30. The Supreme Court has further clarified that Section 4C constitutes a standalone tax on income, independent of the normal charge under Section 4 of the Ordinance fileciteturn1file4L48-L54. This effectively means that Super Tax under Section 4C is legally enforceable from Tax Year 2022 onward, including at the enhanced rates introduced through subsequent Finance Acts.  

However, and most importantly for UEP, the Court has provided a crucial qualification in respect of E&P companies governed by the Fifth Schedule and PCAs. The judgment clearly holds that Sections 4B and 4C shall apply to E&P companies only to the extent that their application does not result in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes provided in the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCAs fileciteturn1file3L8-L16. It has further been clarified that Section 4C shall not apply to E&P companies where its application would cause taxation to exceed the threshold stipulated in Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule fileciteturn1file6L9-L17.  

In essence, while the constitutional challenge to Super Tax has been decided against taxpayers, the statutory ceiling embedded in the Fifth Schedule remains fully intact. The Supreme Court has recognized that petroleum operations are governed by a sector-specific fiscal regime, and that Super Tax cannot override or frustrate this legislative safeguard. Accordingly, the liability of UEP cannot be determined in isolation but must be computed in the context of the aggregate tax cap under Rule 4 read with the applicable PCA.  

The Court has also directed that the Commissioner Inland Revenue must undertake a fresh determination of liability in respect of each E&P company by examining the terms and conditions of its respective PCA alongside the applicable tax law fileciteturn1file3L16-L24. This provides an important procedural protection. Any recovery action must be preceded by a PCA-based assessment and an opportunity of hearing. Liability, therefore, is not automatic and must be technically evaluated in light of the Fifth Schedule framework.  

In practical terms, UEP’s exposure will now depend on a year-wise computation of aggregate effective tax rates for Tax Years 2022 onwards. Where the combined incidence of normal tax and Super Tax remains within the Fifth Schedule ceiling, the levy may be sustained. However, to the extent that imposition of Super Tax results in exceeding the prescribed aggregate threshold, such excess would not be legally enforceable in light of the Supreme Court’s express findings.  

The constitutional phase of litigation has effectively concluded. The matter now transitions from vires to technical computation and application of the Fifth Schedule cap. We recommend an immediate internal review of year-wise tax computations, segregation of Fifth Schedule income from any other income streams, and preparation of a detailed PCA-aligned submission in anticipation of fresh proceedings by the tax authorities.

**Technical Note**  
**E&P Companies Opting for 40% under Paragraph (4A) – Impact of Subsequent PCA Amendments and Levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B & 4C**

This note examines the position of petroleum exploration and production (E&P) companies that exercised the one-time irrevocable option under paragraph (4A) of the Fifth Schedule to pay tax at 40% of profits and gains, net of royalty, from Tax Year 2012 onward, and whose respective Petroleum Concession Agreements (PCAs) were subsequently amended to reflect this election. The analysis considers the impact of levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 in light of the recent Supreme Court judgment dated 27 January 2026.

1. Effect of Exercising the One-Time Option under Paragraph (4A)  

Paragraph (4A) introduced a legislative settlement mechanism. An E&P company could irrevocably opt to pay tax at 40% of profits and gains net of royalty from Tax Year 2012 onward, subject to withdrawal of pending litigation and settlement of outstanding liabilities up to Tax Year 2011. The option was expressly stated to be one-time and irrevocable.

Importantly, in practice, once this option was exercised, the respective PCAs were amended to align with the revised fiscal regime. The tax rate and related fiscal terms were contractually embedded into the amended PCA framework. Therefore, the 40% regime did not remain merely a statutory rate; it became part of the contractual fiscal bargain between the State and the E&P undertaking.

This has material legal consequences. The fiscal terms governing income tax for such companies now stand not only under the Fifth Schedule but also contractually entrenched through amended PCAs.

2. Nature of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C  

Section 4B (introduced through Finance Act 2015) and Section 4C (introduced via Finance Act 2022 and subsequently amended) impose Super Tax as an additional levy on income. The Supreme Court has upheld the constitutional validity of both provisions and has clarified that Section 4C is a standalone tax on income, independent of the normal charge under Section 4.

Therefore, as a matter of general law, Super Tax is an additional charge over and above normal income tax. However, that general principle is subject to the special regime applicable to E&P companies under the Fifth Schedule and their PCAs.

3. Supreme Court’s Qualification for E&P Companies  

While upholding Sections 4B and 4C, the Supreme Court categorically held that their application to E&P companies is subject to an overriding limitation. The levy cannot operate so as to cause taxation to exceed the aggregate rate of taxes provided under the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCAs. The Court further clarified that Super Tax cannot be imposed to the extent that it breaches the threshold stipulated in Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule.

The Court recognized that petroleum operations are governed by a sector-specific fiscal regime, reflecting high-risk, capital-intensive investment structures. That legislative safeguard cannot be nullified by imposing an additional levy that overrides the agreed tax ceiling.

4. Position Where PCAs Were Amended After Exercising 40% Option  

Where an E&P company exercised the one-time option under paragraph (4A), and the PCA was subsequently amended to reflect the 40% rate as the governing income tax rate, the fiscal position becomes even stronger.

In such cases:

– The 40% rate is not merely a statutory election; it forms part of the amended contractual framework between the State and the contractor.  
– The amended PCA reflects the negotiated fiscal equilibrium post-settlement of historical disputes.  
– The tax ceiling must therefore be interpreted in light of both the Fifth Schedule and the amended PCA terms.  

If the amended PCA embeds 40% as the applicable income tax rate and contemplates that as the effective aggregate fiscal incidence on profits (net of royalty), then any additional Super Tax that increases the effective burden beyond that ceiling would conflict with both:

(a) Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule; and  
(b) The amended contractual fiscal regime under the PCA.  

In light of the Supreme Court’s clear finding that Super Tax cannot override the Fifth Schedule ceiling, its application in such circumstances would be legally unsustainable to the extent of excess.

5. Practical Interpretation  

For E&P companies that:

– exercised the one-time irrevocable option in 2012;  
– amended their PCAs accordingly; and  
– are already subject to 40% tax on profits and gains net of royalty;  

the key question is whether imposition of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C would cause the aggregate tax incidence to exceed the permissible ceiling under the Fifth Schedule read with the amended PCA.

If the answer is yes, then in view of the Supreme Court judgment, Super Tax cannot be enforced to that extent.

6. Conclusion  

The Supreme Court has upheld the constitutional validity of Super Tax but has simultaneously preserved the fiscal ceiling applicable to E&P companies under the Fifth Schedule and their PCAs. For companies that opted for the 40% regime in 2012 and whose PCAs were subsequently amended to reflect that election, the fiscal position is contractually and statutorily anchored.

Accordingly, Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C is not automatically payable in addition to the 40% regime. Its enforceability depends on whether the aggregate tax burden, after inclusion of Super Tax, exceeds the ceiling under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule as read with the amended PCA and governing mining legislation.

The legal landscape after the Supreme Court’s decision is therefore not a blanket imposition of Super Tax on E&P companies, but a ceiling-based, PCA-specific determination. The decisive question is not whether Super Tax exists, but whether it can operate without breaching the fiscal bargain embedded in the amended PCA framework.
