Dear [Name],  

We have carefully reviewed the short order dated 27 January 2026 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Appeal No. 1243 of 2020 and connected matters, authored by the Hon’ble Chief Justice Mr. Justice Amin-ud-Din Khan. The judgment conclusively decides the vires and applicability of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, including its specific application to oil and gas exploration and production (E&P) companies such as United Energy Pakistan Limited.  

Below is our detailed analysis of the discussion and final conclusions of the Court, particularly as they relate to the E&P sector.

1. Background and Scope of Adjudication  

The Supreme Court clubbed multiple appeals and transfer cases involving challenges to:  

– Section 4B (Super Tax for rehabilitation of IDPs, introduced via Finance Act 2015), and  
– Section 4C (Super Tax on High Earning Persons, introduced via Finance Act 2022 and subsequently amended).  

Importantly, the Court expressly noted that the judgment also determines the applicability of these provisions to income arising to oil exploration and petroleum companies assessed under their respective Petroleum Concession Agreements (PCAs) fileciteturn1file7L23-L40.  

2. Findings on Section 4B (Applicable from Tax Year 2015 onwards)  

The Court unequivocally upheld Section 4B as intra vires the Constitution and declared it to be a valid tax on income falling within Entry 47 of the Fourth Schedule fileciteturn1file9L4-L10.  

The Court rejected arguments that it was discriminatory or beyond legislative competence and confirmed that it validly applies from Tax Year 2015 onwards at the prescribed rates.  

For UEP, this means that any constitutional challenge to Section 4B stands finally settled against taxpayers.

3. Findings on Section 4C – Constitutionality and Retrospective Application  

The Supreme Court held Section 4C to be intra vires and applicable from Tax Year 2022 onwards at the rates prescribed in Division IIB fileciteturn1file9L46-L54.  

Significantly, the Court set aside the High Courts’ view that Section 4C could not apply to Tax Year 2022. It held that the legislature is competent to enact retrospective fiscal legislation, and there is no bar in the Ordinance preventing such imposition where returns had not yet been filed fileciteturn1file4L17-L30.  

Further, the Court affirmed that Section 4C is a standalone, self-contained tax on income, independent of Section 4 fileciteturn1file4L48-L54.  

Accordingly, Super Tax under Section 4C validly applies from Tax Year 2022 onwards, including at amended rates for Tax Year 2023 (Finance Act 2023).  

4. Crucial Findings for E&P Companies (Including UEP)  

This is the most material portion for UEP.  

The Court specifically addressed the application of Sections 4B and 4C to E&P companies operating under the Fifth Schedule and PCAs. It held:  

– Sections 4B and 4C shall apply to E&P companies, but  
– Only to the extent that their application does not result in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes provided in the Fifth Schedule and respective PCAs fileciteturn1file3L8-L16.  

Further, the Court categorically ruled that Section 4C shall not apply to E&P companies to the extent that its application would result in taxation exceeding the threshold stipulated in Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule fileciteturn1file6L9-L17.  

The Court emphasized that Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule represents a sector-specific legislative safeguard recognizing the unique risks and capital intensity of petroleum operations. Any super tax that overrides this ceiling would be inconsistent with the statutory scheme fileciteturn1file6L12-L23.  

At the same time, the Court clarified that Section 4C will apply to other income of E&P companies from sources falling under sub-sections (i), (ii), and (iii) of Section 4C(2) fileciteturn1file6L1-L4.  

Importantly, the Court directed that:  

– The Commissioner Inland Revenue must first determine the E&P company’s liability,  
– Undertake a PCA-specific assessment by placing the PCA terms in juxtaposition with applicable tax laws, and  
– Issue a fresh notice after affording opportunity of hearing before recovery fileciteturn1file3L16-L24.  

5. Practical Conclusion for United Energy Pakistan Limited  

In light of the above, the position for UEP can be summarized as follows:  

a. Constitutional Challenge Concluded  
The vires of Sections 4B and 4C stand finally upheld. The legal ground challenging legislative competence is no longer sustainable.  

b. Section 4C Applies from Tax Year 2022  
Super Tax under Section 4C validly applies from Tax Year 2022 onward, including at enhanced rates introduced by subsequent Finance Acts.  

c. Sectoral Protection Remains for PCA Income  
For income governed by the Fifth Schedule and UEP’s specific PCA, Super Tax cannot push the aggregate tax burden beyond the ceiling stipulated in Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule. This is a significant protective finding.  

d. Case-by-Case Determination Required  
The Department must undertake a PCA-specific determination. Liability is not automatic; it must be computed in the context of the contractual and statutory tax ceiling applicable to UEP.  

e. Other Non-PCA Income  
Any income of UEP not governed by Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule (for example, ancillary income streams) may fall fully within Section 4C without the benefit of the Fifth Schedule ceiling.  

6. Recommended Way Forward  

In view of the judgment, we recommend:  

– Immediate recalculation of effective tax rate for each relevant tax year vis-à-vis Rule 4 Fifth Schedule ceiling;  
– Segregation of PCA-governed income and other income streams;  
– Review of pending assessment or recovery proceedings in light of the Supreme Court’s direction for fresh determination;  
– Preparation for detailed PCA-based submissions before the CIR to ensure the aggregate rate cap is strictly enforced.  

The Supreme Court has closed the constitutional chapter but preserved a technically robust and contractually anchored defense for E&P companies under the Fifth Schedule framework. The battle now shifts from “vires” to “computation and ceiling application.”  

We will be pleased to prepare a year-wise exposure matrix and strategy note for ongoing and future proceedings in light of this judgment.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Designation]  
[Your Firm Name]

Subject: Supreme Court Order – Levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C – United Energy Pakistan Limited  

Dear [Name],  

We write to apprise you of the recent order passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Appeal No. 1243 of 2020 (authored by Mr. Justice Amin-ud-Din Khan), wherein the matter relating to levy of Super Tax under Sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 has been adjudicated.  

The Hon’ble Court has upheld the constitutional validity of the levy of Super Tax under Section 4B, as originally introduced for rehabilitation of temporarily displaced persons, and has also examined the subsequent legislative framework under Section 4C, which imposed Super Tax on high-earning persons and companies. The judgment affirms the competence of Parliament to levy such tax under the Constitution, including its application to specified income thresholds and corporate taxpayers.  

In practical terms, the decision reinforces the enforceability of Super Tax under both Sections 4B and 4C for the relevant tax years covered by the amendments. For E&P companies such as United Energy Pakistan Limited, which typically fall within the higher income brackets prescribed under Section 4C, the exposure remains significant, particularly considering the graduated rates introduced through subsequent Finance Acts.  

It is important to note that the Court’s findings may materially impact ongoing assessment proceedings, pending appeals, and positions taken in returns for the affected tax years. The revenue authorities are likely to rely upon this judgment in support of demands raised or proceedings initiated under Sections 4B and 4C.  

We recommend that a detailed impact assessment be undertaken for each relevant tax year to evaluate:  

– Quantum of exposure (including principal tax, default surcharge under Section 205, and potential penalties);  
– Status of ongoing litigation or appellate proceedings; and  
– Whether any protective claims, rectification applications, or accounting adjustments may be warranted in light of the ruling.  

We will be pleased to arrange a discussion to walk through the judgment in detail and align on the way forward from a compliance and litigation strategy perspective.  

Kind regards,

Hi Jan,  

Further to my earlier email, I would like to clarify two important procedural aspects which are practically critical in Pakistan.

As discussed, based on Article 7 of the Pakistan–Italy Convention fileciteturn0file1, the payments to RINA would constitute business profits taxable only in Italy, provided no Permanent Establishment is created in Pakistan. In such a case, Pakistan should not have the right to tax the income and, strictly from a treaty perspective, no withholding would be required.

However, from a practical remittance standpoint, the position is more nuanced. Under Pakistani tax law, the payer acts as a withholding agent, and the State Bank of Pakistan generally does not allow outward remittance unless tax has been deducted at source or the withholding agent holds a valid exemption certificate. In practice, banks require evidence that either withholding has been made or that an exemption / lower deduction certificate has been issued by the Commissioner Inland Revenue.

Therefore, even though obtaining an exemption certificate is not legally mandatory in treaty cases—because treaty protection can be claimed directly—remittance without deduction in the absence of a certificate may become operationally problematic. To avoid delays or objections at the time of remittance, we recommend applying for an exemption certificate before the Commissioner Inland Revenue under section 159 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, clearly invoking Article 7 of the treaty and confirming that no PE exists in Pakistan. This provides administrative comfort both to the company and the bank handling the foreign remittance.

In parallel, we should ensure that:

– A valid Italian Tax Residency Certificate is obtained from RINA.  
– Written confirmation is secured that no personnel will be present in Pakistan beyond the three-month threshold under Article 5(2)(i) fileciteturn0file1.  
– The contract reflects that services are primarily rendered from Italy and no fixed place or services PE is intended.

Separately, for Sindh Sales Tax purposes, the position is different. Since RINA is a non-resident service provider and the recipient (EETL) is located in Sindh, the reverse charge mechanism would apply. Accordingly, the liability to pay Sindh Sales Tax would rest with the resident recipient of the services. EETL would be required to discharge the applicable Sindh Sales Tax under reverse charge and report it in the relevant Sindh Revenue Board return, subject to input tax adjustment eligibility, if applicable.

In summary, while the treaty position supports non-taxability in Pakistan in absence of a PE, we recommend proactively obtaining an exemption certificate to ensure smooth remittance through banking channels and to mitigate any withholding compliance exposure.  

Please let me know if you would like us to proceed with preparing the exemption application along with the supporting treaty analysis and documentation checklist.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

Hi Jan,

Thank you for your email. I have reviewed the technical proposal issued by RINA Consulting S.p.A. for “Technical Assistance for FSRU Exquisite Exchange” fileciteturn0file0 together with the Pakistan–Italy Double Taxation Convention, 1984 fileciteturn0file1. Based on the scope described in the proposal—namely review of manoeuvring simulation studies, HAZID and QRA reviews, and potentially real-time navigation simulations and risk assessments—the services clearly fall within the category of engineering and technical consultancy services. There is no transfer of intellectual property, no right to use equipment, and no licensing of any patent, process, design, or know-how as such.

From a treaty perspective, the first issue is characterization of income. Article 12 of the Pakistan–Italy Convention defines royalties as consideration for the use of, or the right to use, copyright, patent, trademark, design, secret formula or process, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, or information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience fileciteturn0file1. In the present case, RINA is not granting any right to use its intellectual property or equipment; it is rendering technical studies and issuing reports. Therefore, the payments do not qualify as “royalties” under Article 12. The income is more appropriately characterized as business profits under Article 7 of the Convention fileciteturn0file1.

Under Article 7, the business profits of an Italian enterprise are taxable only in Italy unless the enterprise carries on business in Pakistan through a Permanent Establishment (PE) fileciteturn0file1. Accordingly, Pakistan can tax the income only if a PE of RINA is constituted in Pakistan. Article 5 of the Convention is therefore critical. In particular, Article 5(2)(i) provides that the furnishing of services, including consultancy services, in Pakistan through employees or other personnel will constitute a PE where such activities continue for the same or a connected project for a period or periods aggregating more than three months fileciteturn0file1.

Based on the proposal, most activities appear to be desk-based and performed from RINA’s home office in Italy, with workshops possibly conducted via videoconference. There is no explicit reference to prolonged on-site presence in Pakistan. If the services are performed entirely outside Pakistan and RINA’s personnel do not remain in Pakistan for an aggregate period exceeding three months in relation to this project, no PE should arise. In that case, by virtue of Article 7, Pakistan would not have the right to tax the income. Conversely, if RINA’s personnel are physically present in Pakistan and the aggregate duration exceeds the three-month threshold, a services PE risk would arise and the income attributable to such PE would become taxable in Pakistan.

From a domestic law perspective, payments to non-residents for technical services ordinarily attract withholding tax under section 152 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. However, treaty provisions override domestic law to the extent they are more beneficial to the taxpayer. Where RINA is a tax resident of Italy (supported by a valid Tax Residency Certificate) and no PE is created in Pakistan, the treaty position would prevail and withholding in Pakistan should not apply to the business profits. Practically, this requires obtaining an Italian TRC, ensuring proper documentation of the treaty claim, and completing the necessary procedural compliance before remittance.

It is also relevant to note that the Convention expressly covers Pakistan income tax, super tax and surcharge fileciteturn0file1. Therefore, if Pakistan does not have taxing rights under Article 7 in the absence of a PE, no income tax or super tax exposure should arise in respect of these payments.

Separately, we should evaluate the indirect tax position. Depending on where the services are considered to be rendered and consumed, reverse charge implications under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 may need to be examined. This analysis would be independent of the DTT and will depend on the invoicing structure and place of performance.

In summary, subject to confirmation that RINA will not have a presence in Pakistan exceeding the three-month threshold and upon obtaining an Italian TRC, the payments should be treated as business profits taxable only in Italy under Article 7, with no Pakistani income tax withholding. I would recommend obtaining written confirmation from RINA regarding the absence and duration of any on-site presence and structuring the engagement documentation accordingly.

If required, I can prepare a brief internal advisory note for management summarizing the treaty position and outlining the compliance steps for remittance.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

Hi Jan,

Thank you for sharing the scope and the DTT. I have reviewed the technical proposal of RINA Consulting S.p.A. dated 5 February 2026 for “Technical Assistance for FSRU Exquisite Exchange” fileciteturn0file0 along with the Pakistan–Italy Double Taxation Convention (1984) fileciteturn0file1.

Based on the scope, the services include review of manoeuvring studies, HAZID and QRA reviews, and potentially real-time navigation simulation, risk assessment and safety studies. These are clearly technical / engineering consultancy services and do not involve transfer of any patent, process, or right to use equipment.

1. Characterization of income under the DTT

Under Article 12 of the Pakistan–Italy Convention, “royalties” cover payments for use of copyright, patent, trademark, design, secret formula, process, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, or information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience fileciteturn0file1.

In our case, RINA is not granting any right to use intellectual property or equipment. They are performing technical studies and issuing reports. Therefore, the payment does not qualify as “royalty” under Article 12.

Accordingly, the income falls under Article 7 (Business Profits) fileciteturn0file1.

2. Permanent Establishment (PE) exposure

Under Article 7, Italy has the exclusive right to tax business profits of an Italian enterprise unless it has a Permanent Establishment (PE) in Pakistan fileciteturn0file1.

Article 5 defines PE. Relevant here is the services clause in Article 5(2)(i), which creates a PE where services (including consultancy) are furnished in Pakistan for more than three months in aggregate for the same or connected project fileciteturn0file1.

From the proposal, most activities (Option 1 and even Option 2) appear to be performed from RINA’s home office in Italy, with workshops possibly via videoconference. There is no indication of site presence in Pakistan unless specifically required.

Therefore:

– If RINA performs all services from Italy (desk-based reviews, simulations, reports) without presence in Pakistan, no PE should arise.  
– If their personnel visit Pakistan and the aggregate presence exceeds 3 months for the same project, a services PE risk will arise.

You may confirm from RINA whether any physical presence in Pakistan is envisaged and, if so, expected duration.

3. Withholding tax position in Pakistan

Under domestic law, technical services to non-residents are generally subject to withholding under section 152 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

However, treaty provisions override domestic law to the extent they are more beneficial.

If:

– RINA is tax resident of Italy (TRC required), and  
– It does not create a PE in Pakistan,

then under Article 7, Pakistan has no taxing right, and the payment should not be subject to income tax in Pakistan.

In practice, this means:

– Obtain Italian Tax Residency Certificate (TRC).  
– File application for treaty relief with FBR (if required) before remittance.  
– Withhold at 0% under treaty protection, subject to procedural compliance.

If PE is triggered, then the income attributable to the PE would be taxable in Pakistan, and RINA would need to register and file return in Pakistan.

4. Super Tax implications

The treaty covers income tax, super tax and surcharge in Pakistan fileciteturn0file1. However, since Article 7 allocates taxing rights to Italy in absence of PE, Pakistan cannot impose income tax or super tax on such business profits if no PE exists.

5. Sales tax considerations

Separately from income tax:

– Since services are rendered by a non-resident and likely performed outside Pakistan, federal sales tax on services (reverse charge) may need to be examined depending on where the service is considered rendered and used.  
– Given EETL is engaged in LNG terminal operations, we need to confirm whether reverse charge under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 applies.

This is a separate analysis from the DTT and we can review it once we confirm invoicing structure.

6. Practical steps recommended

I recommend the following:

1. Obtain Italian TRC from RINA.  
2. Confirm in writing that no personnel will be stationed in Pakistan for more than 3 months (aggregate).  
3. Insert a clause in contract that services are rendered from Italy and no PE is intended in Pakistan.  
4. Apply treaty position before making remittance.

If you would like, I can prepare a short internal note summarizing the treaty position for your management and also draft a checklist for remittance compliance.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

Dear Amin Sb,  

Thank you for your email and for sharing the signed Contract for Engineering Consultancy Services executed between Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited and the consortium comprising Exponent Engineers (Pvt.) Limited (Lead Consultant) and RINA Consulting S.p.A. (Joint Venture Partner) fileciteturn0file0  

We have reviewed the contract, particularly the consortium structure and payment framework, and set out below our refined comments on the withholding tax implications.

RINA Consulting S.p.A. – Non-Resident (Italy)  

RINA Consulting S.p.A. is a non-resident entity incorporated in Italy and is providing specialized engineering consultancy services, including technical evaluation of conceptual designs, development of engineering designs, and preparation of cost estimates for the berth extension project. These services clearly fall within the scope of technical consultancy services.

From a treaty perspective, the Double Taxation Agreement between Pakistan and Italy does not contain a separate Article dealing specifically with “Fees for Technical Services.” In the absence of an FTS clause, such income is ordinarily examined under the Business Profits Article of the DTA. Under the treaty framework, Pakistan would have the right to tax such income only if RINA constitutes a Permanent Establishment (PE) in Pakistan within the meaning of the DTA. In the absence of a PE, taxation rights would typically rest with Italy.

However, from a withholding compliance standpoint, section 152(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 requires deduction of tax at source on payments to non-residents for services rendered. In the absence of an expressly reduced treaty rate applicable to such services, tax is required to be withheld at the rate prescribed under domestic law, i.e., 15%, subject to treaty relief.  

If RINA intends to claim protection under the Business Profits Article (on the basis of no PE in Pakistan), a formal application for treaty relief under section 152 read with section 107 of the Ordinance would be required, supported by a valid Tax Residency Certificate and relevant declarations. Until such exemption or reduced rate certificate is obtained from the Commissioner, the payer remains legally obliged to deduct tax at the applicable domestic rate.

Exponent Engineers (Pvt.) Limited – Resident Company  

Exponent Engineers (Pvt.) Limited, being a resident company in Pakistan and acting as the Lead Consultant under the consortium arrangement, is subject to withholding under section 153(1)(b) of the Ordinance in respect of payments for services.

Accordingly, tax is required to be deducted at the prescribed rate under Clause 2 of Division III, Part III of the First Schedule to the Ordinance, presently 15% for services, subject to active taxpayer status and any applicable adjustments. The tax deducted will be treated as adjustable against the final tax liability of Exponent Engineers.

Consortium Structure – Practical Withholding Considerations  

Although the contract is executed with the consortium, the tax treatment must follow the substance of payment allocation. Withholding should be applied separately on the portion of consideration attributable to each consortium member, in line with the contract price breakdown in foreign and local currency as reflected in the Appendices to the agreement.  

It is important that invoices are raised distinctly by each entity and that payments are made directly to the respective member to ensure proper characterization for withholding purposes. A consolidated payment without clear segregation may create unnecessary exposure or disputes at the time of audit.

Conclusion  

In summary:  

– Payments to RINA are subject to section 152 withholding at 15%, unless treaty relief is formally obtained on the basis of no PE in Pakistan.  
– Payments to Exponent Engineers are subject to section 153 withholding at 15% as adjustable tax.  
– Proper segregation of consideration between consortium members is essential for accurate compliance.

Please let us know if you would like us to assist in evaluating the PE exposure of RINA or in preparing a treaty relief application to optimize the withholding position.

Dear Amin Sb,  

We have carefully reviewed the Contract for Engineering Consultancy Services executed between Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited (FAP) and the consortium comprising Exponent Engineers (Pvt.) Limited (Lead Consultant) and RINA Consulting S.p.A. (Joint Venture Partner) fileciteturn0file0  

Set out below is a detailed discussion of the transaction from a legal and tax characterization perspective.

Nature of the Arrangement  

The agreement is structured as a consultancy contract for “Technical Consultancy for Extension in Berth – FAP Marine Terminal, Port Qasim, Karachi.” It is not an EPC contract, not a works contract, and not a supply of goods arrangement. The Consultants are engaged to provide engineering consultancy services, including design evaluation, development of engineering designs, and related professional advisory functions.

The contract clearly places the responsibility for execution of works, procurement, and construction outside the scope of the Consultants. The Consultants are responsible for intellectual and technical deliverables, not physical execution. This is critical because it confirms that the arrangement constitutes professional services rather than construction or turnkey execution.

Consortium / Joint Venture Structure  

The contract is executed with a consortium consisting of Exponent Engineers and RINA Consulting S.p.A., with Exponent designated as the Lead Consultant. The relevant clauses confirm that where the Consultants consist of more than one entity, they are jointly and severally liable to the Client for performance of the Contract.

This joint and several liability is important from a risk and tax perspective. Although the contract is signed collectively, the tax treatment must follow the economic allocation of consideration between the consortium members. The consortium itself does not appear to be incorporated as a separate legal entity in Pakistan. Therefore, payments must be examined at the level of each member.

In substance, this is a professional services consortium arrangement rather than a separately taxable joint venture entity, unless operationally a separate NTN or PE is created in Pakistan.

Scope of Services  

The scope includes:  
– Technical evaluation of conceptual designs  
– Development of engineering designs  
– Project cost estimation  
– Reporting and documentation deliverables  
– Professional advisory inputs  

The contract further provides that documents prepared by the Consultants become the property of the Client. This confirms that the output is intellectual property in the form of reports, engineering drawings, technical documentation, and consultancy advice.

The Consultants are required to maintain professional standards, indemnify the Client for negligence, and maintain insurance. These are typical attributes of a professional consultancy contract.

There is no transfer of tangible goods, no permanent transfer of proprietary technology, and no licensing of IP as a standalone transaction. The ownership of deliverables transfers to the Client as part of service performance, which supports characterization as technical consultancy services rather than royalty.

Payment Structure  

The contract contains appendices detailing breakdown of contract price in foreign currency and local currency. This indicates that part of the consideration is likely attributable to the foreign consortium member (RINA), and part to the local member (Exponent Engineers).

The remuneration is described as lump sum or milestone-based consultancy consideration, not reimbursement-only and not success-fee based. There are provisions for additional services and variation, but the base structure is service remuneration.

There is no indication that the Client is purchasing equipment or physical assets from the Consultants. Payments are strictly for professional services.

Governing Law and Location of Services  

The contract is governed by the laws of Pakistan. The services are to be performed at locations specified in Appendix A and as mutually agreed. However, the document does not automatically imply that all services are physically performed in Pakistan. It is common in such engineering arrangements that certain design and evaluation work is performed offshore.

This becomes relevant in analyzing Permanent Establishment exposure for RINA. If RINA’s personnel are physically present in Pakistan beyond treaty thresholds or if a fixed place of business exists, a PE risk may arise. If services are rendered predominantly offshore without a fixed place or dependent agent in Pakistan, treaty protection may apply.

Tax Characterization – Resident Member (Exponent Engineers)  

For Exponent Engineers (Pvt.) Limited, the characterization is straightforward. This is income from services under section 153(1)(b) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Withholding applies at the prescribed rate and the tax is adjustable.

From a sales tax perspective, this would also fall within the ambit of engineering consultancy services under provincial sales tax on services.

Tax Characterization – Non-Resident Member (RINA Consulting S.p.A.)  

For RINA, the characterization is technical consultancy services rendered to a Pakistani client. Under domestic law, section 152 applies to payments to non-residents for services.

From a treaty perspective (Pakistan–Italy DTA), there is no specific “Fees for Technical Services” Article. Therefore, the income would generally fall under Business Profits. Pakistan can tax such income only if RINA has a Permanent Establishment in Pakistan.

The key practical question is whether RINA’s activities create:  
– A fixed place PE  
– A service PE (depending on treaty language and duration thresholds)  
– A dependent agent PE  

This requires factual evaluation of personnel deployment, duration of presence in Pakistan, authority to conclude contracts, and nature of on-site supervision.

If no PE exists, treaty relief may be available, subject to procedural compliance.

Risk Considerations  

There are several technical risk points in this structure:

First, joint and several liability may cause authorities to argue that the consortium is operating as a unified enterprise in Pakistan. Clear invoicing and allocation of scope between Exponent and RINA is therefore essential.

Second, if RINA personnel visit Pakistan for extended periods for supervision or meetings, PE risk may increase.

Third, from a sales tax perspective, the place of supply and reverse charge implications must be reviewed if services are rendered from abroad.

Substance of the Transaction  

In economic substance, this is a pure engineering consultancy arrangement involving:

– Intellectual and professional services  
– Design and advisory outputs  
– No construction execution  
– No supply of equipment  
– No royalty licensing structure  

Therefore, it should be treated as professional consultancy services for tax purposes, not as royalty, not as construction contract, and not as supply of goods.

Conclusion  

The transaction is a structured engineering consultancy engagement under a consortium model, with joint and several liability but economically separable service components attributable to a resident and a non-resident member. The principal tax considerations revolve around withholding under sections 152 and 153, and Permanent Establishment exposure for the Italian entity.

If required, we can further prepare a structured note evaluating PE exposure, treaty position, and documentation strategy to mitigate withholding and audit risk.

Now we’re getting into the real mechanics of the law — and this is exactly where assumptions can become expensive.

You are absolutely right to question the earlier understanding. Under the Sindh Finance Act, 2025, the regime is no longer based on a limited positive list. The law now operates on a broad taxation principle: **all services are taxable unless specifically exempted in the First Schedule**.

Export status does **not** automatically grant exemption.

The exemption for export of services is not general in nature. It applies only to specific categories expressly mentioned in the Schedule (such as certain IT services, call center services, research services, etc.), and even those are subject to strict conditions including realization of foreign exchange through banking channels and SBP reporting.

Management consultancy services (generally falling under CPC 8311 / 83117 – business and management services) are **not included** in the specific export-exempt categories. Therefore, even if:

- The client is located outside Pakistan, and  
- Payment is received in foreign currency,

the transaction does not automatically qualify for exemption unless it falls within a specifically notified export category.

If the services are correctly classified as management consultancy, the default position under the amended law is that Sindh sales tax at **15%** would apply.

Below is a refined and corrected email draft reflecting this position:

---

**Subject:** Sindh Sales Tax Position – Management Consultancy Services Provided to Overseas Entity  

Dear [Client Name],  

Further to our discussion, we have revisited the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 and carefully reviewed the sales tax implications of classifying the proposed engagement as management consultancy services, generally falling under CPC 8311 / 83117 (business and management advisory services).

Under the revised Sindh Sales Tax on Services framework, the taxation model has materially changed. The law now applies on a broad-base principle whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempted in the First Schedule. The standard rate is 15%, unless a reduced or higher rate is expressly prescribed.

It is important to clarify that the concept of “export of services” does not automatically grant exemption from Sindh sales tax. Export-related exemptions are available only for specific service categories expressly mentioned in the Schedule, such as certain IT-enabled services and call center services, and are subject to realization of foreign exchange and regulatory compliance conditions.

Management consultancy services are not included within those specifically exempted export categories. Accordingly, even where the recipient is located outside Pakistan and payment is received in foreign currency through banking channels, the transaction would generally remain subject to Sindh sales tax if classified as management consultancy.

Based on the current understanding that the services fall within the management consultancy category, Sindh sales tax at the standard rate of 15% would apply.

We recommend reviewing the detailed scope of services and contractual wording before finalization, as classification will be determinative in confirming the final tax position.

Please share the draft agreement and service description so we may provide a conclusive view.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair  

---

In tax law, geography alone does not determine taxability — classification does. And classification, in turn, determines the outcome.

**Subject:** Sindh Sales Tax Implications – Management Consultancy Services for Overseas Client  

Dear [Client Name],  

We refer to your proposed arrangement for provision of management consultancy services to your overseas entity and have examined the implications under the Sindh Finance Act, 2025, which has significantly restructured the Sindh Sales Tax on Services regime effective 1 July 2025.

The amended framework has shifted Sindh from a positive list system to a broader taxation model whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempted. The standard rate remains 15%, subject to higher or reduced rates prescribed under the Second Schedule. Management consultancy services fall within the CPC classification relating to business and management services and, in principle, are chargeable to Sindh sales tax at the standard rate unless they qualify as export of services under the prescribed conditions.

In the context of services provided to an overseas client, the critical consideration is whether the transaction qualifies as export of services. For this purpose, it must be clearly established that:  

- the recipient of services is located outside Pakistan;  
- the services are used and consumed outside Pakistan; and  
- consideration is received in convertible foreign exchange through normal banking channels and appropriately reported to the State Bank of Pakistan.  

Proper documentation will be essential. The service agreement should explicitly identify the foreign entity as the contractual recipient, define the scope of services as being delivered for overseas operations, and clearly stipulate payment terms in foreign currency. Supporting records such as invoices, bank realization evidence, and remittance documentation must be maintained to substantiate export status in case of review by the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB).

If these conditions are fully satisfied, the transaction may qualify for export treatment under the Sindh Sales Tax law, thereby mitigating local sales tax exposure. However, if any element indicates local consumption or benefit within Sindh, the standard 15% sales tax would apply.

Given the broadened definition of taxable services and enhanced compliance scrutiny under the revised regime, we strongly recommend reviewing the draft agreement and billing structure before execution to ensure alignment with export criteria and to avoid unintended exposure.

Please share the draft engagement terms and proposed invoicing model so that we may conduct a detailed review and advise on the optimal structure from a Sindh sales tax perspective.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

- Issuance of SRB-compliant tax invoices;  
- Charging and depositing Sindh sales tax at 15% on the value of services; and  
- Filing of periodic sales tax returns in accordance with SRB regulations.

We would suggest that you share the draft agreement and detailed scope of services so that we may confirm the final classification and ensure the arrangement is structured in a tax-efficient and compliant manner from the outset.

Management consultancy (CPC 8311 / 83117 type business management services) general category ہے اور اس کیلئے blanket export exemption نہیں دی گئی۔

---

**Subject:** Sindh Sales Tax Position – Management Consultancy Services to Overseas Entity  

Dear [Client Name],  

Further to our earlier discussion, we have revisited the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 and carefully examined the sales tax implications of categorizing the proposed services as management consultancy falling under CPC 8311 / 83117 (business and management services).

Under the amended Sindh Sales Tax on Services framework, the taxation principle has materially changed. The law now operates on a broad-base approach whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempted in the First Schedule. The standard rate remains 15%, unless a higher or reduced rate is expressly prescribed.

Management consultancy services do not fall within the categories specifically exempted for export of services under the Act. While certain IT-enabled services, call center services, and specific technology-based services are granted export-related exemptions subject to foreign exchange realization and SBP reporting conditions, business management and advisory services are not covered within those exemption entries.

Accordingly, the mere fact that the recipient of services is located outside Pakistan does not automatically exempt the transaction from Sindh sales tax. Unless the service squarely falls within an explicitly exempt export category under the Schedule, the default position would be that Sindh sales tax at 15% is applicable.

Therefore, if the services are classified as management consultancy under CPC 8311 / 83117, the transaction would generally remain taxable, even if consideration is received in foreign exchange.

We recommend that we carefully review the scope of services and contractual characterization before finalizing the structure, as classification will be determinative in assessing the correct Sindh sales tax treatment.

Please share the draft agreement and service description so we may confirm the final tax position with precision.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

For proper appreciation of the issue, the relevant provisions may be summarized as follows:

- **Section 153(1)(a)** requires prescribed persons to deduct tax at source from payments for goods.  
- **Section 168(1)** provides that tax deducted at source shall be treated as tax paid on behalf of the person from whose income the deduction is made.  
- **Section 168(3)** stipulates that such tax shall be allowed as a credit against the tax liability of the person for the relevant tax year.  
- **Section 161(1)** empowers the Commissioner to treat a person as an assessee-in-default where tax required to be deducted has not been deducted or paid.  
- **Section 170(4)** authorizes the Commissioner to adjust any refund due to a person against any outstanding tax liability.  
- **Rule 42 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002** prescribes issuance of a certificate of deduction/collection of tax as evidence of tax deducted and paid.  
- **Section 165 read with Rule 44** requires furnishing of withholding statements to the Commissioner, forming the basis of system-based reconciliation and credit availability.

The statutory scheme therefore contemplates two essential conditions for allowability of credit to the deductee under section 168:

i. Tax must have been deducted in accordance with the Ordinance; and  
ii. Such tax must have been paid or credited to the Federal Government Treasury.

Subject: Preliminary View on 30% Investment Limit – Employees Contributory Fund  

Dear [Name],  

Further to our discussion regarding the 30% investment cap under the Employees Contributory Funds (Investment in Listed Securities) Regulations, 2018, I have carried out a preliminary reading of the relevant provisions.  

The Regulations provide that the limit is to be assessed “at the time of making investment” and restrict total investment in listed equity securities to thirty percent of the size of the Fund or Trust fileciteturn0file0. The term “size of Fund” is defined as total assets of the fund including realized profit fileciteturn0file0.  

Based on a plain reading, it appears that the 30% threshold should logically be tested on a fair value / NAV basis at the time a new investment decision is made. Since the “size of Fund” refers to total assets (which are determined on a current value basis), the exposure in listed equities should also be considered at current market value rather than historical cost to ensure consistency in the calculation.  

Accordingly, if the fair value of existing equity investments has increased due to market appreciation and exceeds 30%, this may not automatically constitute a breach, provided that at the time of making the last investment the exposure was within the prescribed limit. However, further investment in that category should not be made unless the exposure falls back within the threshold.  

That said, I would like to clarify that this view is based solely on a preliminary reading of the Rules, and this is not an area of my specialized expertise. Before drawing any firm conclusion or implementing any position, I would strongly recommend obtaining a formal opinion from a regulatory or capital markets expert. It would also be prudent to seek confirmation from the audit side to ensure alignment from a compliance and reporting perspective.  

Please let me know if you would like me to coordinate further discussions or obtain an external opinion.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

اور definition میں “size of Fund or Trust” کا مطلب ہے:

> total assets of the contributory fund or trust including realized profit at cutoff date fileciteturn0file0

اب یہاں دو چیزیں کلیدی ہیں:

1. **“at the time of making investment”**
2. **“size of Fund” (یعنی total assets)**

یہ ریگولیشن ongoing daily mark-to-market breach کو address نہیں کر رہا، بلکہ یہ “investment decision point” کو regulate کر رہا ہے۔

یعنی جب آپ نئی investment کر رہے ہیں، اُس وقت آپ کو دیکھنا ہے کہ:

- اُس وقت fund کا total asset size کیا ہے (عام طور پر latest NAV / total assets)
- اور اُس وقت equity (یا متعلقہ category) میں total exposure کتنا ہے

اور یہ exposure practical طور پر **current fair value / NAV basis** پر دیکھا جاتا ہے — نہ کہ historical cost پر۔

کیوں؟

کیونکہ “size of Fund” itself ایک dynamic concept ہے (total assets)، جو NAV پر based ہوتا ہے۔ اگر denominator fair value basis پر ہے تو numerator بھی fair value basis پر ہی logically assess کیا جائے گا۔ ورنہ mismatch ہو جائے گا۔

اب آپ کی مثال لیتے ہیں:

Fund size = 100 ارب  
Cost of equity investment = 10 ارب  
Fair value = 35 ارب  

اگر آپ آج نئی investment کر رہے ہیں تو سوال یہ ہوگا:

“اس وقت equity exposure کتنا ہے؟”

یہ exposure **market value basis** پر دیکھا جائے گا — یعنی 35 ارب۔

تو calculation ہو گی:

35 ÷ 100 = 35%

یعنی regulatory exposure 35% ہے — نہ کہ 10%۔

اب یہاں ایک اور subtle مگر اہم بات:

ریگولیشن کہتا ہے limit apply ہو گی **at the time of making investment**۔

اگر market appreciation کی وجہ سے exposure 30% سے اوپر چلا گیا ہے، تو:

- یہ automatically violation نہیں سمجھا جائے گا
- مگر آپ مزید investment نہیں کر سکتے جب تک exposure واپس permissible limit میں نہ آ جائے

یہ بالکل ویسا ہی ہے جیسے UCITS funds یا pension regulations میں ہوتا ہے — appreciation allowed ہے، fresh breach allowed نہیں۔

اگر کوئی آڈیٹر آپ سے پوچھے گا تو وہ یہی دیکھے گا:

1. جب آخری equity purchase ہوئی تھی اُس وقت exposure 30% سے کم تھا یا نہیں؟
2. current position appreciation کی وجہ سے exceed ہوئی یا deliberate additional investment سے؟

اگر appreciation کی وجہ سے 35% ہو گیا تو compliance maintained ہے، لیکن آپ مزید equity نہیں خرید سکتے۔

خلاصہ:

- 30% calculation **fair value / current NAV basis** پر ہوگی۔
- cost basis پر calculation کرنا regulatory intent کے خلاف ہے۔
- breach evaluate ہوگا investment decision date پر۔
- appreciation allowed ہے، active breach allowed نہیں۔

یہ وہ جگہ ہے جہاں ریگولیشن کا لفظی متن اور fund management کی معاشی منطق ایک دوسرے سے ملتے ہیں۔ قانون اکثر static لگتا ہے، مگر market dynamic ہے — اور regulator اس dynamic nature کو implicitly recognize کرتا ہے۔

اگر آپ چاہیں تو میں اس پر ایک concise technical note بھی draft کر سکتا ہوں جو آپ audit file میں رکھ سکیں۔

Subject: Preliminary View – 30% Investment Limit under Employees Contributory Fund Regulations  

Dear [Name],  

Further to our recent discussion regarding the 30% investment cap prescribed under the Employees Contributory Funds (Investment in Listed Securities) Regulations, 2018, I have revisited the relevant provisions for a preliminary assessment.  

The Regulations stipulate that the limit is to be tested “at the time of making investment” and that total investment in listed equity securities shall not exceed thirty percent of the size of the Fund or Trust fileciteturn0file0. The “size of Fund” is defined as total assets of the fund including realized profit fileciteturn0file0.  

On a plain reading, it appears that the 30% threshold should be evaluated on a fair value / NAV basis at the time of making a new investment. Since the size of the Fund is determined by reference to total assets (which are generally measured at current value), it would be consistent to assess the equity exposure at current market value rather than historical cost.  

Accordingly, where equity exposure has increased beyond 30% purely due to market appreciation, such increase may not, in itself, constitute a regulatory breach—provided that at the time of the last investment decision, the exposure was within the prescribed limit. However, in such circumstances, further investment in that category should not be undertaken unless and until the exposure falls back within the permissible threshold.  

That said, I would like to emphasize that the above understanding is based on a preliminary reading of the Rules, and this is not my core area of specialization. Before adopting any definitive position, it would be advisable to obtain a formal opinion from a regulatory or capital markets expert. I will also recheck this interpretation with our audit department to ensure alignment from a compliance and reporting perspective.  

Once I have feedback from the audit side, I will revert accordingly.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

parts:
This is a very important and practical regulatory question — and exactly the type auditors tend to raise.

Let’s go directly to the regulatory language.

Under the Employees Contributory Funds (Investment in Listed Securities) Regulations, 2018, Regulation 3 states:

> “Total investment, **at the time of making investment**, shall not exceed thirty per cent of the size of the Fund or Trust…” fileciteturn0file0

Further, “size of Fund or Trust” is defined as:

> total assets of the contributory fund or trust including realized profit at cutoff date fileciteturn0file0

Now, two phrases are critical:

1. **“at the time of making investment”**
2. **“size of Fund” (i.e., total assets)**

The regulation is clearly transaction-based — it regulates the decision point of making an investment, not daily mark-to-market movements.

The next question is: should the 30% limit be tested using cost or fair value?

The logical and regulatory interpretation is that the test should be applied on a **fair value / current NAV basis**, not historical cost. Here’s why:

- “Size of Fund” refers to total assets, which in practice is determined on NAV / fair value basis.
- If the denominator (fund size) is dynamic and fair value-based, the numerator (investment exposure) must also be evaluated at fair value. Otherwise, you create a mismatch and distort the exposure ratio.

Now applying your example:

Fund size = 100 billion  
Cost of equity investment = 10 billion  
Fair value of equity investment = 35 billion  

If you are evaluating compliance at the time of making a new investment, the exposure is:

35 ÷ 100 = 35%

Not:

10 ÷ 100 = 10%

Because regulatory exposure reflects economic exposure — and economic exposure is measured at current value.

However — and this is very important — the regulation says the limit applies **“at the time of making investment.”**

This means:

- If equity exposure has increased from 10% to 35% purely due to market appreciation, that does not automatically constitute a regulatory breach.
- But you cannot make further equity investments until the exposure falls back within the 30% threshold.

In other words:

Appreciation is not a violation.  
Active additional investment beyond the cap is.

This is consistent with global pension and fund regulations: limits restrict new allocations, not passive valuation movements.

If an auditor reviews this, they will typically test:

1. What was the exposure at the date of the last equity purchase?
2. Was it within 30% at that time?
3. Did any breach occur due to additional purchases, or only because of market movement?

Conclusion:

- The 30% cap should be assessed on a fair value / NAV basis.
- The test is applied at the time of making investment.
- Market appreciation beyond 30% does not automatically create a violation.
- Further investment is restricted until exposure falls within the limit.

This interpretation aligns both with the wording of the regulation and with sound risk-governance principles.

Hi Mazhar, hope you are doing well. 

Thank you for sharing the draft working and proposed commercial framework in respect of the silo development initiative. After undertaking a preliminary review of the proposed structure, we believe it would be commercially and fiscally prudent to first align on the preferred structural model with both FAP Terminal and the prospective investors before finalizing documentation. The tax outcome will depend fundamentally on how ownership, control, risk allocation, and return mechanics are ultimately structured. Accordingly, we outline below the principal structuring alternatives and their respective tax implications for consideration.

Option 1 – Investor-Owned Asset with Throughput-Based Compensation

Under this model, investors would legally own the silo assets during the agreed 10-year tenure, while FAP would operate and manage the facility. Investors would earn a fixed per-ton return strictly linked to actual throughput, and FAP would retain an option to acquire the assets at a commercially reasonable residual value after Year 8.

From a tax perspective, investors may be entitled to claim depreciation, provided ownership and asset risk are demonstrable in substance. The per-ton earnings would generally constitute business income in the hands of investors, potentially subject to withholding under section 153 depending on classification. FAP would treat the payments as deductible business expenditure. However, if the 90% cargo commitment effectively guarantees recovery of capital and return, the arrangement could be scrutinized as a finance lease in substance. Therefore, utilization risk must remain commercially genuine, and documentation must avoid any language suggesting guaranteed internal rate of return. Proper drafting will be critical to sustain this characterization.

Option 2 – Structured Finance Lease Arrangement

Alternatively, the transaction could be structured explicitly as a finance lease, whereby investors finance the construction and FAP is treated as lessee for tax purposes. Lease rentals would be payable over the term, with ownership transferring either at the end or through the agreed buy-back mechanism.

In such case, depreciation may shift to FAP if the lease is regarded as a finance lease under tax principles, and lease rentals would be deductible for FAP while investors would recognize rental income. This structure offers clarity and reduces recharacterization risk because the legal form would align with the economic substance; however, it removes the variable throughput-based risk-sharing element and converts the arrangement into a structured financing model.

Option 3 – Contractual Joint Development Model

A further alternative would be to structure the arrangement as a formal joint development agreement with defined revenue-sharing mechanics. However, this introduces higher complexity. There is potential risk of classification as an Association of Persons (AOP) if not carefully drafted, which would trigger separate tax compliance and profit allocation implications. This model increases audit exposure and administrative burden and should only be considered if there are strong commercial drivers.

Service Concession Overlay Consideration

Separately, it will be important to review FAP’s underlying concession agreement with PQA to confirm whether newly constructed silo infrastructure automatically forms part of concession assets or is subject to reversionary rights. If such regulatory overlay exists, it may influence the preferred structuring route and asset ownership position.

Recommended Way Forward

From a risk-managed tax perspective, the most sustainable structures appear to be either a clearly defined investor-owned asset model with genuine throughput risk or a straightforward FAP-owned asset model with volume commitments and commercial incentives. The hybrid approach, where capital recovery is economically assured yet labeled as throughput-based, poses the greatest recharacterization exposure.

We therefore recommend arranging a discussion to align on the intended economic substance, ownership preference, risk allocation, depreciation entitlement, withholding exposure, and exit mechanics. Once the commercial objective is clearly crystallized, we can refine the documentation to ensure the tax treatment aligns with substance and remains defensible.

Subject: Proposed Silo Investment Structure – Detailed Tax Analysis and Recommended Structuring Approach  

Dear Mazhar,  

Thank you for your patience. After carefully reviewing the commercial framework shared, I am setting out below a more structured and reasoned analysis of the tax position, focusing on substance, defensibility, and risk mitigation.

1. Fundamental Principle – Substance Over Form  

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the tax treatment of an arrangement depends on its real economic substance rather than the label assigned to it. Therefore, describing the arrangement as a “project investment model” does not by itself determine its tax character. The decisive factors will be:

– Who bears commercial and utilization risk?  
– Who has control over the asset?  
– Who is economically assured recovery of capital?  
– Whether return is contingent or effectively guaranteed?  

The current commercial terms suggest that although the structure is not equity-based, the economic profile requires careful calibration to avoid recharacterization.

2. Commercial Risk vs Capital Protection  

The proposed features include:

– Fixed per-ton earning  
– 90% cargo commitment  
– Preferential routing of investor cargo  
– Compensation if cargo is diverted  
– Protection from dilution due to future silo expansion  
– Defined residual value mechanics  
– Buy-back / extension formula  

Collectively, these terms significantly reduce the investor’s downside exposure. If, in practice, the model ensures recovery of investment plus return over 10 years with limited volume volatility, the tax authorities may view the arrangement as structured financing rather than entrepreneurial risk participation.

This distinction is critical.

If utilization risk is genuine and commercially variable → it supports a business income characterization.

If capital recovery is economically secured → it resembles a finance lease or infrastructure financing arrangement.

3. Likely Tax Characterization Scenarios  

A. Investor-Owned Asset Model (Throughput-Based Business Return)  

If investors legally and beneficially own the silos, bear utilization risk, and earn income strictly based on actual throughput without guaranteed minimum recovery, then:

– Investors may claim tax depreciation.  
– Per-ton earnings would constitute business income.  
– Withholding exposure would depend on final classification under section 153 (likely as services if structured accordingly).  
– FAP would treat payments as deductible business expenditure.  

However, this position is defensible only if the agreement avoids language implying guaranteed yield or fixed IRR recovery.

B. Finance Lease / Financing Model  

If economic analysis demonstrates that:

– Capital recovery is reasonably assured,  
– Utilization risk is contractually mitigated,  
– Return is structured to replicate financing yield,  

then the arrangement may be regarded as a finance lease in substance.

In that case:

– Depreciation entitlement may shift to FAP under tax principles.  
– Payments would be treated as lease rentals or financing cost.  
– Withholding classification would change accordingly.  
– Recharacterization risk reduces if structure is transparently aligned with economic reality.  

C. Joint Development / AOP Risk  

If drafting introduces joint control, shared project rights, or pooled economic outcomes beyond a simple payment mechanism, there is risk of classification as an Association of Persons (AOP). This would trigger:

– Separate tax registration,  
– Separate return filing,  
– Allocation of profit among members,  
– Significant compliance complexity.  

This exposure should be consciously avoided unless commercially intended.

4. Depreciation and Accounting Considerations  

The 10-year depreciation assumption and residual value schedule must align with tax treatment. If investor claims depreciation, asset ownership and asset risk must be demonstrable. If FAP effectively controls and bears asset risks, tax authorities may argue depreciation should vest with FAP regardless of legal title.

5. Withholding Tax Clarity  

From FAP’s perspective, incorrect head of withholding is a primary operational risk. The classification must be settled at structuring stage to avoid future audit exposure under incorrect deduction provisions.

6. Sales Tax Overlay  

Since FAP remains the operator providing port and storage services, the per-ton mechanism must be carefully structured so that it does not unintentionally create a secondary taxable service between FAP and investors under Sindh Sales Tax.

7. Recommended Structuring Path  

From a risk-managed standpoint, two clean alternatives are preferable:

Option 1 – Genuine Risk-Based Investor Model  
If this route is selected, cargo commitment and capital protection features should be commercially balanced so that throughput variability remains meaningful. The agreement should avoid any indication of assured return.

Option 2 – Explicit Infrastructure Financing / Lease Model  
If commercial objective is capital mobilization with predictable recovery, it is more defensible to structure transparently as financing or lease. This reduces litigation risk because tax characterization will align with economic substance.

Hybrid models — where return is economically secured yet labelled as throughput-linked — present the highest audit vulnerability.

8. Regulatory Overlay  

A review of the concession arrangement with Port Qasim Authority is necessary to confirm:

– Whether silo infrastructure forms part of concession assets;  
– Whether reversionary rights apply;  
– Whether independent ownership during tenure is permissible.  

This may materially influence asset ownership structuring.

9. Way Forward  

Given the tenure (10+ years) and capital magnitude, we recommend aligning internally on the intended economic outcome first:

– Is the objective genuine risk-sharing?  
– Or is it infrastructure financing?  

Once that is clearly defined, we can refine the documentation to ensure the tax treatment is sustainable and defensible.

We are available today to discuss and finalize a preferred direction so that structuring risk is addressed before commercial negotiations are concluded.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

Subject: Silo Investment Proposal – Recommended Legal Capacity and Structuring Framework  

Dear Mazhar,  

Thank you for your patience. Based on the full commercial terms shared and considering both tax defensibility and commercial practicality, I am setting out below a more detailed and structured recommendation on the most appropriate legal capacity and structuring approach under which this arrangement should be implemented.

1. Starting Point – Define the True Economic Objective  

Before selecting the legal form, the key strategic question is this:

Is FAP seeking genuine risk-sharing infrastructure development, or is FAP effectively raising structured capital for expansion?

The legal capacity must follow the economic substance. If we mismatch the two, recharacterization risk becomes material.

From the terms currently proposed — particularly the 90% cargo commitment, preferential routing, residual value mechanics, and capital protection features — the commercial profile appears closer to infrastructure financing than pure entrepreneurial risk investment.

Therefore, I will analyze the viable structuring capacities and then recommend the most defensible option.

-----------------------------------------

Option 1 – Investor as Independent Infrastructure Owner (Risk-Based Model)

Legal Capacity:
Investor owns silo assets for the tenure under a Project Development and Operations Agreement with FAP.

Key Features:
– Legal and beneficial ownership remains with investor during tenure.  
– Investor bears utilization risk (no guaranteed minimum return).  
– Return strictly linked to actual throughput.  
– FAP operates as facility manager/operator.  
– Buy-back at commercially negotiated fair value, not formulaic capital recovery.  

Tax Position:
– Investor claims depreciation.  
– Income treated as business income.  
– FAP deducts per-ton payments as operating expense.  
– Withholding under section 153 depending on classification.  

Risk Assessment:
This model is defensible only if genuine throughput variability exists. The present 90% cargo commitment and volume protection clauses materially weaken this position because they reduce business risk.

If we proceed under this capacity, the contract must be redrafted to reflect real commercial uncertainty. Otherwise, tax authorities may argue that the structure is merely disguised financing.

-----------------------------------------

Option 2 – Structured Infrastructure Financing / Finance Lease Model (Recommended)

Legal Capacity:
Investor participates as Infrastructure Financier or Lessor under a Finance Lease / Infrastructure Financing Agreement.

Key Features:
– Investor funds construction.  
– FAP is treated as lessee or economic user.  
– Payment structure defined as lease rentals or infrastructure usage charges.  
– Clear amortization profile aligned with capital recovery.  
– Purchase option at pre-agreed residual value.  

Tax Consequences:
– Characterization aligns with financing substance.  
– Depreciation likely shifts to FAP (depending on tax treatment of finance lease).  
– Investors recognize rental/financing income.  
– Withholding applied under correct head (likely lease or service classification).  
– Reduced recharacterization exposure because legal form matches economic substance.  

Why This is Structurally Stronger:
Given the cargo commitment, operational control by FAP, and capital protection mechanics, the arrangement economically resembles financing. Structuring transparently as such reduces litigation risk.

In my professional view, this is the most sustainable and defensible approach under Pakistani tax principles.

-----------------------------------------

Option 3 – Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) Structure

Legal Capacity:
A separate SPV incorporated for silo ownership, jointly funded by investors (but not equity in FAP).

Possible Structures:
– SPV leases silos to FAP.  
– SPV earns lease income.  
– Investors hold equity in SPV.  

Tax Implications:
– SPV taxed separately.  
– Dividends to investors subject to applicable tax regime.  
– Clear separation of ownership and operational control.  

Advantages:
– Ring-fences project risk.  
– Avoids AOP classification if structured as corporate entity.  
– Cleaner accounting and financing presentation.  

Disadvantages:
– Additional compliance and governance overhead.  

This model is viable if investors prefer institutional clarity and ring-fenced exposure.

-----------------------------------------

Structure to Avoid – Informal Joint Venture / Revenue Share

If documentation uses language suggesting:

– Joint undertaking  
– Shared project profits  
– Co-management rights  

There is risk of classification as Association of Persons (AOP), which would trigger:

– Separate tax registration  
– Separate return filing  
– Profit allocation complexities  
– Increased audit scrutiny  

Given the scale and visibility of FAP, this exposure is not advisable unless commercially necessary.

-----------------------------------------

Depreciation and Ownership Clarity

The 10-year depreciation schedule must match legal and tax ownership. If investor claims depreciation but FAP controls and economically consumes the asset, authorities may challenge depreciation entitlement.

Ownership must be supported by:

– Asset risk  
– Insurance responsibility  
– Replacement risk  
– Residual value uncertainty  

Without these, depreciation position weakens.

-----------------------------------------

Concession Overlay – Critical Review Required

We must also examine FAP’s concession agreement with Port Qasim Authority to determine:

– Whether new infrastructure automatically vests in concession framework;  
– Whether independent ownership during tenure is permissible;  
– Whether reversionary rights apply.  

This may influence whether investor ownership is legally sustainable.

-----------------------------------------

Final Recommendation

Based on the commercial safeguards currently embedded in the proposal, the most appropriate and defensible legal capacity is:

Infrastructure Financing / Finance Lease Model  

This aligns with:

– FAP’s operational control  
– Capital protection mechanics  
– Volume commitments  
– Pre-determined exit valuation  

Trying to preserve an “investment participation” label while economically guaranteeing recovery would create avoidable tax exposure.

If the commercial intention is genuine risk participation, then terms must be recalibrated to remove capital protection features.

-----------------------------------------

Next Step

I recommend a structured internal alignment session to finalize:

– Desired economic substance  
– Risk tolerance  
– Ownership intention  
– Exit mechanics  

Once agreed, we can prepare a detailed tax structuring memo and assist in drafting defensible contractual clauses.

Given the urgency, we remain available to discuss today and finalize the preferred route.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

Subject: Recommended Legal Capacity and Structuring Approach – Silo Investment Arrangement  

Dear Mazhar,  

Further to your request, I am setting out below my clear recommendation on the most appropriate legal capacity and structuring approach under which this arrangement should be implemented, considering tax defensibility, regulatory alignment, and long-term risk management.

1. Commercial Substance Assessment  

Based on the proposed terms:

- Investors fund construction of silos on FAP land  
- FAP leads execution and retains operational control  
- Investors earn fixed per-ton entitlement  
- 90% cargo commitment exists  
- Capital recovery profile is largely predictable  
- Pre-agreed residual value / buy-back mechanics are embedded  
- Volume protection clauses are included  

These features significantly reduce investor downside risk. In substance, the arrangement resembles structured infrastructure financing rather than a pure risk-based business venture.

Accordingly, the legal capacity must reflect this reality.

2. Most Appropriate Legal Capacity – Infrastructure Financing / Lease Model  

In my professional view, the most sustainable and defensible structure would be:

A clearly defined Infrastructure Financing / Finance Lease arrangement.

Under this model:

• Investors participate in the capacity of financiers / lessors.  
• FAP is treated as lessee / economic user of the asset.  
• Construction is funded by investors but operational control remains with FAP.  
• Payments are structured as lease rentals or infrastructure usage charges.  
• A defined purchase option at agreed residual value is documented.  

Why this is preferable:

a) Alignment of Form and Substance  
The economic profile already indicates predictable capital recovery. Structuring it transparently as financing eliminates recharacterization exposure.

b) Reduced Tax Litigation Risk  
When documentation aligns with commercial reality, the risk of FBR challenging the arrangement as a disguised lease or financing is significantly reduced.

c) Clear Withholding Position  
Payments can be classified appropriately (e.g., lease rental), ensuring correct withholding head from day one.

d) Depreciation Clarity  
Tax depreciation treatment can be aligned with finance lease principles, avoiding later disputes over beneficial ownership.

3. Alternative – SPV-Based Lease Structure (If Investors Prefer Ring-Fencing)

If investors require institutional clarity and risk segregation, a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) may be incorporated:

- SPV owns silos.  
- SPV leases assets to FAP.  
- Investors hold equity in SPV (not in FAP).  

Advantages:
- Ring-fenced liability  
- Cleaner ownership structure  
- Avoids AOP risk  
- Institutional comfort for larger investors  

This is commercially cleaner where multiple investors are involved.

4. Structure to Avoid – Hybrid “Throughput Investment” with Capital Protection  

The least advisable approach is to retain the current hybrid format:

- Labeling it as throughput-based investment  
- While embedding cargo guarantees and capital recovery protection  

Such a structure creates maximum audit vulnerability because it appears to be financing in substance but is not documented as such.

This is precisely the type of arrangement that may attract recharacterization under “substance over form” principles.

5. AOP Exposure – Must Be Avoided  

The agreement must not:

- Refer to joint undertaking  
- Share project profits  
- Create co-management rights  

Otherwise, risk of Association of Persons (AOP) classification arises, triggering separate tax compliance and complexity.

6. Concession Agreement Review – Mandatory  

Before finalization, FAP must confirm:

- Whether silo infrastructure legally vests under concession framework  
- Whether third-party ownership during tenure is permissible  
- Whether any regulatory approval is required  

This is critical to ensure the ownership structure is legally sustainable.

7. Final Recommendation  

Given the commercial safeguards currently embedded in the proposal, the most appropriate and defensible legal capacity is:

Infrastructure Financing / Finance Lease Model  
(possibly through an SPV if investor profile requires it)

This structure:

- Aligns economic reality with legal documentation  
- Minimizes recharacterization risk  
- Provides clarity on withholding  
- Reduces future audit exposure  
- Ensures depreciation position is defensible  

If FAP’s strategic objective is instead genuine risk-sharing infrastructure development, then the commercial terms must be materially revised to remove capital protection features.

I am available to align internally and prepare a short structuring note for management approval so that negotiations proceed on a tax-secure footing.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair
