Subject: Proposed Silo Investment Model – Tax Structuring Analysis and Recommended Approach  

Dear Mazhar,

Thank you for your follow-up. Based on a detailed review of the commercial terms now shared, I am setting out below a consolidated tax and structuring analysis together with our recommended way forward.

At the outset, while the proposal is described as a “project-specific investment model” and not an equity participation in FAP, the ultimate tax characterization will depend on substance over form — particularly ownership, risk allocation, capital recovery mechanics, and certainty of return.

1. Core Tax Characterization Risk

The commercial features currently contemplated — fixed per-ton entitlement, 90% cargo commitment, FAP-led execution and operational control, defined tenure of 10 years, buy-back / extension pricing linked to residual value, and protection against volume dilution — collectively indicate that the investor’s downside risk may be commercially limited.

If the structure economically assures capital recovery plus return, even if phrased as throughput-based, the tax authorities may recharacterize the arrangement as:

– A finance lease; or  
– A structured financing arrangement; or  
– In certain drafting scenarios, a joint venture / AOP exposure.

Therefore, documentation discipline will be critical.

2. Analysis of Current Model – Likely Treatment

Based on the terms shared, the arrangement presently leans closer to a structured financing model rather than a pure throughput-risk investment. Key reasons:

• FAP leads project execution and operational management.  
• Investors do not appear to bear meaningful operational or utilization risk due to 90% cargo commitment and allocation mechanics.  
• Residual value formula and buy-back mechanics are pre-agreed.  
• Non-compete and volume protection clauses limit commercial uncertainty.

In such scenario, the tax authority could argue that investors are effectively financing infrastructure for FAP, and the per-ton payment is economically akin to lease rental or financing return.

3. Withholding Tax Implications

Depending on final characterization:

If treated as service payments → exposure under section 153 (services).  
If treated as lease rentals → section 155 may become relevant.  
If treated as business income of resident investor → withholding under section 153(1)(b) may still apply depending on contractual structure.

From FAP’s perspective, clarity on classification is essential to avoid disputes on incorrect withholding heads.

4. Depreciation Entitlement

Depreciation claim will depend on beneficial ownership.

If investor retains genuine asset ownership and bears asset risk → investor may claim depreciation.

If arrangement is recharacterized as finance lease → depreciation may shift to FAP under tax principles.

Therefore, legal title alone will not be sufficient; economic substance must support ownership.

5. AOP Risk (Joint Venture Exposure)

If revenue-sharing language, joint management rights, or pooled profit mechanics are introduced, there is risk of classification as an Association of Persons under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. That would trigger separate tax registration, compliance, and profit allocation complexity. The current model should avoid language suggesting “joint undertaking” or “shared profits.”

6. Sales Tax Overlay

Since FAP will continue to provide port handling and storage services, Sindh Sales Tax implications must also be aligned. Any per-ton payment mechanism should not inadvertently create a secondary taxable supply characterization between FAP and investors.

7. Recommended Structuring Direction

From a defensibility standpoint, two clean alternatives are preferable:

Option A – Genuine Investor-Owned Asset with Real Utilization Risk  
If this route is selected, the 90% cargo commitment and volume protection clauses should be commercially softened to demonstrate real throughput variability. No guaranteed IRR language should appear in financial modelling or agreements.

Option B – Clearly Structured Financing / Lease Model  
If commercial objective is assured capital recovery, it would be more robust to structure transparently as a finance lease or infrastructure financing arrangement. This reduces recharacterization risk because legal form matches economic reality.

Hybrid models where capital recovery is economically locked yet labelled as throughput-based create the highest audit exposure.

8. Concession Agreement Check

Before finalization, we strongly recommend reviewing the underlying concession arrangement with Port Qasim Authority to confirm whether silo infrastructure automatically forms part of concession assets or triggers reversionary rights. This may materially influence ownership structuring.

9. Next Step

Given the quantum and tenure involved, I recommend a structured working session with FAP commercial and legal teams to finalize:

– Ownership position  
– Risk allocation  
– Return mechanism  
– Exit mechanics  
– Withholding treatment  
– Depreciation entitlement  

Once the economic substance is clearly defined, we can prepare a defensible tax memo and assist in drafting appropriate contractual clauses.

Given urgency, we are available today for a short call to align and move toward a preferred structure.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

:::writing{id="59384" variant="email" subject="Permanent Withdrawal from Recognized Provident Fund – Position under Income Tax Ordinance, 2001"}
Dear [Client Name],  

This is with reference to your query regarding the frequency of permanent withdrawals from a Recognized Provident Fund (“RPF”) and the position under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”) and the Income Tax Rules, 2002 (“the Rules”).  

After reviewing the relevant provisions of the Ordinance and the Rules, we note that there is no provision which prescribes any numerical restriction on the number of permanent withdrawals that may be made by an employee during the course of employment. The Ordinance does not impose any capping on frequency.  

The tax framework governing provident funds is primarily contained in:  

- Section 2(47) of the Ordinance (definition of “recognized provident fund”);  
- Part I of the Sixth Schedule to the Ordinance (conditions for recognition and exemption); and  
- Rules relating to recognition and maintenance of provident funds under the Income Tax Rules, 2002.  

Under Part I of the Sixth Schedule, the emphasis of law is on the conditions for recognition, investment of funds, limits on employer contributions, and taxation of accumulated balance in certain circumstances (for example, cessation of employment before completing the prescribed service period). The law does not regulate the number of withdrawals per se.  

Further, the Ordinance does not prescribe any monetary cap for permanent withdrawals. Instead, tax consequences are triggered in specific situations, such as:  

- Where the accumulated balance becomes taxable due to premature cessation of employment (as per the relevant clauses of Part I of the Sixth Schedule); or  
- Where the fund ceases to satisfy the conditions of recognition.  

Therefore, from a strict income tax perspective:  

1. There is no restriction under the Ordinance or the Rules on how many times permanent withdrawal may be allowed.  
2. The amount and grounds of withdrawal are generally governed by the approved trust deed and rules of the provident fund.  
3. Provided the withdrawal is in accordance with the approved rules of the RPF and the fund continues to meet the conditions of Part I of the Sixth Schedule, such withdrawals do not, by themselves, violate the tax law.  

Accordingly, the frequency of permanent withdrawals is a matter of the fund’s internal regulations and not a statutory limitation under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.  

However, it remains important to ensure that repeated withdrawals do not conflict with the approved scheme of the RPF, as any violation could potentially affect its recognized status, which would have adverse tax implications.  

Should you require, we may also examine your specific RPF trust deed to confirm alignment with the tax framework.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Firm Name]

:::writing{id="76125" variant="email" subject="Permanent Withdrawal from Recognized Provident Fund – Position under Rules 103 to 106 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002"}
Dear [Client Name],  

Further to your query regarding the frequency of permanent withdrawals from a Recognized Provident Fund (“RPF”), we have examined Rules 103 to 106 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 in detail, read with Part I of the Sixth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.  

Under Rule 103, withdrawals from accumulated balance are strictly purpose-based. The permitted purposes include expenses relating to illness of the subscriber or his family, transfer of balance to an approved pension fund under the Voluntary Pension System, purchase of a motor cycle or scooter, overseas passage for health or education, marriage and funeral expenses, performance of Haj, purchase or construction of a residential house or site, repairs or renovation of a residential house, payment of life insurance premiums (subject to assignment requirements), purchase of shares of a public limited company in accordance with the Rules, purchase or construction of house or agricultural land after attaining the age of fifty years, repayment of a loan from a financial institution, withdrawal without assigning any reason after attaining fifty years of age, and withdrawal while proceeding on leave preparatory to retirement. Accordingly, any withdrawal must clearly fall within one of these specified purposes.  

Rule 104 prescribes monetary ceilings for each category. For example, withdrawals for illness, motor cycle purchase, overseas passage, and marriage or funeral expenses are limited to six months’ salary or the accumulated balance, whichever is lower. Withdrawals for Haj are restricted to six months’ salary or a specified monetary cap or accumulated balance, whichever is lowest. Withdrawals for purchase or construction of a house may extend up to thirty-six months’ salary or accumulated balance, whichever is lower. Certain withdrawals after attaining fifty years of age may be allowed up to twenty-four months’ salary or a percentage (such as sixty percent or eighty percent, depending on the purpose) of the accumulated balance. Withdrawal on leave preparatory to retirement may be allowed up to ninety percent of accumulated balance. Therefore, while the Rules do not impose a simple numerical cap, each withdrawal is independently subject to quantitative limits.  

The issue of frequency is specifically governed by Rule 105. As a general principle, a second withdrawal is not permitted until the earlier withdrawal has been fully repaid. However, there are express exceptions. Subsequent withdrawals may be permitted in respect of life insurance premium payments even if earlier withdrawals have not been repaid. Certain withdrawals may also be allowed notwithstanding non-repayment of earlier withdrawals taken for performance of Haj or other specified purposes. In addition, subsequent transfers to an approved pension fund are permitted without restriction. Therefore, frequency is not absolutely barred, but it is conditionally regulated depending upon the nature of the earlier and subsequent withdrawals.  

Rule 106 determines whether repayment is mandatory. Withdrawals made for transfer to an approved pension fund, purchase or construction of house, payment of life insurance premiums, purchase of shares, withdrawals after attaining fifty years of age (including withdrawal without assigning reason), and withdrawal on leave preparatory to retirement are not required to be repaid. In other cases, repayment is mandatory in equal monthly installments (up to forty-eight months) together with mark-up calculated at the prescribed rate. In case of default in repayment, the Commissioner is empowered to add the withdrawn amount or outstanding balance to the employee’s total income in the year of default and assess tax accordingly.  

In view of the above, the correct legal position is that the Income Tax Rules, 2002 do not prescribe a fixed number of times an employee may permanently withdraw from a recognized provident fund. However, withdrawals are tightly structured: they must be for permitted purposes, within prescribed monetary limits, and subject to the repayment and second-withdrawal restrictions contained in Rules 105 and 106. Any deviation from these provisions may result in tax consequences or jeopardize compliance under Part I of the Sixth Schedule.  

Please let us know if you would like us to apply the above framework to a specific factual scenario or proposed withdrawal.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Firm Name]  
:::

:::writing{id="76125" variant="email" subject="Permanent Withdrawal from Recognized Provident Fund – Position under Rules 103 to 106 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002"}
Dear [Client Name],  

Further to your query regarding the frequency of permanent withdrawals from a Recognized Provident Fund (“RPF”), we have now specifically examined Rules 103 to 106 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 read with Part I of the Sixth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.  

At the outset, it is important to clarify that the tax law does not provide an unrestricted right of withdrawal, nor does it impose a simple numerical cap. Instead, the framework under Rules 103 to 106 regulates (i) the purposes for which withdrawal is permissible, (ii) the monetary limits applicable to each category, and (iii) the circumstances in which second or subsequent withdrawals may be allowed.  

Rule 103 exhaustively lists the permitted purposes for withdrawals from accumulated balance, such as illness, marriage and funeral expenses, performance of Haj, purchase or construction of house, purchase of agricultural land (in specified cases), repayment of loan, purchase of shares, insurance premiums, transfer to an approved pension fund, and certain withdrawals after attaining the age of fifty years (including withdrawal without assigning any reason under clause (j)(iv)). Accordingly, withdrawals are purpose-driven and must strictly fall within one of the enumerated clauses of Rule 103(1).  

Rule 104 then prescribes monetary ceilings linked to salary or accumulated balance, depending upon the nature of withdrawal. For example, withdrawals for illness, motor cycle purchase, overseas passage, marriage or funeral expenses are generally capped at six months’ salary or accumulated balance, whichever is lower; withdrawals for house purchase or construction may extend up to thirty-six months’ salary; certain withdrawals after age fifty are restricted to twenty-four months’ salary or specified percentages of accumulated balance; and in some cases (such as leave preparatory to retirement), up to ninety percent of accumulated balance may be permitted. Therefore, while frequency is not directly capped, each withdrawal must independently comply with the quantitative limits prescribed under Rule 104.  

The key provision relevant to your query on frequency is Rule 105 (Second Withdrawals). As a general rule under Rule 105(1), no second withdrawal is permitted until the first withdrawal has been fully repaid. However, sub-rules (2) to (6) carve out important exceptions. For instance, subsequent withdrawals for purposes specified in clause (h) of Rule 103(1) (insurance premium) may be permitted even if earlier withdrawals have not been repaid. Similarly, certain withdrawals may be allowed notwithstanding non-repayment of earlier withdrawals for Haj or other specified purposes. In addition, withdrawals under clause (aa) (transfer to approved pension fund) may be permitted subsequently without restriction.  

Rule 106 further clarifies whether repayment is mandatory. Withdrawals under clauses (aa), (f), (h), (i), (j) and (k) of Rule 103(1) are not required to be repaid. In other cases, repayment is mandatory in installments (up to forty-eight months) together with mark-up as prescribed. Importantly, in case of default in repayment, the Commissioner may add the withdrawn amount (or outstanding balance) to the employee’s total income for the year of default and assess it accordingly.  

In light of the above, the correct legal position is that the Income Tax Rules, 2002 do not impose a fixed numerical cap on permanent withdrawals. However, frequency is indirectly regulated through the mechanism of Rule 105, which generally prohibits a second withdrawal until repayment of the earlier one, subject to specified exceptions. Further, each withdrawal must satisfy the permitted purpose under Rule 103 and the monetary limits under Rule 104, and where repayment is required under Rule 106, compliance with the repayment schedule is essential to avoid adverse tax consequences.  

Accordingly, the permissibility of repeated permanent withdrawals is not unlimited but is structured and conditional under the Rules. Any withdrawal must strictly comply with Rules 103 to 106 to ensure continued recognition of the fund under Part I of the Sixth Schedule and to avoid potential addition to the employee’s taxable income in case of default.

The concept of a recognized provident fund is defined in section 2(47) of the Ordinance, and the substantive tax treatment is governed by Part I of the Sixth Schedule. The Sixth Schedule prescribes the conditions subject to which a provident fund is granted and retains recognition, including limits on employer contributions, investment of funds, and taxation of accumulated balances in specified circumstances (for example, where an employee ceases employment before completion of the prescribed qualifying service period). Notably, neither section 2(47) nor any clause of Part I of the Sixth Schedule prescribes any restriction on the number of withdrawals that an employee may make during service.  

Under the Income Tax Rules, 2002, the relevant framework is contained in the Rules dealing with recognition of provident funds (including, inter alia, Rules 98 to 110). These Rules regulate the procedure for application for recognition, conditions for approval, maintenance of accounts, investment restrictions, amendment of trust deeds, and reporting obligations to the Commissioner. The Rules require that the fund must operate strictly in accordance with its approved trust deed and rules, and any amendment to the governing document generally requires prior approval of the Commissioner. However, the Rules do not impose any numerical cap or frequency-based limitation on permanent withdrawals.  

Accordingly, from a strict reading of the Ordinance and the Rules, there is no statutory limitation on how many times a permanent withdrawal may be allowed to an employee. The tax law does not regulate frequency; rather, it regulates compliance with recognition conditions and determines taxability of accumulated balance in specified events.  

The practical control mechanism, therefore, lies in the approved trust deed and fund rules. If the trust deed permits permanent withdrawals for specified purposes (such as housing, marriage, medical needs, etc.), and such withdrawals are made strictly in accordance with those approved rules, the mere repetition of withdrawals does not contravene the Ordinance or the Rules. However, if withdrawals are allowed outside the approved framework or in a manner inconsistent with the conditions of recognition laid down in Part I of the Sixth Schedule and the relevant Rules, there is a risk that the Commissioner may invoke powers relating to withdrawal of recognition, which could have adverse tax consequences for the fund and its members.  

In conclusion, under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 read with the Income Tax Rules, 2002, there is no statutory capping on the number of permanent withdrawals. Dear Sir, hope you are doing well. 

Further to our earlier verbal discussion, wherein you had indicated that the proposed arrangement may be structured under the concept of “export of services” on the basis that management consultancy services would be provided to an overseas entity, we have undertaken a preliminary review of the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 to confirm the implication.

The standard rate of Sindh sales tax is 15%, unless a reduced or higher rate is expressly prescribed for particular categories.

It is important to clarify that the concept of export of services does not provide a blanket exemption. Export-related exemptions are available only for specific service categories expressly mentioned in the Schedule, such as certain IT-enabled services, call centre services, research services and similar technology-based services, and even those are subject to strict conditions, including realization of consideration in foreign exchange through banking channels and compliance with regulatory reporting requirements.

Management consultancy services, generally falling under CPC 8311 / 83117 (business and management advisory services), are not included within the specifically exempted export categories. Accordingly, the mere fact that the recipient of services is located outside Pakistan and payment is received in foreign currency does not automatically render the transaction exempt from Sindh sales tax.

Based on the current understanding that the proposed services constitute management consultancy, the transaction would remain subject to Sindh sales tax at the standard rate of 15%. In light of this position, the following compliance requirements would apply:

Registration with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB), if not already obtained;

Issuance of SRB-compliant tax invoices;

Charging and depositing Sindh sales tax at 15% on the value of services; and

Filing of periodic sales tax returns in accordance with SRB regulations.

We recommend reviewing the detailed scope of services and draft agreement to ensure correct classification before final execution.

Please let us know if you require our assistance in obtaining SRB registration, structuring the arrangement appropriately, or concluding the matter from a compliance perspective. We would be pleased to support you through the registration and implementation process to ensure full regulatory alignment from the outset.

Kind regards,

Subject: Clarification Regarding Taxability of Research Services under Sindh Sales Tax Framework  

Dear Sir,  

Thank you for your feedback and for highlighting the position that research services may qualify within the export-related exemptions under the amended Sindh Sales Tax regime effective July 1, 2025. We have carefully revisited the classification aspect in light of the CPC structure and the amended Sindh Sales Tax on Services framework to address this point comprehensively.  

At the outset, it is correct that the Sindh Sales Tax model now follows a broad-based principle whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempted in the First Schedule. Export-related relief is not automatic merely because the recipient is located outside Pakistan and consideration is realized in foreign exchange. The exemption applies only where the service falls squarely within the specifically notified categories and all prescribed conditions are strictly satisfied.  

The critical issue, therefore, is proper service classification. Under CPC Version 2.1, genuine “research and experimental development services” are classified under Division 81 (CPC 811–813), which cover basic research, applied research, and experimental development in natural sciences, engineering, social sciences, and interdisciplinary fields. These involve systematic original investigation undertaken to generate new knowledge, develop new products, processes, or materially improve existing ones.  

In contrast, management consultancy services fall under CPC 8311 (e.g., strategic management consulting, financial management consulting, operational advisory, business restructuring, etc.). These services involve advisory and operational assistance to management and do not constitute research in the technical or scientific sense contemplated under Division 81.  

The distinction is not merely academic. If the scope of work primarily involves advisory support, business strategy formulation, financial modeling, performance evaluation, policy advisory, or management oversight, the essential character of the service remains management consultancy, even if analytical inputs or studies are involved. The CPC rules require classification based on the most specific description and the essential character of the service. A consultancy assignment does not transform into “research services” merely because it includes analysis or reporting.  

Accordingly, unless the contractual scope clearly demonstrates systematic R&D activity — such as scientific experimentation, technological development, structured applied research, or generation of new intellectual output — it would be difficult to sustain classification under CPC 811–813. In such case, the transaction would remain taxable at the standard rate of 15% under the Sindh Sales Tax regime.  

However, if the arrangement is genuinely structured as research and experimental development services within the meaning of Division 81, and if it falls within the specific export-exempt categories notified in the Schedule (subject to fulfillment of foreign exchange realization and documentary conditions), a different tax treatment may be supportable. That determination will depend strictly on the contractual substance rather than the label assigned to the services.  

We therefore recommend a detailed clause-by-clause review of the draft agreement and scope of services to assess whether the services qualify as technical R&D or remain management consultancy in substance. Proper structuring at the outset is essential to mitigate classification risk and future exposure during SRB audit or scrutiny.  

We would be pleased to review the draft documentation and advise on the most defensible tax position before finalizing the arrangement.  

Kind regards,  

[Your Name]

Subject: Clarification on Research Services Exemption under Sindh Sales Tax Framework  

Dear Sir,  

Thank you for your further input regarding the taxability of research services. We have revisited the matter in light of the relevant entry of the First Schedule to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services framework to ensure the position is fully aligned with the statutory provisions.  

As previously discussed, with effect from July 1, 2025, the Sindh Sales Tax regime operates on a broad-based principle whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempted under the First Schedule. Therefore, classification and applicability of any exemption must be strictly tested against the wording of the relevant Schedule entry.  

In this regard, Entry No. 15 of the First Schedule refers to:  

**“81 – Research and development services”**, with the specific condition that **the exemption shall be applicable only to the services provided or rendered to educational institutions recognized by the Higher Education Commission of Pakistan (HEC) and/or Sindh Higher Education Commission.**  

This is a conditional exemption. It does not provide a blanket exemption for all research services exported or rendered to any overseas entity. Rather, the exemption is restricted to a very specific scenario:  

1. The service must fall within CPC Division 81 (Research and Development services — i.e., genuine basic research, applied research, or experimental development as per CPC 811–813); **and**  
2. The recipient must be an educational institution recognized by HEC and/or Sindh HEC.  

Both conditions must be satisfied cumulatively.  

Accordingly, even if a service qualifies technically as research and development under CPC 81, the exemption under Entry 15 would not apply unless the recipient is a recognized educational institution as specified. If the services are rendered to a corporate entity, foreign holding company, group entity, or any non-HEC-recognized institution, the exemption would not be available under this entry.  

Further, if the services in substance constitute management consultancy (CPC 8311) rather than research and experimental development (CPC 81), the exemption would not apply in any case, irrespective of the recipient. As per CPC classification principles, the essential character of the service determines its classification. Advisory, strategic, financial, or operational assistance generally remains management consultancy even if analytical work is involved.  

Therefore, based on the current understanding that the proposed services are being provided to an overseas non-educational entity and are advisory in nature, the exemption under Entry 15 of the First Schedule would not be applicable. In such case, the services would remain subject to Sindh sales tax at the standard rate of 15%, along with the applicable compliance requirements.  

We strongly recommend a careful review of the scope of work and recipient profile to determine whether the services can legitimately fall within CPC 81 and whether the statutory conditions of the First Schedule are fulfilled. Any classification adopted should be defensible on substance, particularly in the event of SRB scrutiny.  

We remain available to review the agreement in detail and assist in structuring the arrangement in a tax-efficient and compliant manner.  

Kind regards,  

[Your Name]

According to a document from CPC-Code-10.07.2025.pdf, research services are specifically classified under **Section 8 – Business and production services**, Division 81 “Research and development services”【turn1file14†L33-L41】.

Now let’s evaluate this properly and not mix apples with mangoes.

The CPC clearly distinguishes between:

1. **Research and experimental development services (Division 81)**  
2. **Licensing of R&D products (73330)**  
3. **Market research services (which are excluded from R&D and classified elsewhere, e.g., 83700)**  

That distinction is critical for tax purposes.

---

## 1️⃣ Core Taxable Research Services – Division 81

Division 81 covers genuine R&D services. These include:

### A. Natural Sciences & Engineering (811)

Basic research (8111) – theoretical or experimental work undertaken primarily to acquire new knowledge without specific commercial application【turn1file11†L6-L13】.

Applied research (8112) – original investigation directed toward a specific practical objective【turn1file10†L13-L17】.

Experimental development (8113) – systematic work aimed at producing new materials, products, processes or substantially improving existing ones【turn1file10†L60-L65】.

Examples that clearly fall under taxable research services:

- Biotechnology research (81113, 81123, 81133)【turn1file11†L18-L26】【turn1file9†L6-L15】
- Medical and pharmaceutical R&D (81115, 81125, 81135)【turn1file11†L43-L45】【turn1file9†L33-L36】
- Engineering and technology R&D (81114, 81124, 81134)【turn1file11†L39-L42】【turn1file9†L28-L32】

These are clearly research services and, where taxable under local sales tax laws, should be mapped under CPC 811 (as applicable subclass).

---

### B. Social Sciences & Humanities Research (812)

Basic research (8121) – theoretical work to acquire knowledge【turn1file9†L46-L53】

Applied research (8122) – directed toward a specific objective【turn1file9†L72-L76】

Experimental development (8123) – systematic work to create new systems/services【turn1file7†L24-L28】

Importantly, the CPC explicitly excludes **market research services** from these categories【turn1file7†L9-L10】.

So if a company claims “research services,” we must ask:

- Is it scientific/academic R&D? → Division 81  
- Is it business/consumer survey research? → Likely 83700 (not Division 81)  

That distinction materially affects tax classification.

---

### C. Interdisciplinary Research (813)

Where research spans both natural sciences and social sciences, it falls under CPC 813 (81301–81303)【turn1file13†L11-L20】.

This would apply, for example, to:

- Tech + behavioral research  
- Environmental + economic impact studies  
- Public health + data science projects  

---

### D. Research and Development Originals (814)

CPC 81400 covers “scientific originals” — inventions, blueprints, formulas created on own account for later sale【turn1file13†L24-L31】.

This is not research service per se — it is the creation of intellectual property.

Tax treatment may differ where:

- You provide R&D services (811–813), versus  
- You sell/license the outcome (73330)  

---

## 2️⃣ Licensing of R&D Outcome – NOT Research Service

If a party grants rights to use research results, that falls under:

**73330 – Licensing services for the right to use R&D products**【turn1file14†L11-L17】.

This is crucial. Licensing is not research service. It is IP licensing.

In tax terms:

- Performing research = CPC 811/812/813  
- Licensing research output = CPC 73330  

Completely different characterization.

---

## 3️⃣ What Should Be Considered Taxable “Research Services”?

Based strictly on CPC structure, the following should qualify as research services:

✔ Basic scientific research (8111, 8121)  
✔ Applied research (8112, 8122)  
✔ Experimental development services (8113, 8123)  
✔ Interdisciplinary R&D (813)  
✔ Contract R&D services provided to a client  

These are service transactions.

However, the following are NOT research services under Division 81:

✘ Market research (classified separately)【turn1file7†L9-L10】  
✘ Licensing of R&D output (73330)【turn1file14†L11-L17】  
✘ Drafting legal IP documents (82130)  
✘ General consultancy that does not involve original investigation  

---

## 4️⃣ Practical Tax Risk Areas

From a tax advisory perspective, the biggest classification disputes typically arise where:

- Management consultancy is wrongly labelled as “research”
- Market surveys are labelled as “applied research”
- Engineering consultancy is confused with experimental development
- IP licensing is treated as service instead of royalty

The CPC rules clearly state that classification must prefer the most specific description【turn1file2†L14-L20】.

So we must always determine:

What is the essential character of the service?

If it is systematic original investigation → Division 81  
If it is advisory → likely 831 (management consulting)  
If it is consumer data analysis → market research  
If it is right to use IP → 73330  

---

## 5️⃣ Conclusion

Appropriate research services that are taxable under CPC would fall under:

- 811xx – Natural sciences & engineering R&D  
- 812xx – Social sciences & humanities R&D  
- 8130x – Interdisciplinary R&D  
- 81400 – R&D originals (where applicable)  

Licensing of research output is classified separately under 73330 and should not be treated as research service.

I have carefully reviewed the notice issued under section 122(9) for Tax Year 2015, particularly the portion relating to the Technical Service Fee (TSF) paid to ICTSI Mauritius Limited, as reflected on pages 1 to 3 of the notice fileciteturn0file0.

Now let us critically evaluate the legal and procedural deficits in the notice strictly in light of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and the Income Tax Rules, 2002.

First: Misapplication of Section 20 and Section 174(2)

The officer alleges that the expenditure is not incurred “wholly and exclusively” for business purposes and refers to section 20 and section 174(2). However, the notice does not identify any material defect in the books of account nor does it invoke section 32 or section 121 for best judgment assessment. Section 174(2) deals with maintenance and production of accounts. Non-satisfaction of the officer cannot automatically convert into disallowance unless:

• books are rejected on cogent grounds; or  
• specific falsity, inflation, or non-genuineness is demonstrated.

Merely stating that the taxpayer “failed to demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt” is not the statutory test under section 20. The correct test is whether the expenditure is incurred for the purposes of business. The burden initially lies on the taxpayer to substantiate incurrence — not to prove commercial wisdom beyond doubt. Courts have consistently held that tax authorities cannot sit in judgment over commercial expedence unless the transaction is sham or colourable.

The notice does not allege sham, fictitious payment, or non-payment. It merely questions adequacy of evidence and benefit. That is a weak legal foundation.

Second: Incorrect Standard of Proof – “Beyond Reasonable Doubt”

The repeated use of the phrase “beyond reasonable doubt” (page 1 and 2) is legally flawed fileciteturn0file0. That is a criminal law standard. Income tax proceedings are civil in nature. The applicable standard is preponderance of evidence. The officer has applied a higher evidentiary threshold not recognized under the Ordinance.

This is not just semantic. It shows misunderstanding of evidentiary burden.

Third: Transfer Pricing Adjustment under Section 108 – Procedural Gaps

The officer invokes section 108 read with Chapter VI of the Income Tax Rules 2002 and alleges that:

• no independent enterprise would pay such fee  
• no local comparable is paying  
• the fee is profit shifting to Mauritius  

However, several procedural deficiencies exist:

1. No identification of most appropriate method (CUP, TNMM, Cost Plus, etc.)  
2. No FAR analysis (Functions, Assets, Risks)  
3. No benchmarking study  
4. No computation of arm’s length price  
5. No adjustment mechanics provided  

Section 108 does not allow disallowance per se. It allows substitution of arm’s length price. The officer must determine the ALP using one of the prescribed methods under Rules 27 to 31 (Chapter VI as applicable for that year). Simply saying “none of the local companies pay” is not a valid CUP unless functional comparability is established.

Terminal operators with different ownership structures and group integration models are not automatically comparable.

Fourth: Commercial Expediency Test – Exceeding Jurisdiction

The notice questions why services were not obtained from Manila instead of Mauritius and whether Manila benefited (page 2) fileciteturn0file0.

This line of reasoning exceeds jurisdiction. The tax department cannot dictate intra-group structuring unless it is shown to be artificial or lacking substance. Section 108 addresses pricing — not business structuring decisions. The officer has conflated corporate structuring with tax avoidance without invoking any anti-avoidance provision such as section 109 (transactions without economic substance) or section 111.

No GAAR-type reasoning is properly articulated.

Fifth: Allegation of “Profit Shifting to Tax Haven”

The statement that the fee was incurred “to shift profits to a tax heaven i.e. Mauritius” (page 2) fileciteturn0file0 is speculative. There is:

• no analysis of treaty implications  
• no examination of effective tax rate in Mauritius  
• no reference to tax sparing  
• no discussion of whether withholding tax was deducted under section 152  

Without factual tax rate comparison and treaty application, the allegation remains conjectural.

Sixth: Disallowance of Sales Tax Component under Section 20

The officer proposes to disallow sales tax of Rs. 114,983,000 under section 20 (page 3) fileciteturn0file0.

This is legally questionable. If the underlying service is allowable, sales tax paid thereon (being cost component if not adjustable) forms part of expenditure under accounting principles. Disallowance of sales tax requires showing that it is refundable, adjustable, or not incurred. The notice does not analyze whether the sales tax was input-adjustable or cost.

Seventh: Absence of Specific Definite Information

Section 122(5A) (and by implication 122(9)) requires “definite information.” The notice states discrepancies were treated as definite information from audit. However:

• No new information external to return is cited  
• No third-party evidence  
• No contradictory material  

The notice is largely inferential. Courts have repeatedly held that “change of opinion” or reappraisal of same record is not definite information.

Eighth: Failure to Address Withholding Compliance

If the payment was made to a non-resident, compliance under section 152 should have been examined. If withholding was properly deducted and deposited, that strengthens genuineness. The notice ignores this aspect entirely.

Ninth: No Segregation of Capital vs Revenue in TSF

The officer alleges that services were low value or non-chargeable but does not classify whether the payment resulted in:

• enduring benefit (capital nature under section 21), or  
• operational advisory (revenue nature)

The reasoning remains internally inconsistent — at one point alleging no service, at another alleging low-value service.

That logical contradiction weakens the proposed adjustment.

Tenth: Comparative Table – Incomplete and Selective

The table comparing FOTCO, Fauji Akbar Portia, Engro Vopak etc. (page 2) fileciteturn0file0 lacks:

• ownership pattern comparison  
• international group affiliation analysis  
• scope of technical integration  
• concession agreement differences  

Transfer pricing comparability requires functional similarity, not merely industry similarity.

Conclusion

From a professional tax litigation perspective, the notice on the Technical Service Fee suffers from:

• Misapplication of burden of proof  
• Incorrect evidentiary standard  
• Procedural non-compliance under section 108  
• Absence of benchmarking methodology  
• Speculative profit shifting allegation  
• No structured ALP computation  
• Conflation of commercial judgment with tax adjustment  
• Weak “definite information” foundation  

The adjustment as framed appears legally vulnerable at appellate forums unless supported by detailed FAR and benchmarking analysis.

In transfer pricing disputes, precision matters. Allegation without methodology is like assessing customs duty without valuation rules — structurally unstable.

**Input Tax Adjustment and Its Calculation Along with Allied Matters**

Since the digital subscription services are treated as taxable services under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, OUP SMC is entitled to claim adjustment of input tax against the output tax charged on such digital supplies, subject to fulfillment of the prescribed statutory conditions. Input tax will be admissible where the underlying services are acquired for business purposes, are directly or proportionately attributable to taxable digital operations, and are supported by valid tax invoices issued by duly registered suppliers under the Sindh sales tax regime. In addition, the tax charged by the supplier must have been properly declared and deposited in accordance with the law.

Admissible input tax would typically include sales tax paid on local IT services, software development, platform maintenance, digital infrastructure support, marketing and advertising services, professional advisory services, and other taxable operational services used in providing the online educational platforms. However, input tax will not be available in respect of exempt supplies such as printed books, non-business expenditures, or services procured from unregistered persons (unless otherwise specifically allowed). Further, offshore recharges or foreign service costs not subjected to Sindh sales tax would not qualify as adjustable input tax under the provincial framework.

The calculation mechanism is straightforward in principle: output tax charged on digital subscription revenue for a tax period is reduced by the admissible input tax incurred during the same period, and the net amount is payable to SRB. For instance, if digital subscription revenue for a month amounts to PKR 10,000,000 and sales tax is applied at 3%, the output tax would be PKR 300,000. If admissible input tax for the same period is PKR 220,000, the net sales tax payable would be PKR 80,000. The same computation would apply under the standard rate; however, the overall tax incidence and input recovery efficiency would differ depending upon whether the reduced-rate option or the standard rate is adopted.

Given that OUP SMC also makes exempt supplies (i.e., printed books), proper apportionment becomes essential where common expenses relate to both taxable digital services and exempt activities. In such cases, only the portion of input tax attributable to taxable services can be claimed, and a reasonable and consistently applied allocation basis—commonly revenue-based—should be adopted and documented. Inadequate segregation or absence of an apportionment methodology may result in disallowance during audit proceedings.

It is also important to consider that if the reduced-rate option (such as 3% under CPC 843 in Sindh) is exercised, certain limitations may apply regarding input tax carry-forward or adjustment mechanics under the relevant rules. Therefore, a financial impact assessment should be conducted to evaluate whether the reduced rate or the standard rate yields a more efficient tax position, particularly where the cost structure involves significant taxable inputs.

From a compliance perspective, maintaining proper documentation, segregating digital operations within the accounting system, reconciling input tax ledgers with monthly SRB returns, and ensuring consistency between ERP records and filed returns are critical. Input tax adjustment is fundamentally documentation-driven, and disciplined record management significantly mitigates exposure during departmental scrutiny or audit.

**Input Tax Adjustment and Its Calculation Along with Allied Matters**

Since the digital subscriptions are treated as taxable services under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, OUP SMC will be entitled to claim input tax adjustment on sales tax paid on services used or consumed for providing such taxable services, subject to admissibility conditions prescribed under the Act and Rules.

**Admissibility of Input Tax**

Input tax may be claimed where:

- The supplier is duly registered with SRB.
- A valid tax invoice containing prescribed particulars is available.
- The service is directly attributable to the taxable digital activity.
- The tax has been properly deposited by the supplier (as reflected in SRB system, where applicable).

Typical admissible input services may include:

- Local IT and software development services,
- Platform maintenance and technical support,
- Marketing and advertising services,
- Professional advisory services,
- Office utilities and other taxable support services.

However, input tax will not be admissible on:

- Services used for exempt supplies (e.g., printed books),
- Non-business or personal expenses,
- Services received from unregistered persons (unless otherwise allowed),
- Offshore recharges not subjected to Sindh sales tax.

**Calculation Mechanism**

The input tax adjustment is computed monthly as follows:

Output Tax (on digital subscriptions)  
Less: Admissible Input Tax (on taxable services used for digital operations)  
= Net Sales Tax Payable to SRB  

For example, if digital subscription revenue for a month is PKR 10,000,000 and tax is charged at 3%, output tax will be PKR 300,000. If admissible input tax amounts to PKR 220,000, the net payable will be PKR 80,000.

If the standard rate (15%) is applied instead of the reduced rate, the output tax increases proportionately; however, input tax recovery may become more efficient depending on the cost structure.

**Apportionment in Case of Mixed Supplies**

Since OUP SMC also makes exempt supplies (i.e., printed books), input tax attributable to common expenses must be apportioned between taxable and exempt activities in accordance with the apportionment rules. Only the portion attributable to taxable digital services can be claimed. This requires maintaining a reasonable and consistent allocation basis (for example, revenue-based or activity-based allocation).

Failure to properly apportion may lead to disallowance during audit.

**Reduced Rate Option – Impact on Input Tax**

If OUP SMC opts for the reduced rate (e.g., 3% under CPC 843 in Sindh), the option must be exercised in accordance with prescribed rules. Typically, reduced-rate regimes may restrict carry-forward of excess input tax or limit adjustment flexibility. Therefore, a financial evaluation should be undertaken before finalizing the option, especially where input-heavy cost structures exist.

**Documentation and Controls**

From a compliance perspective, it is advisable to:

- Maintain a separate cost center for digital operations,
- Ensure proper segregation of invoices for taxable vs exempt activities,
- Reconcile input tax ledger with SRB return monthly,
- Maintain supplier tax payment confirmations where necessary.

Input tax adjustment is not merely a mechanical deduction; it is a documentation-driven entitlement. Proper structuring at the accounting level significantly reduces exposure during audit proceedings.
In paragraph form

**E-invoicing requirements, if any**

Since the sales tax on these digital products is to be discharged under the relevant provincial sales tax law — in this case, the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 — the federal FBR e-invoicing regime (which is primarily designed for goods under the Sales Tax Act, 1990) is not applicable.

Under the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) framework, there is presently no mandatory real-time e-invoicing integration requirement specifically prescribed for online content services classified under CPC 84311. Accordingly, OUP SMC is not currently required to integrate its ERP system with any SRB live invoice transmission portal for these digital subscriptions.

However, SRB requires that all taxable services be properly invoiced in accordance with the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules, 2011. Therefore, each tax invoice must contain:

- SRB registration number,
- name and address of the customer,
- description of service (clearly reflecting digital subscription / online content),
- applicable CPC classification (for internal consistency and audit defensibility),
- gross value,
- amount of Sindh sales tax charged,
- and total invoice value.

While real-time e-invoicing may not be mandatory at this stage, the ERP system should be structured to generate compliant tax invoices and maintain digital records capable of being exported or submitted electronically in case SRB expands its electronic monitoring regime in future. Given the increasing digitization trend in provincial tax administrations, system readiness is advisable from a governance and risk-management perspective.

In summary, no separate SRB e-invoicing integration is currently required for these digital products; however, compliant electronic invoice generation and proper documentation remain mandatory under provincial law.

Under the current structure, a clear and defensible position already exists — namely that the digital services are supplied from the centralized head office in Sindh. Where contracts are executed, invoicing is generated, revenue is recorded, customer management is handled, and platform administration is controlled from Karachi, the “place of business of the supplier” principle becomes a strong jurisdictional basis. This is not a theoretical argument; it is a commercially grounded and legally recognized position that has been relied upon in multi-provincial service models.

That said, the provincial sales tax framework in Pakistan — particularly in relation to digital services — is still evolving. Other provinces may attempt to assert a consumption-based argument on the basis that users access the services within their territory. Such a contention is legally debatable and could potentially lead to litigation. The issue is arguable on both sides; however, the Sindh-based centralized supply position is reasonable and defensible.

From a practical standpoint, one should not assume that if another province were to raise a demand, an automatic refund would seamlessly be available from Sindh. Inter-provincial refund mechanisms are not streamlined. While a refund may be legally claimable if tax has already been discharged in Sindh in good faith, the process would involve formal proceedings, documentation, and verification. It is therefore important to recognize that while refund is legally supportable, it may not be administratively frictionless.

Based on experience with other clients operating across provinces, overlapping enforcement is not common where the supplier’s operational, contractual, billing, and financial control functions are demonstrably centralized in one province. In several cases, provincial authorities have withdrawn or moderated their position once it is established that sales tax has already been paid elsewhere and that the taxpayer has acted consistently and transparently. Courts generally take a practical view and are reluctant to allow double taxation in substance, even where jurisdictional debates exist.

Accordingly, while the matter remains technically debatable and litigation cannot be entirely ruled out, the current Sindh-based reporting position has solid legal and commercial grounding. The key protection lies in maintaining consistency, proper documentation of centralized operations, clear contractual positioning, and disciplined compliance. If these elements are properly managed, the likelihood of sustained overlapping taxation exposure remains moderate rather than high.

If another province seeks to assert sales tax jurisdiction over these digital products on a consumption basis, the position would become one of competing provincial claims. In principle, sales tax on services is intended to be levied only once on the same supply. Therefore, if Sindh sales tax has already been charged and deposited, and another province successfully establishes that tax was legally payable in its jurisdiction instead of Sindh, the taxpayer would generally be entitled to seek refund or adjustment from Sindh, subject to the statutory refund procedure and documentary substantiation.

However, practically speaking, obtaining an inter-provincial refund is neither automatic nor administratively simple. Refunds under provincial sales tax laws require formal application, reconciliation of tax payments, verification by the tax authority, and satisfaction that tax was indeed paid in excess or under a mistaken jurisdictional assumption. Inter-provincial coordination mechanisms remain limited, and such situations can result in temporary cash flow exposure until the matter is resolved.

From our practical experience with other clients operating digital or multi-provincial service models, it is relatively uncommon for multiple provinces to aggressively pursue overlapping tax claims where the supplier’s registered office, contract execution, billing, and operational control are demonstrably located in one province (e.g., Sindh in the present case). In most cases, authorities tend to respect the “place of business of supplier” principle where documentation clearly supports that position. That said, the risk cannot be entirely ruled out, particularly in a consumption-based interpretation environment and in sectors involving online or digital services accessed across provincial boundaries.

Accordingly, while the likelihood of immediate overlapping enforcement may be moderate rather than high — provided the Sindh-based supply model is properly documented and consistently applied — the risk is not theoretical. It is advisable to maintain clear documentation demonstrating that contracts, invoicing, platform administration, and commercial management are centrally operated from Karachi. This strengthens the defensibility of Sindh as the primary taxing jurisdiction.

In the unlikely event that another province successfully establishes jurisdiction and tax becomes payable there, a refund from Sindh would legally be claimable, though timing and procedural aspects would need to be managed carefully.

In short, dual taxation should not arise as a matter of law, but procedural friction can occur in practice. The key safeguard is strong structural documentation supporting the chosen place of taxation.

If any other province attempts to assert sales tax jurisdiction over these digital supplies, the matter would become legally debatable and may potentially lead to litigation. However, it is important to note that a defensible and already adopted position exists in the present structure — namely, that the entire commercial operation is centralized at the head office in Sindh. 

Where contracts are executed, billing is generated, revenue is recorded, platform administration is managed, and financial control is exercised from the head office, the “place of business of supplier” principle becomes a strong jurisdictional anchor. This is not a casual argument; it is a recognized interpretative position that has been relied upon in multi-provincial service models.

That said, provincial sales tax laws in Pakistan are still evolving, and digital services especially remain an area where competing interpretations can arise. Therefore, while our position is legally reasonable and commercially defensible, it would be inaccurate to say that litigation risk is zero. The issue is arguable — and because it is arguable, it is also contestable.

With respect to refund, practically speaking, one should not assume that an automatic refund will be granted by Sindh if another province raises a demand. Inter-provincial adjustments are not seamless in Pakistan. Even if a legal case for refund exists, the process can be lengthy and documentation-heavy. Refund is legally claimable, but not frictionless.

However, strong arguments do exist in support of refund if it is demonstrated that:

- Tax was already discharged in Sindh in good faith,
- The supply was treated consistently as Sindh-based,
- No suppression or misclassification occurred,
- And there is no double benefit claimed.

In past matters across jurisdictions, courts have often taken a practical view. In certain cases, provincial authorities have withdrawn or softened demands once it is demonstrated that sales tax has already been paid elsewhere and that the taxpayer has acted transparently and consistently. Courts generally disfavor double taxation in substance, even where technical jurisdictional disputes exist.

Therefore, the key safeguard is not fear — it is structure. If the head office in Sindh is demonstrably the commercial nerve center, and documentation supports centralized supply, the position is reasonable and defensible. It may be debated; it may even be litigated; but it is not weak.

The practical recommendation remains:

- Continue reporting in Sindh consistently.
- Maintain clear evidence of centralized operations.
- Avoid mixed or shifting tax positions across provinces.
- Keep reconciliations clean and defensible.

In summary, while the matter is debatable and litigation is theoretically possible, the adopted Sindh-based position has solid grounding. Refund from another authority is not automatic, but reasonable arguments would exist if ever required to pursue it. The strength of the case will depend entirely on consistency, documentation, and commercial substance — not merely legal wording.

**E-Invoicing Requirements, if any**

Since the sales tax on these digital products is discharged under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 before the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB), the federal FBR e-invoicing regime (applicable to goods under the Sales Tax Act, 1990) is not relevant in the present case.

Under the current SRB framework, mandatory real-time e-invoicing integration has, by and large, been implemented for specific sectors — most notably restaurants operating through POS integration. The electronic integration requirements primarily target food chains and similar retail outlets to ensure real-time sales reporting. Such regime is not generally extended to online educational content services or CPC 84311 (on-line books supplied electronically).

Accordingly, OUP SMC is not presently required to integrate its ERP system with any SRB real-time e-invoice transmission platform for its digital subscription products.

That said, the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules, 2011 require issuance of proper tax invoices containing prescribed particulars, including:

- SRB registration number,
- name and address of the customer,
- description of service (clearly identifying digital subscription / online access),
- gross value,
- amount of Sindh sales tax charged,
- and total invoice value.

From a governance perspective, the ERP should remain capable of generating compliant tax invoices and maintaining proper electronic records, particularly in view of SRB’s increasing digitization initiatives. While real-time e-invoicing is not applicable in the instant case, statutory invoice compliance and record retention remain mandatory under provincial law.

**Details of compliances resulting from registration with tax authority**

As stated earlier, no fresh registration is required since Oxford University Press Pakistan (SMC-Private) Limited is already duly registered with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB). However, once the digital products are formally treated as taxable services under the relevant CPC classification, certain ongoing compliance obligations arise under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011.

Primarily, OUP SMC will be required to issue proper sales tax invoices in accordance with the prescribed requirements of the Act and the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules, 2011. Each invoice must contain complete particulars, including SRB registration number, description of the digital service provided, gross value of supply, amount of Sindh sales tax charged at the applicable rate, and total invoice value. Care should be taken to ensure that digital subscriptions are clearly segregated from exempt printed book supplies to avoid classification disputes.

In addition, monthly sales tax returns must be filed within the prescribed due date (currently the 18th of the following month in Sindh), reflecting output tax on digital supplies and any admissible input tax adjustments. Proper reconciliation between invoicing records, ERP revenue reports, and the figures declared in the SRB return should be maintained to ensure consistency and audit defensibility.

Apart from periodic return filing and tax payment, OUP SMC must maintain adequate records of contracts, subscription data, and supporting documentation for a minimum statutory retention period, as these may be called for during audit or scrutiny proceedings by SRB.

Below is the updated advisory content that can be shared with management.

---

## Updated Advisory – Post Registration & Operational Compliance Framework  

### 1. System Integration Post Registration with Tax Authority  

Once OUP SMC proceeds with registration under the relevant provincial sales tax law (recommended: Sindh Sales Tax, if adopting Sindh as primary jurisdiction), the following system integrations become necessary:

**a) ERP / Billing System Configuration**

The invoicing module must be configured to:

- Classify digital subscriptions under CPC 84311 (On-line books supplied electronically).
- Auto-apply applicable provincial sales tax rate (3% if opting reduced rate in Sindh; otherwise 15%).
- Segregate printed book sales (exempt under Sixth Schedule) from digital receipts.
- Clearly reflect:
  - Gross subscription value  
  - Provincial Sales Tax  
  - Final tax under section 6A (Income Tax – 1%/2% deduction by intermediary)

Failure to segregate may jeopardize printed book exemption and create audit exposure.

**b) Payment Gateway Mapping (Section 6A Compliance)**

Payment intermediaries must be formally notified in writing that:

- OUP SMC supplies digitally delivered services under section 6A.
- Tax must be deducted at:
  - 1% on digital payments  
  - 2% on COD  
- Deduction must be on gross invoice value including provincial sales tax.

A reconciliation mechanism must be embedded monthly between:

- Gross ERP sales  
- Payment gateway settlement statements  
- Section 6A withholding certificates  
- Bank receipts  

This avoids mismatch during assessment proceedings.

**c) POS / Digital Invoice Integration**

If required by provincial authority (especially Sindh), digital platform invoicing may need integration with SRB’s e-portal or API system once notified. System capability for API-based invoice transmission should be kept ready.

---

### 2. E-Invoicing Requirements  

At present:

- **Federal FBR e-invoicing** applies to goods under Sales Tax Act, 1990.
- Digital subscriptions are not goods.
- Therefore, FBR e-invoicing does not apply.

However, under provincial sales tax:

- Sindh is gradually expanding digital invoice reporting.
- If classified under CPC 84311 and registered with SRB, invoice reporting through the SRB portal will be mandatory.
- Punjab and KPK currently require periodic return reporting but not real-time invoice transmission (subject to change).

Practical step:
System should generate tax-compliant invoice containing:
- SRB registration number  
- CPC classification  
- Tax rate applied  
- Gross value  
- Tax charged separately  

---

### 3. Compliance Obligations After Registration  

Once registered for provincial sales tax:

**Monthly Compliance**

- Monthly Sales Tax Return (usually by 18th of next month in Sindh)
- Payment of output tax after adjustment of admissible input tax
- Reconciliation between:
  - ERP revenue  
  - Sales tax return  
  - Income under section 6A  

**Annual / Audit Exposure**

- Possible provincial audit under Section 25 of SST Act
- Maintenance of:
  - Subscription contracts  
  - Hosting agreements  
  - Royalty arrangements  
  - Intercompany recharge agreements  
  - CPC classification justification  

**Income Tax Compliance**

Even though section 6A is final tax:

- Gross receipts must still be declared in annual return.
- Income to be shown under “Final Tax Regime – Digital Services”.
- Section 6A deductions must be reconciled via withholding statements (Annexure).

---

### 4. Input Tax Adjustment & Calculation  

Now the interesting part — the economics.

If Sindh 3% reduced rate option is exercised:

- Output tax = 3% of gross subscription value.
- Input tax adjustment may be restricted (subject to Rule 42I conditions).
- Often reduced rate schemes restrict carry-forward of excess input.

If standard 15% is applied:

- Output tax = 15%.
- Full input tax adjustment allowed (subject to admissibility).
- Better for cost-heavy digital operations.

Example:

If monthly digital revenue = PKR 10,000,000  

Under 3%:
Output tax = 300,000  
If input tax = 250,000 → net payable = 50,000  

Under 15%:
Output tax = 1,500,000  
If input tax = 250,000 → net payable = 1,250,000  

However, pricing impact must be evaluated because schools may not claim input tax.

Key input tax considerations:

Admissible:
- Local hosting charges (if Sindh registered supplier)
- Local IT services
- Platform support charges
- Marketing services
- Professional services

Not admissible:
- Intercompany offshore recharge (outside provincial jurisdiction)
- Exempt supplies proportion (if printed books and digital bundled)

Apportionment may be required if mixed supplies exist.

---

### 5. Practical Risk Controls  

To avoid litigation:

1. Explicitly mention on invoice:  
   “Tax under section 6A deducted by intermediary as final tax.”

2. Maintain province-wise revenue analysis.

3. Keep clear documentation that service is supplied from Karachi (place of business principle).

4. Avoid bundling digital access value invisibly inside printed book price — must be separately priced.

---

### Strategic Observation  

This is not merely a tax registration issue. It is a structural shift from:
- Publishing model  
to  
- Digital service provider model  

The law has now explicitly captured e-learning under “digitally delivered services.” The opportunity here is compliance clarity before audit pressure arrives.

Digital tax frameworks globally are evolving. Pakistan has now formally entered that phase. Businesses that systemize early will sleep better during scrutiny.

If required, I can also prepare:
- A compliance checklist for IT team  
- A financial comparison note: 3% vs 15% model  
- Draft communication to payment intermediaries  

The digital economy isn’t just about content. It’s about documentation.

### **Computation of Aggregate Tax Incidence under the Fifth Schedule and Governing PCA – Rule 1 Segregation and Ceiling-Sensitive Application of Section 4C**

It is respectfully submitted that our client has duly examined and determined the aggregate tax incidence on income arising under Rule 1 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule for Tax Year 2022. As contemplated in paragraph (viii) of the judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court dated January 27, 2026, the aggregate tax incidence necessarily comprises income tax chargeable under the Fifth Schedule, surcharge (where applicable), and super tax under section 4C, if lawfully leviable. The detailed working of income computed under Rule 1, the corresponding tax computation, and reconciliation with the return of income and audited financial statements were duly filed along with the return for Tax Year 2022 and are already available on record with your good office. The computation has been undertaken strictly within the statutory parameters of the Fifth Schedule and in conformity with the fiscal provisions contained in the governing Petroleum Concession Agreement (PCA).

In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the relevant PCA, including the Supplemental Agreement dated March 18, 2014 for Kirthar Block, expressly incorporates the fiscal option under Sub-Rule 4A of Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule, enabling the Working Interest Owner to pay tax at the rate of forty percent (40%) on profits and gains derived from joint operations, effective from tax year 2012 onwards. fileciteturn4file0 The Supplemental Agreement further clarifies that once exercised, the rate of forty percent (40%) shall not be increased for the term of the Agreement, and that subsequent amendments to Sub-Rule 4A or otherwise shall not affect the stabilized fiscal position agreed between the parties. This contractual stabilization reinforces the statutory framework governing petroleum taxation under the Fifth Schedule.

Consistent with Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule, income arising from petroleum exploration and production under each PCA has been treated as a separate business undertaking. Such income has been clearly segregated from income from other sources (if any), computed independently as a distinct undertaking, and fully reconciled with the audited financial statements and the return of income for Tax Year 2022. The relevant computation schedules, reconciliation statements, and supporting workings already form part of the return documentation and are available on record.

With respect to the applicability of section 4C, paragraph (viii) of the Federal Constitutional Court judgment unequivocally directs that sections 4B and 4C shall apply to E&P companies only to the extent that such application does not result in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes prescribed under the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCA. The Court has further mandated that the departmental determination must be undertaken PCA-wise, restricted strictly to income arising under Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule, and that section 4C shall not apply where its application results in exceeding the threshold stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule, in the absence of express legislative intent.

In light of these binding directions, any determination of super tax liability must necessarily be tested against the aggregate tax ceiling prescribed under the Fifth Schedule and the governing PCA. Our client respectfully submits that its petroleum income for Tax Year 2022 has already been subjected to tax in accordance with the applicable rate structure under the Fifth Schedule and the stabilized fiscal terms incorporated in the PCA and its Supplemental Agreement. The aggregate tax incidence has therefore been computed strictly within the fiscal parameters governing the petroleum undertaking. Accordingly, any levy of super tax under section 4C must be examined in a ceiling-sensitive manner consistent with paragraph (viii) of the judgment. To the extent that application of section 4C would result in taxation exceeding the aggregate threshold prescribed under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule and/or the governing PCA, such application would not be legally sustainable in view of the binding judicial pronouncement and the contractual stabilization embodied in the PCA.

The notice seeks particulars regarding the applicable tax regime governing each PCA, computation of aggregate tax incidence, working of income under Rule 1 segregated from other income, and evidence as to whether section 4C results in exceeding the prescribed ceiling. In this regard, it is respectfully submitted that copies of the relevant PCAs and supplemental agreements have already been furnished to your good office; the return of income for Tax Year 2022 contains complete computation of income under Rule 1 and tax payable thereon; the segregation and reconciliation workings are already on record; and the aggregate tax position has been determined strictly in accordance with the Fifth Schedule and the governing PCA. The Company has therefore fully complied with the requisitions contained in the notice under section 176(1).
