**Reply to Notice under section 176(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**  
**Determination of Applicability and Computation of Super Tax under Section 4C**

Dear Madam,

We refer to your notice issued under section 176(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“Ordinance”) dated February 19, 2026, whereby the Company has been required to furnish particulars for determination of applicability and computation of Super Tax under section 4C in light of paragraph (viii) of the judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court dated January 27, 2026.

This reply is being submitted respectfully in compliance with the requisitions contained in the said notice and in continuation of the information and documentation already furnished to your good office.

---

### 1. Preliminary Submissions and Legal Framework

Prime Global Energies Limited (“the Company”) is an Exploration and Production (E&P) company engaged in petroleum exploration and production activities under duly executed Petroleum Concession Agreements (“PCAs”) with the Federal Government. The taxation of such operations is governed by Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Ordinance, which constitutes a special fiscal regime for petroleum undertakings.

In terms of Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule, where a person carries on petroleum exploration or production under an agreement with the Federal Government, such business is treated as a separate business undertaking. The income arising therefrom is required to be computed and taxed in accordance with the provisions of the Fifth Schedule and the applicable PCA.

Accordingly, the Company’s petroleum income for Tax Year 2022 has been computed and offered to tax strictly in accordance with the Fifth Schedule and the governing PCAs.

---

### 2. Furnishing of Petroleum Concession Agreements – Already on Record

Your good office had previously issued a notice under section 176 requiring submission of copies of the relevant PCAs. In compliance thereof, the Company furnished complete copies of the applicable PCAs vide its letter dated February 17, 2026 (DT-2930), wherein the same were enclosed as Annexure A. The said letter and enclosures are already part of the departmental record. fileciteturn2file0  

Accordingly, the contractual framework governing each petroleum area operated by the Company, including the fiscal terms agreed with the Federal Government, stands duly provided to your good office.

Therefore, the requirement in the present notice regarding the applicable tax regime governing each PCA is already satisfied, as the PCAs themselves define the fiscal structure under which the Company operates.

---

### 3. Applicable Tax Regime under the Fifth Schedule

Each PCA executed by the Company constitutes an “agreement” within the meaning of Rule 1 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule. Consequently, the income derived from petroleum exploration and production under each PCA is treated as a separate business undertaking.

The applicable tax regime governing such income is the special petroleum regime under the Fifth Schedule, read together with the specific fiscal provisions contained in the respective PCA.

For Tax Year 2022, the Company has:

- Computed taxable income arising under Rule 1 separately from any other income;  
- Applied the rate of tax prescribed under the Fifth Schedule; and  
- Determined tax liability in accordance with the fiscal structure applicable to its petroleum operations.

---

### 4. Computation of Aggregate Tax Incidence

In compliance with your notice, the Company has examined the aggregate tax incidence on income arising under Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule for Tax Year 2022.

The aggregate tax incidence, as contemplated in paragraph (viii) of the Federal Constitutional Court judgment, includes:

- Income tax under the Fifth Schedule;  
- Surcharge, if applicable; and  
- Super tax under section 4C, if lawfully chargeable.

The detailed working of income under Rule 1, computation of tax thereon, and reconciliation with the return of income and audited financial statements were duly filed with the return for Tax Year 2022 and are already available on record.

The Company respectfully submits that the computation of tax has been undertaken strictly within the parameters of the Fifth Schedule and the governing PCA, and that the aggregate tax incidence has been determined accordingly.

---

### 5. Segregation and Reconciliation of Rule 1 Income

As directed in the notice, the Company confirms that income arising from petroleum exploration and production under each PCA has been:

- Segregated from income from other sources (if any);  
- Computed separately as a distinct undertaking in accordance with Rule 1; and  
- Reconciled with the audited financial statements and the return of income for Tax Year 2022.

The relevant schedules and reconciliation statements form part of the return documentation already filed and are available with your office.

---

### 6. Application of Section 4C in Light of Federal Constitutional Court Judgment

Paragraph (viii) of the judgment dated January 27, 2026 clearly directs that:

- Sections 4B and 4C shall apply to E&P companies only to the extent that such application does not result in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes provided in the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCA;  
- The departmental determination must be undertaken PCA-wise;  
- The exercise must be restricted to income arising under Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule; and  
- Section 4C shall not apply where its application results in exceeding the threshold stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule, in the absence of express legislative intent.

In light of the above binding directions, any determination of super tax under section 4C must be tested against the aggregate tax ceiling prescribed under the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCA.

The Company respectfully submits that:

- Its petroleum income has already been subjected to tax in accordance with the applicable rate structure under the Fifth Schedule;  
- The aggregate tax incidence has been computed within the fiscal parameters governing the PCA; and  
- Any levy of super tax under section 4C must be examined strictly in a ceiling-sensitive manner in compliance with paragraph (viii) of the judgment.

To the extent that application of section 4C would result in taxation exceeding the aggregate threshold prescribed under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule and/or the governing PCA, such application would not be sustainable in view of the binding judicial directions.

---

### 7. Compliance with Notice and Availability of Record

The notice seeks particulars regarding:

- The applicable tax regime governing each PCA;  
- Computation of aggregate tax incidence;  
- Working of income under Rule 1 segregated from other income; and  
- Evidence as to whether section 4C results in exceeding the prescribed ceiling.

It is respectfully submitted that:

- Copies of the relevant PCAs have already been furnished to your good office;  
- The return of income for Tax Year 2022 contains complete computation of income under Rule 1 and tax payable thereon;  
- The segregation and reconciliation workings are already on record; and  
- The aggregate tax position has been determined in accordance with the Fifth Schedule and the governing PCA.

Accordingly, the Company has fully complied with the requisitions contained in the notice under section 176(1).

---

### 8. Request for Determination in Accordance with Law

The Company respectfully requests that any determination of super tax liability for Tax Year 2022 be undertaken strictly:

- PCA-wise;  
- Restricted to income arising under Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule;  
- In conformity with the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCA; and  
- In faithful adherence to paragraph (viii) of the Federal Constitutional Court judgment.

The Company remains available to provide any further clarification or to attend a hearing, should your good office deem it necessary prior to making any determination, as contemplated by the judgment.

We trust that the above submissions sufficiently address the requirements of the captioned notice.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
**Prime Global Energies Limited**

Assistant Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Unit-4, Zone-II  
Large Taxpayers Office  
Karachi  

**Subject: Reply to Notice under section 176(1) – Determination of applicability and computation of Super Tax under section 4C – Tax Year 2022**  
**Prime Global Energies Limited**

Dear Madam,

We refer to your notice issued under section 176(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“Ordinance”) dated February 19, 2026 in the matter of determination of applicability and computation of Super Tax under section 4C for Tax Year 2022, in light of paragraph (viii) of the judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court dated January 27, 2026.

This reply is submitted respectfully in compliance with the directions contained in the notice and in continuation of the information already furnished to your good office.

At the outset, it is submitted that the Company is an Exploration & Production (E&P) company whose petroleum operations are governed by the Fifth Schedule to the Ordinance read with the relevant Petroleum Concession Agreements (“PCAs”) executed with the Federal Government under the applicable petroleum regulatory framework. The taxation of such operations constitutes a separate business undertaking in terms of Rule 1 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule.

**1. Furnishing of Petroleum Concession Agreements**

Your good office had earlier issued notice under section 176 calling for copies of the PCAs. In compliance thereof, the Company had furnished complete copies of the relevant PCAs vide our letter dated February 17, 2026 (DT-2930), wherein the same were enclosed as Annexure A. The said letter and enclosures are already on record of your office.

Accordingly, the contractual framework governing the Company’s petroleum operations, including the fiscal terms agreed with the Federal Government, stands duly provided and forms part of the departmental record.

**2. Applicable Tax Regime Governing Each PCA**

Each of the Company’s petroleum areas is governed by a duly executed PCA with the Federal Government. In terms of Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule, income arising from petroleum exploration and production under such agreement is treated as a separate business undertaking and is taxed in accordance with the Fifth Schedule.

The applicable fiscal regime is therefore the special petroleum taxation regime under the Fifth Schedule, read with the terms and conditions of the respective PCA. The income arising under Rule 1 has been computed and offered to tax strictly in accordance with the rates and principles prescribed therein.

**3. Computation of Aggregate Tax Incidence under the Fifth Schedule**

In accordance with your notice, the Company has examined the aggregate tax incidence on income arising under Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule for Tax Year 2022.

The aggregate tax incidence includes:

- Income tax under the Fifth Schedule;
- Any surcharge, where applicable; and  
- Super tax under section 4C, if applicable.

The computation of taxable income under the Fifth Schedule, along with the working of tax payable, was duly filed with the return of income for Tax Year 2022 and is fully reconciled with the audited financial statements and tax return.

It is respectfully submitted that the Company’s petroleum income has been taxed in accordance with the applicable rate structure under the Fifth Schedule and within the fiscal parameters prescribed therein and under the respective PCA.

**4. Segregation of Income under Rule 1**

As required in the notice, the Company confirms that income arising from petroleum exploration and production under each PCA has been treated as a separate business undertaking under Rule 1 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule.

Such income has been:

- Computed separately from income from other sources (if any);  
- Properly segregated in the return of income; and  
- Reconciled with the financial statements.

The workings in this regard form part of the return documentation already available with your office.

**5. Effect of Section 4C vis-à-vis Fifth Schedule and PCA Ceiling**

Paragraph (viii) of the judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court clearly directs that:

- Section 4C shall apply to E&P companies only in a manner that does not result in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes provided in the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCA;  
- The determination is to be undertaken PCA-wise;  
- The exercise is to be restricted to income arising under Rule 1; and  
- In the absence of express legislative intent, section 4C cannot be applied where it causes taxation to exceed the threshold stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule.

In light of the above, the Company has examined whether the application of section 4C to its Rule 1 income would result in exceeding the aggregate tax ceiling prescribed under the Fifth Schedule and/or the respective PCA.

It is respectfully submitted that:

- The aggregate tax incidence on the Company’s petroleum income has been computed strictly within the fiscal framework of the Fifth Schedule and the PCA;  
- Any levy of super tax under section 4C must be tested against the aggregate ceiling prescribed therein; and  
- To the extent that application of section 4C would result in exceeding the protected threshold, the same would not be sustainable in view of the binding directions of the Federal Constitutional Court.

The Company therefore respectfully submits that the determination, if any, may kindly be undertaken strictly in accordance with paragraph (viii) of the judgment and after affording the Company an opportunity of hearing, as mandated therein.

**6. Information Already on Record**

The notice seeks particulars relating to:

- Applicable tax regime for each PCA;  
- Computation of aggregate tax incidence;  
- Working of Rule 1 income; and  
- Evidence regarding aggregate ceiling.

It is respectfully submitted that:

- Copies of all relevant PCAs have already been furnished (vide letter dated February 17, 2026);  
- The computation of income and tax under the Fifth Schedule was filed with the return; and  
- The relevant reconciliation and workings are already part of the record.

In view of the above, the Company submits that it has complied with the requirements of the notice under section 176(1).

**7. Conclusion**

Prime Global Energies Limited has consistently computed and discharged its tax liability for Tax Year 2022 in accordance with:

- The Fifth Schedule to the Ordinance;  
- The applicable Petroleum Concession Agreements; and  
- The prevailing law governing petroleum operations.

The Company remains fully prepared to assist your good office in any PCA-wise determination exercise as contemplated by the Federal Constitutional Court and respectfully requests that no adverse inference be drawn, as the requisite documentation and computations already stand furnished.

We trust that the above would sufficiently address the requirements of the captioned notice. However, should your good office require any specific clarification or hearing in terms of paragraph (viii) of the judgment, the Company shall be pleased to assist.

Yours faithfully,  

For and on behalf of  
Prime Global Energies Limited

I have carefully read the similar draft response titled “Reply to Notice under section 4C – Determination of applicability and recovery of Super Tax” submitted before LTO Karachi. fileciteturn1file0  

This draft is structured as a constitutional, statutory and fiscal-protection based defence against the application of section 4C to petroleum operations, and its architecture is quite clear:

First, it is positioned as a WITHOUT PREJUDICE preliminary reply, expressly reserving jurisdictional and constitutional objections, especially pending detailed Federal Constitutional Court reasoning.

Second, it builds its foundation on paragraph (viii) of the FCC short order and treats that paragraph as the controlling legal compass. The entire response is framed around the proposition that super tax cannot apply where it breaches the aggregate petroleum fiscal ceiling.

Third, it relies heavily on section 3B of the Regulation of Mines and Oilfields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948, arguing that:
- The non obstante clause gives it overriding force.
- The Schedule to the Mining Act fixes/caps petroleum taxation at 40%.
- That cap operates as a fiscal shield.

Fourth, it harmonizes:
- Rule 1 (separate undertaking),
- Rule 4 (40% reference),
- The Mining Act fiscal concession,
- The FCC direction.

The draft argues that:
- The Ordinance ensures tax does not fall below 40%.
- The Mining Act ensures tax does not exceed 40%.
- Therefore, the permissible range is effectively fixed at 40%.
- Any super tax exceeding that threshold violates both statute and FCC directions.

Fifth, it emphasizes PCA continuity — especially in relation to Sui Area — arguing that:
- Licences, renewals and authorizations constitute valid “agreements” under Rule 1.
- There was no break in Federal authorization.
- Post-Finance Act 2017, petroleum regime became fully applicable.

Sixth, it takes a defensive procedural position:
- All PCAs and workings already furnished.
- Aggregate tax computation already demonstrates 40%.
- Therefore, no further submission required.

Finally, the relief sought is straightforward:
- Drop the proposed levy.
- Hold that petroleum income already stands taxed at the maximum permissible 40%.

In essence, the draft is built on three pillars:
1. Constitutional direction (FCC para viii),
2. Special law override (Mining Act section 3B),
3. Aggregate fiscal ceiling doctrine (40% cap as upper limit).

It is a strong ceiling-based defence model rather than a computational rebuttal model.

From a strategic standpoint, this draft is ideal where:
- The company’s petroleum income is already taxed at 40%;
- The factual matrix clearly fits within Rule 1 income;
- There is no internal vulnerability in segregation or reconciliation.

The intellectual battleground in such cases is not arithmetic — it is hierarchy of laws and fiscal protection architecture.

We refer to your notice bearing barcode No. 100000271615381 issued under section 176(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Ordinance) dated February 19, 2026, whereby our above-mentioned client has been required to furnish particulars for determination of applicability and computation of Super Tax under sections 4B and 4C of the Ordinance in light of paragraph (viii) of the judgment of the Federal Constitutional Court dated January 27, 2026.

The petroleum exploration and production sector functions under a distinct fiscal and contractual regime, embedded in statutory protections and long-term stabilization commitments extended by the Federal Government. These commitments were designed to ensure certainty and predictability of the tax framework in a high-risk, capital-intensive industry that is critical to Pakistan’s energy security and macroeconomic stability.

3.	In this backdrop, the Pakistan Petroleum Exploration & Production Companies Association (PPEPCA), representing E&P companies operating in Pakistan, has formally taken up the matter with the Chairman, Federal Board of Revenue, vide its letter dated February 23, 2026 (copy is enclosed as 
Annexure ‘A’). In the said representation, it has been specifically highlighted that the fiscal regime governing PCAs incorporates stabilization clauses pursuant to which payments to the Federal Government, including income tax and other fiscal levies, were contractually frozen as of the execution date of the respective PCAs and were to remain protected throughout the term of such agreements. 

4.	The representation further underscores that any subsequent legislative changes inconsistent with the agreed fiscal stabilization framework cannot be made applicable to E&P companies operating under valid PCAs. The letter further highlights that the Federal Constitutional Court, while deciding the super tax litigation, expressly acknowledged the sanctity of the PCA stabilization framework and directed that any application of sections 4B and 4C must remain within the aggregate tax ceiling prescribed under the Fifth Schedule and the respective PCAs.

5.	Without prejudice to any constitutional or jurisdictional objections available in law, our client respectfully sets out below its position in compliance with the notice issued under section 176(1) of the Ordinance, strictly in accordance with the Fifth Schedule, the governing PCAs, and the binding directions of the Federal Constitutional Court.
6.	FURNISHING OF PETROLEUM CONCESSION AGREEMENTS – ALREADY ON RECORD

6.1	Your good office had previously issued a notice No. ACIR/Z-II/LTO/KHI/2025-26/228 dated February 11, 2026 under section 176 of the Ordinance, requiring submission of copies of the relevant PCAs. In compliance thereof, our client furnished complete copies of the applicable PCAs vide our letter DT 2930 dated February 17, 2026, wherein the same were enclosed as Annexure ‘B’. The said letter and enclosures are already part of the departmental record.

6.2	Accordingly, the contractual framework governing each petroleum area operated by our client, including the fiscal terms agreed with the Federal Government, stands duly provided to your good office. Therefore, the requirement in the present notice regarding the applicable tax regime governing each PCA is already satisfied, as the PCAs themselves define the fiscal structure under which our client operates.

7.	EXERCISE OF ONE-TIME OPTION UNDER RULE 4(4A) AND CONTRACTUAL EMBEDDING OF THE 40% FISCAL REGIME

7.1	It is respectfully submitted that our client expressly exercised the one-time irrevocable option available under paragraph (4A) of Rule 4 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Ordinance, thereby entering into a settled and stabilized fiscal regime with effect from tax year 2012 onward. The exercise of this option was subject to statutory conditions, including withdrawal of pending litigation concerning the applicable tax rate and discharge of outstanding tax liabilities up to tax year 2011. Upon fulfillment of these requirements and formal exercise of the option, the fiscal arrangement attained finality and became irrevocable, creating a binding and concluded fiscal settlement between the Federal Government and the respective Working Interest Owners, including our client.

7.2	Following the valid exercise of this option by our client, the relevant PCAs were amended through supplemental agreements to incorporate and reflect the revised fiscal structure. Copies of all respective supplemental agreements have already been furnished to your good office in response to earlier notices under section 176 of the Ordinance and form part of the departmental record. 

7.3	It is pertinent to clarify that the stabilization language and fiscal embedding of the 40% regime is consistently reflected across all amended PCAs submitted to your office. For illustrative purposes only, reference may be made to the Supplemental Agreement dated March 18, 2014 in respect of Kirthar Block, wherein the 40% tax rate was expressly incorporated into the contractual framework and protected for the term of the Agreement. 

7.4	The amended provisions categorically stipulate that once the option is exercised, tax shall be payable at the rate of forty percent (40%) of profits and gains from tax year 2012 onward and that such rate shall not be increased for the duration of the Agreement. For the sake of brevity, the operating paragraph of the aforesaid amended PCA is reproduce below: 
 
7.5	Accordingly, the 40% rate is not merely a statutory prescription under the Fifth Schedule; it forms an integral and contractually stabilized component of the fiscal regime governing our client’s petroleum undertakings under each of the submitted PCAs. The example cited above is representative in nature, and similar fiscal stabilization clauses are embedded in all amended PCAs already placed on record before your good office.

8.	FEDERAL CONSTITUTIONAL COURT JUDGMENT – CEILING-SENSITIVE APPLICATION OF SUPER TAX

8.1	The Federal Constitutional Court has recently upheld the constitutional validity of Super Tax under sections 4B and 4C of the Ordinance and clarified that section 4C constitutes a standalone levy on income. Nevertheless, the Court has categorically held that in the case of E&P companies governed by the Fifth Schedule and their respective PCAs, Super Tax cannot be applied in a manner that results in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule read together with the respective PCAs and the governing mining legislation.

8.2	The Court has further directed that the determination must be undertaken PCA-wise, restricted strictly to income arising under Rule 1 of the Fifth Schedule, and tested against the aggregate fiscal ceiling embedded in the statutory and contractual framework. Therefore, while the levy of Super Tax is constitutionally valid in general application, its enforceability in the case of E&P companies is expressly subject to the aggregate cap prescribed under the petroleum regime.


8.3	AGGREGATE FISCAL CEILING UNDER THE AMENDED PCA FRAMEWORK AND NON-APPLICABILITY OF ADDITIONAL SUPER TAX

8.4	In the case of companies that opted for the 40% regime and whose PCAs were subsequently amended to reflect that rate, the fiscal ceiling must necessarily be examined in light of both the Fifth Schedule and the amended contractual framework. Where the 40% rate represents the agreed and permissible aggregate tax incidence under the PCA structure, the imposition of additional Super Tax under sections 4B or 4C would result in exceeding the statutory and contractual ceiling.

8.5	In such circumstances, and in view of the binding findings of the Federal Constitutional Court, Super Tax would not be enforceable to the extent that it breaches the aggregate cap. Accordingly, while Super Tax remains constitutionally valid in principle, its application to E&P companies that have adopted the 40% regime must be determined strictly on a PCA-specific basis. Where the amended PCA embeds forty percent (40%) as the governing fiscal settlement and the aggregate threshold under Rule 4 read with Sub-Rule 4A has already been achieved, no additional Super Tax under sections 4B or 4C would be legally payable.

9.	STATUTORY FISCAL PROTECTION UNDER THE MINING ACT, 1948 – SECTION 3B

9.1	Without prejudice to the above, the Mining Act, 1948 is the governing statute for petroleum exploration and production and provides overriding fiscal protection to petroleum companies operating under licences and leases granted by the Federal Government. Section 3B of the Mining Act provides:
“3B. Concessions to petroleum exploration companies:

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, every company, whether incorporated in Pakistan or outside Pakistan, to whom a licence or a lease to explore, prospect and mine petroleum is granted under this Act, not being a company such as is referred to in sub section (1) of section 3A, shall be entitled to the concessions specified in the Schedule, in addition to the concessions for the time being admissible to it under any other law.”
9.2	By virtue of the non obstante clause in section 3B, the concessions in the Schedule to the Mining Act apply notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, including the Ordinance.

9.3	One of the substantive statutory concessions contained in the Schedule to the Mining Act is the fixation/capping of income tax on profits and gains derived from onshore petroleum operations at forty percent (40%). Consequently, the aggregate tax incidence on protected petroleum income cannot exceed this statutory ceiling in the absence of express legislative intent to override it.

10.	Harmonious Construction – No Conflict Between Rule 4 And Mining Act 

10.1	Rule 4(2) of Part I of the Fifth Schedule reflects the legislative intent that taxation of petroleum exploration and production income should not fall below the prescribed benchmark rate of forty percent (40%). At the same time, the Schedule to the Regulation of Mines and Oilfields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948, read with section 3B thereof, provides overriding statutory protection by fixing or effectively capping the income tax incidence on petroleum profits at forty percent (40%). The protection under section 3B operates notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force.

10.2	When these provisions are read harmoniously, a coherent fiscal framework emerges: The Ordinance, through Rule 4, ensures that the tax burden on petroleum income is not reduced below forty percent, while the Mining Act, through its overriding concession regime, prevents the aggregate tax incidence from exceeding that same threshold. In effect, the permissible taxation band for protected petroleum income stands aligned at forty percent (40%).

10.3	This interpretation is not merely theoretical but has been expressly endorsed by the Federal Constitutional Court. The Court has categorically directed that sections 4B and 4C cannot be applied to E&P companies to the extent that its application would result in taxation exceeding the threshold stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule, in the absence of clear and express legislative intent to override such protection. Accordingly, any determination under sections 4B and 4C must necessarily remain within the fiscal ceiling embedded in the petroleum regime.

11.	Special Law Prevails Over General Law

11.1	The Mining Act is a special statute governing petroleum exploration and production and contains an express overriding clause. Where a special law provides a protected fiscal regime, the general provisions of the Ordinance must yield to it, particularly when the Federal Constitutional Court has expressly mandated such an approach.

Rule 4(2) of Part I of the Fifth Schedule reflects the legislative intent that taxation of petroleum exploration and production income should not fall below the prescribed benchmark rate of forty percent. At the same time, the Schedule to the Regulation of Mines and Oilfields and Mineral Development (Government Control) Act, 1948, read with section 3B thereof, provides overriding statutory protection by fixing or effectively capping the income tax incidence on petroleum profits at forty percent. The protection under section 3B operates notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force.

When these provisions are read harmoniously, a coherent fiscal framework emerges: the Ordinance, through Rule 4, ensures that the tax burden on petroleum income is not reduced below forty percent, while the Mining Act, through its overriding concession regime, prevents the aggregate tax incidence from exceeding that same threshold. In effect, the permissible taxation band for protected petroleum income stands aligned at forty percent.

This interpretation is not merely theoretical but has been expressly endorsed by the Federal Constitutional Court. The Court has categorically directed that section 4C cannot be applied to E&P companies to the extent that its application would result in taxation exceeding the threshold stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule, in the absence of clear and express legislative intent to override such protection. Accordingly, any determination under section 4C must necessarily remain within the fiscal ceiling embedded in the petroleum regime.

### **II. Federal Constitutional Court Judgment – Ceiling-Sensitive Application of Super Tax**

The Federal Constitutional Court has recently upheld the constitutional validity of Super Tax under sections 4B and 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and clarified that section 4C constitutes a standalone levy on income. However, the Court has categorically held that in the case of E&P companies governed by the Fifth Schedule and their respective PCAs, Super Tax cannot be applied in a manner that results in exceeding the aggregate rate of taxes stipulated under Rule 4 of the Fifth Schedule read together with the respective PCAs and the governing mining legislation.

In the case of companies that opted for the 40% regime and whose PCAs were subsequently amended to reflect that rate, the fiscal ceiling must necessarily be examined in light of both the Fifth Schedule and the amended contractual framework. Dear Sir,  

We refer to your reminder dated 17-02-2026 issued in continuation of notice dated 10-04-2025 under section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2022, whereby recovery of alleged super tax amounting to Rs. 1,027,977,626 has been proposed fileciteturn0file0L1-L4.  

We also refer to our earlier detailed reply dated April 30, 2025 fileciteturn0file1L1-L4, wherein comprehensive legal and factual submissions were placed on record.  

The reminder further makes reference to the short order of the Hon’ble Federal Constitutional Court dated 27.01.2026 in the matter of DG Khan Cement & Others. In light of the said decision, and without reiterating contentions that now stand concluded against taxpayers, we respectfully submit the following updated position strictly confined to surviving issues.  

---

### 1. Computation of “Total Income” for the Purpose of Section 4C  

Even assuming, without prejudice, that section 4C is applicable to Tax Year 2022 in view of the recent constitutional pronouncement, the computation mechanism remains subject to statutory interpretation and cannot operate independent of Chapter III of the Ordinance.  

Section 4C levies super tax on “income” as determined under the Ordinance. The expression “total income” is a defined statutory term under section 2(59), read with section 9, and necessarily contemplates income computed after giving effect to all admissible deductions, allowances, and set-offs expressly permitted by law.  

Our client had substantial brought-forward business losses and unabsorbed depreciation available for set-off during the subject year. These allowances are not discretionary concessions; they are statutory rights crystallized under sections 56 and 57 read with relevant provisions governing depreciation and amortization. Denial of such set-off for the limited purpose of section 4C would amount to creating a parallel tax base not envisaged by the legislature.  

Accordingly, even if the charge under section 4C survives, the super tax base must first be reduced by:  

- carried forward business losses; and  
- unabsorbed depreciation / amortization allowances.  

Upon proper computation after giving full effect to the above statutory set-offs, the taxable base for the purpose of section 4C is reduced to nil. In the absence of positive “total income” computed in accordance with the Ordinance, no super tax can be sustained.  

---

### 2. Pending Rectification under Section 221 – Direct Impact on 4C Base  

It is respectfully reiterated that a rectification application under section 221 remains pending against the assessment order dated 31-10-2024 passed under section 122(5A).  

The rectification application specifically addresses:  

- non-adjustment of valid refunds determined under section 170(4); and  
- short allowance of withholding tax credits.  

These are apparent errors on the face of record. Once corrected, the assessed tax liability itself stands materially altered. Since super tax under section 4C is consequential upon assessed total income, any computation at this stage — without first disposing of rectification — would be premature and legally unsustainable.  

Proceedings under section 4C must therefore await final determination of rectification issues, failing which the exercise would be based on an unstable and incomplete assessment foundation.  

---

### 3. Principle of Computation Consistency  

The reminder indicates intention to finalize proceedings on the basis of material available on record. We respectfully submit that the material on record includes:  

- the return as filed;  
- statutory set-offs available under the Ordinance;  
- pending rectification; and  
- complete documentary evidence previously furnished.  

Super tax cannot be computed in isolation from the ordinary computation provisions. Any attempt to disallow statutory deductions solely for section 4C purposes would amount to reading words into the statute which do not exist. Taxing statutes must be construed strictly; no charge can be created by implication.  

---

### 4. Without Prejudice – Demand is Arithmetically Inflated  

Even on the department’s working, the figure of Rs. 1,027,977,626 assumes a positive taxable base which is factually and legally disputed. Once lawful loss adjustments and depreciation are incorporated, the arithmetic collapses. A charging provision cannot operate on hypothetical income.  

---

### Conclusion  

In view of the above, and strictly confining ourselves to issues not concluded by the recent constitutional decision, it is respectfully submitted that:  

- the computation mechanism under section 4C must allow full statutory set-offs;  
- pending rectification proceedings materially affect the tax base; and  
- on correct computation, no super tax liability survives for Tax Year 2022.  

We therefore request that proceedings under section 4C be dropped, or in the alternative, kept in abeyance until rectification is finally adjudicated and lawful computation principles are applied.  

We remain available to provide any further clarification or documentary support that your office may require.  

Yours faithfully,  

For and on behalf of  
K-Electric Limited

K-Electric Limited

**To:**  
The Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
LTO Karachi  

**Subject: Response to Addendum Notice under Section 4C – Tax Year 2023**

Dear Sir,

We refer to the Addendum Notice issued under section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”) for Tax Year 2023, whereby super tax liability has been recomputed at Rs. 341,953,016 and proposed to be recovered under sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 4C of the Ordinance.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the super tax computation carried out in the notice is based on a mechanical aggregation of taxable income, dividend income, and capital gains without proper appreciation of the legal framework governing section 4C, particularly the scope of “income” as defined in sub-section (2) of section 4C read with Division IIB of Part I of the First Schedule.

**1. Legal Position under Section 4C**

Section 4C is a charging provision which must be strictly construed. The levy of super tax is attracted only on “income” as defined in section 4C(2), and the computation mechanism cannot extend beyond what the statute explicitly provides.

Dividend income and capital gains are separate and distinct heads of income under the Ordinance and are subject to specific tax regimes. Dividend income is generally taxed under a separate final tax regime or special rate structure, and capital gains are taxed under a distinct mechanism under section 37 and related provisions. The inclusion of such incomes in the base for super tax requires careful interpretation in light of legislative intent and applicable judicial precedents.

The notice proceeds on the assumption that:

Taxable income (Others): Rs. 3,347,282,164  
Dividend income: Rs. 2,229,339  
Capital gains: Rs. 70,018,603  
Total income for section 4C: Rs. 3,419,530,166  

Super tax @ 10%: Rs. 341,953,016  

However, the above working does not examine whether dividend income and capital gains, already subjected to specific tax treatment under separate regimes, are to be included again for the purpose of section 4C in the manner adopted in the notice.

**2. Earlier Computation and Legitimate Expectation**

It is pertinent to note that the original notice computed super tax at Rs. 133,449,000, which itself demonstrates that the department initially adopted a different basis of computation. The subsequent enhancement to Rs. 341,953,016 reflects a material change in interpretation without any change in underlying facts.

Such revision requires detailed reasoning and legal justification, particularly where the liability is being enhanced substantially. In absence of a speaking order explaining the statutory basis for inclusion of all components in the manner adopted, the proposed recovery is not sustainable.

**3. Judicial Proceedings on Section 4C**

It is further submitted that the levy and scope of super tax under section 4C has been subject to extensive litigation before various High Courts and the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan. The legal contours of the provision, including its constitutional validity and computation mechanism, are evolving and remain contentious in several respects.

In such circumstances, coercive recovery proceedings without proper adjudication and opportunity of hearing would not be justified.

**4. Without Prejudice – Computation Clarification**

Without prejudice to the above legal submissions, it is submitted that even on the department’s own working, super tax liability requires proper reconciliation with:

• Income subjected to separate final tax regimes  
• Any adjustments allowable under section 4C(2)  
• Any tax already discharged or available credits, if applicable  

The computation requires detailed verification rather than summary recovery.

**5. Prayer**

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully requested that:

a) The proposed recovery proceedings under section 4C(4) and (5) may kindly be kept in abeyance;  
b) Detailed opportunity of hearing may be provided to explain the legal and computational position; and  
c) The impugned computation may be revisited in light of statutory provisions and applicable judicial principles.

We remain available to provide any further clarification required in this matter.

Yours faithfully,  
Authorized Representative  
Engro Vopak Terminal Limited

Under section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011, tax is chargeable on taxable services provided or rendered in Sindh. The charging mechanism presupposes the existence of a “taxable service” and a “taxable person.” The definition of “taxable person” under section 2 requires a person who provides or renders taxable services or who is liable to pay tax under reverse charge. Likewise, section 9(2) read with section 3(2) imposes reverse charge liability where a resident person receives taxable services from a non-resident service provider. In all these provisions, the legislative scheme is premised on the existence of two distinct persons — a provider and a recipient — and a supply of service for consideration.

In the instant case, there is no such supply between independent persons. A branch and its head office are not separate taxable persons under the SSTSA, 2011. The Act does not contain any deeming fiction treating them as distinct persons for service tax purposes. Therefore, the fundamental condition for levy under section 3 — namely provision of a service by one person to another — is absent. One cannot, in law, render services to oneself.

Further, the auditor’s agreed-upon procedures report confirms that the amounts charged as “Head Office costs” represent allocation of general and administrative expenses incurred at corporate level and apportioned to the Pakistan Branch on the basis of turnover ratio. These include corporate expenses, salaries and staff costs, legal and professional expenses, rent, utilities, travel and related overheads. There is no markup, no profit element, and no specific service deliverable. It is a cost allocation mechanism to ensure appropriate financial reporting and cost attribution across jurisdictions. Such internal allocation cannot be equated with provision of management consultancy or other taxable service classifiable under any CPC code.

The substance of the matter becomes even clearer when examined in the light of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Section 105 of the Ordinance specifically deals with taxation of non-resident persons carrying on business in Pakistan through a permanent establishment (which includes a branch). Subsection (2) of section 105 requires that the profits attributable to the permanent establishment be computed as if it were a distinct and separate enterprise dealing independently with the non-resident. However, this fiction is expressly limited to computation of taxable profits for income tax purposes. It does not create a separate legal personality for all statutory purposes; rather, it is a computational mechanism to determine attributable income.

In practice, section 105 allows allocation of head office expenditures to the Pakistan permanent establishment to determine its taxable profits. Such allocations are recognized for income tax purposes as deductible business expenditure subject to arm’s length principles and transfer pricing considerations. The fact that the Income Tax Ordinance specifically provides a framework for attributing head office costs to a permanent establishment reinforces that these are internal business expenses for profit attribution, not independent cross-border service transactions. They are recognized as part of the same enterprise’s consolidated cost structure.

This income tax treatment reflects the economic substance — namely, that no service is rendered by a third party, but costs are merely allocated for internal accounting and tax computation purposes.

The SSTSA, 2011 levies sales tax on taxable services provided in Sindh

Chargeability (Sec. 8) – Sales tax is charged at the statutory rate on the value of a taxable service. When SSTSA and ITO are read together, it is clear the head office cost allocations under Section 105 cannot magically become “taxable services.” Section 105(1)(c) forbids treating internal management allocations as branch expenses – it effectively negates any notion of a management “service” charged. ### 4. CHARGING MECHANISM UNDER SECTION 3 AND REVERSE CHARGE UNDER SECTION 9 – NOT ATTRACTED  

**4.1** Section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011 is the substantive charging provision and forms the legal foundation of any levy under the Act. It imposes sales tax only where a *taxable service* is provided or rendered in Sindh in accordance with the statutory framework. The existence of a taxable service is therefore the sine qua non for levy. The Act does not tax book entries, internal allocations, or accounting adjustments in isolation. The charge arises only where there is an identifiable service transaction involving (i) a service provider, (ii) a service recipient, (iii) an activity constituting a taxable service, and (iv) consideration flowing in respect of that activity. Unless these essential ingredients co-exist, Section 3 cannot be invoked.

Statutory Framework: Sindh SSTSA, 2011
The SSTSA, 2011 levies sales tax on taxable services provided in Sindh
. Critical definitions include:

Taxable Service (Sec. 3): The Act applies only to services specified in the Second Schedule of the SSTSA. No open‐ended definition of service exists; it must be one of the listed types.
Person (Sec. 2): A “person” covers companies or associations incorporated in or outside Pakistan
, etc. Thus UEPL’s foreign head office is a “person” under SSTSA, and so is its Pakistan branch (as the same legal company).
Consideration: Although not explicitly defined in the SSTSA, by analogy to federal law (and recent amendments), any payment or reimbursement for rendering a taxable service is treated as consideration. Notably, an amendment effective July 2024 clarifies that “reimbursement of expenditures incurred by a services provider for rendering taxable services shall form part of the consideration”
.
Chargeability (Sec. 8) – Sales tax is charged at the statutory rate on the value of a taxable service. The chain requires (i) a person (provider) in Sindh rendering a taxable service to another person, and (ii) payment of consideration. Section 8 confirms tax is levied at the rate (now 15%) on the “value” of the taxable service, as defined in Section 5.

Liability and Reverse Charge (Sec. 9) – Generally the service provider collects and remits the tax. Section 9(3) empowers SRB to prescribe special liability (for example, withholding) on recipients for certain services. The Board’s Withholding Rules, 2011 (under SSTSA Sec. 9) list classes of services (such as advertising) where the recipient is obliged to withhold tax. However, reverse charge under Section 9 applies only if a “taxable service” is provided to a Sindh person by a non-resident. Here, even if one assumed a notional service, it is not a taxable service in substance (see below).

Registration (Sec. 24) – A person “providing taxable services” or liable for tax under Section 9 must register. UEPL’s Pakistan branch neither provides any second-schedule service in Sindh, nor receives a taxable service from a distinct non-resident person. By corporate law, UEPL’s Mauritius head office and its Pakistan branch are one legal entity. A branch is not a separate juristic person; it carries on the same business in a different place. The SSTSA contains no deeming fiction treating a foreign head office as a separate taxpayer vis-à-vis its branch. In fact, courts have recognized that section 2(63)’s definition of “person” includes companies “incorporated…in Pakistan or elsewhere,” so the branch and its head office are legally one person

Here there is only one enterprise. One cannot “render a service to oneself” under the Act’s logic; such allocations are internal. No contract exists with a third-party service supplier. Therefore, Section 3(1) (charging of tax on taxable services provided in Sindh) and Section 9(2) (reverse charge on cross-border services) are not triggered. When SSTSA and ITO are read together, it is clear the head office cost allocations under Section 105 cannot magically become “taxable services.” Section 105(1)(c) forbids treating internal management allocations as branch expenses – it effectively negates any notion of a management “service” charged. From a transfer-pricing standpoint (ITO Sec. 108A and Rules), any cross-charge must be at arm’s length. The auditor report shows the Head Office allocation bore no markup or profit margin. In practice, transfer-pricing law would treat a zero-markup cost-allocation as “reimbursement of actual cost,” not a fee for services. SRB’s notice may suggest the branch should register because it allegedly “received Head Office services” from a non-resident. We anticipate and address likely counterarguments:

“Any cross-border allocation of corporate expenses is a service.” The counter is that statutory taxability requires an actual service for consideration

On each point, the legal and factual position is clear: The Head Office charges reflect no independent service exchange or contract. The entire scheme falls outside the SSTSA’s taxing scope.

In light of the above legal analysis and factual evidence, we request that SRB withdraw the registration notice under Section 24. Specifically, we propose that the Board formally acknowledge that the Head Office allocations do not constitute taxable services under the SSTSA, and that UEPL’s branch is neither providing nor receiving a second-schedule service from a separate person.

### 5. CHARGING MECHANISM UNDER SECTION 3 AND REVERSE CHARGE UNDER SECTION 9 – NOT ATTRACTED  

**5.1** Section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011 is the primary charging provision. In other words, the levy is not triggered merely because an amount is booked in the accounts or because a payment is made; rather, it is triggered only when there is an identifiable **service transaction** that can be said to have been **supplied** by a **service provider** to a **service recipient** for **consideration**, and the service is one which is taxable under the Act (i.e., not exempt under the applicable regime).  

**5.2** Section 9 is not an independent charging section; it only determines **who is liable to discharge the tax** once the underlying taxable service is established under Section 3. However, this reverse charge liability cannot be applied in a vacuum. 6.	HARMONIOUS CONSTRUCTION WITH SECTION 105 OF THE INCOME TAX ORDINANCE, 2001

6.1	The correct legal characterization of the impugned arrangement must be examined in the broader statutory context, particularly in light of section 105 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Ordinance). Section 105 specifically governs the taxation of a non-resident carrying on business in Pakistan through a permanent establishment, which expressly includes a branch. The provision establishes a structured mechanism for determining the profits attributable to the Pakistan permanent establishment and reflects the legislative understanding of how internal head office allocations are to be treated in law.

6.2	Under Section 105, profits attributable to the permanent establishment are to be computed as if it were a “distinct and separate enterprise” dealing independently with the head office. However, this “distinct entity” treatment is not a declaration of separate legal personality; it is a limited legal fiction created solely for the purpose of income tax profit attribution. It serves a computational objective aligned with internationally accepted permanent establishment principles. The fiction enables allocation of income and expenses for tax calculation but does not transform the branch and head office into two independent legal persons for all statutory purposes. Outside the narrow confines of profit attribution, the corporate identity of the enterprise remains unified.

6.3	Significantly, Section 105 expressly permits allocation of head office expenditures to the permanent establishment, subject to prescribed limitations and proportionality conditions. At the same time, it disallows deduction for compensation for services, including management services, performed by the head office for the permanent establishment. This dual structure is deliberate and instructive. If head office allocations were intended to be treated as genuine cross-border service transactions, the law would not have curtailed or restricted their deductibility in this manner. The legislative design clearly indicates that such allocations are to be viewed as internal expense adjustments for profit computation, not as service fees giving rise to income or independent consideration.

6.4	The Ordinance does not characterize these allocations as income accruing to or derived by the head office from Pakistan. Instead, they are recognized as part of the consolidated cost base of the same enterprise for the limited purpose of determining net taxable profits of the permanent establishment. The allocation performs a purely computational function: it ensures that an appropriate portion of overall corporate overheads is reflected in the Pakistan branch’s profitability. It does not represent payment for services rendered, nor does it generate a revenue stream in the hands of the head office.

6.5	In this statutory context, it would be legally inconsistent and conceptually unsound to re-characterize the same internal allocation as a “service,” let alone a taxable service, under the SSTSA, 2011. A harmonious interpretation of fiscal statutes requires that they be read coherently and consistently. Section 105 treats head office allocations as internal profit attribution adjustments within a single enterprise. Absent an express legislative mandate to the contrary, those same allocations cannot be artificially converted into taxable supplies under Section 3 of the SSTSA. To do so would distort the nature of the transaction and create a contradiction between income tax and sales tax treatment without statutory basis. Accordingly, internal profit attribution under Section 105 cannot, in law, be elevated into a taxable service for purposes of the sales tax regime.

7.1	It is acknowledged that recent amendments to the SSTSA clarify that reimbursement of expenditure incurred for rendering taxable services shall form part of the consideration for such services. Nevertheless, this clarification must be read in its proper statutory context. The inclusion of reimbursements within the ambit of “consideration” is not a standalone charging provision; it operates only where a taxable service has already been established under section 3. In other words, reimbursement enhances or forms part of the value of a service that is otherwise taxable. It does not, by itself, create taxability where no service exists. The legislative intent is to prevent artificial bifurcation of service fees and reimbursable costs in genuine service arrangements, not to tax internal cost movements that lack an underlying supply.

7.2	In the present case, the foundational requirement of an identifiable service is entirely absent. No independent activity is undertaken by one distinct person for another. The amounts recorded as “Head Office charges” merely reflect allocation of actual corporate overheads within the same legal entity. There is no markup, no profit element, no contractual obligation to render services, and no defined or measurable deliverable provided to the Pakistan Branch. In the absence of a service transaction, the concept of “consideration” in the legal sense contemplated by the SSTSA does not arise. Consideration presupposes a quid pro quo flowing from a recipient to a provider in respect of a defined service. Where there is no provider-recipient relationship and no identifiable service output, the allocation of costs cannot be characterized as consideration.

7.3	Consequently, the internal apportionment of head office expenses does not constitute a taxable event. The statutory provisions relating to reimbursement forming part of consideration are inapplicable because they presuppose an existing taxable supply. Since no such supply exists in the instant case, the reimbursement clarification does not alter the legal position, and no sales tax liability can arise on these internal allocations.

8.	REGISTRATION UNDER SECTION 24 – PRECONDITIONS NOT FULFILLED

8.1	Section 24 of the SSTSA, 2011 governs the requirement to obtain registration. A plain reading of the provision makes it evident that registration is not an autonomous or independent obligation; it is consequential to the existence of tax liability under the Act. The statutory framework contemplates registration only where a person (i) provides taxable services in Sindh, or (ii) is otherwise liable to pay tax under the Act, including under the reverse charge mechanism. Accordingly, compulsory registration in respect of the alleged “Head Office services” would be contrary to both the letter and the intent of the SSTSA, 2011.

7.5	In this context, it would be legally inconsistent and conceptually unsound to treat the same internal allocation as a taxable supply of services under the SSTSA, 2011. A harmonious interpretation of both statutes requires that section 105 be understood as a profit attribution mechanism and not as recognition of a service transaction. Internal allocations recognized for income tax computation cannot, without clear legislative mandate, be re-characterized as taxable services under Section 3 of the SSTSA. Accordingly, internal profit attribution under section 105 cannot be converted into a taxable service for the purposes of the sales tax regime.


8.	CONSIDERATION AND REIMBURSEMENT – NO TAXABLE EVENT

8.1	It is acknowledged that recent amendments to the SSTSA framework clarify that reimbursement of expenditure incurred for rendering taxable services shall form part of the consideration for such services. Nevertheless, this clarification operates only where there is an underlying taxable service in the first place. The statutory inclusion of reimbursements within “consideration” presupposes that a service has been rendered by one person to another and that the reimbursement relates to that identifiable supply. In other words, reimbursement is not independently taxable; it merely forms part of the value of an already established taxable service.

8.2	In the present case, the threshold requirement of an underlying service is absent. No independent service is rendered by one distinct person to another. The so-called “Head Office charges” represent allocation of actual corporate overheads within the same legal entity, without markup, profit element, contractual service obligation, or identifiable deliverable. In the absence of a supply, there can be no consideration in the legal sense contemplated by the Act. Consequently, the internal allocation of costs does not constitute a taxable event, and the provisions relating to reimbursement forming part of consideration are not attracted.


9.	REGISTRATION UNDER SECTION 24 – PRECONDITIONS NOT FULFILLED

9.1	Section 24 of the SSTSA, 2011 governs the obligation to obtain registration. The statutory scheme makes it clear that registration is not an independent or standalone requirement; rather, it is consequential to taxability. A person is required to register only if it (i) provides taxable services in Sindh, or (ii) is otherwise liable to pay tax under the Act, including under the reverse charge mechanism. Thus, the obligation to register arises only where the charging provisions under Section 3 and the liability provisions under Section 9 are first attracted.

9.2	In the present case, as demonstrated above, the Pakistan Branch does not provide any taxable service in Sindh to third parties in relation to the impugned head office allocations. Nor does it receive any taxable service from an independent non-resident service provider within the meaning of Sections 3 and 9. The essential ingredients of a taxable supply are absent. Consequently, no liability to pay tax arises under the Act.

9.3	Registration under Section 24 cannot be imposed in the abstract or merely on the basis of accounting entries. It must be founded upon the existence of a taxable event. In the absence of a taxable supply, there is no statutory trigger for registration. Accordingly, compulsory registration in respect of the alleged “Head Office services” would be contrary to the scheme and intent of the SSTSA, 2011.

### 5. NEGATIVE LIST REGIME – NO DILUTION OF THE “SUPPLY” REQUIREMENT  

**5.1** It is acknowledged that through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025, the legislature transitioned from a positive list regime to a negative list framework, under which all services are taxable unless specifically exempted. However, this structural shift relates only to the *scope* of taxable services and not to the *existence* of a taxable event. The change does not override or modify the fundamental architecture of the Act. The negative list regime cannot convert a non-transaction into a taxable transaction, nor can it impose tax in the absence of a legally recognizable supply. The charging mechanism remains anchored to the occurrence of a taxable service as defined and contemplated under the Act.

**5.2** Section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011 continues to be the charging provision and remains unaltered in substance. It requires that a taxable service be provided or rendered in Sindh before tax can be levied. The expression “taxable service” inherently presupposes the existence of a service transaction between distinct persons for consideration. The negative list merely determines *which categories of services*, if rendered, are subject to tax. It does not dispense with the threshold requirement that a service must in fact be rendered or supplied. Thus, while the tax base may have broadened, the legal meaning of “service,” “supply,” and “consideration” has not been diluted or redefined.

**5.3** Consequently, even under the negative list regime, the essential elements of taxability remain unchanged: there must be (i) a service provider, (ii) a service recipient, and (iii) consideration flowing from one to the other in respect of an identifiable and ascertainable service. Where these elements are absent, the negative list has no application. The mere absence of an exemption does not automatically create liability; taxability arises only where the underlying transaction qualifies as a service within the meaning of the charging provision. In the present case, since no service is rendered between distinct persons, the negative list regime does not alter the legal position, and no tax liability can arise.

---

### 1. Legal Status of the Branch and Head Office – Absence of Two Distinct Persons

At the outset, it is essential to determine whether two legally distinct persons exist for the purposes of Section 3 and Section 9 of the SSTSA, 2011. United Energy Pakistan Limited (“UEP”) is incorporated in Mauritius and carries on petroleum exploration and production operations in Pakistan through its Branch. The Branch is not a separate juristic entity; it is the same corporate person operating in Pakistan.

Under settled principles of company law, a branch has no independent legal personality distinct from its head office. The SSTSA, 2011 does not contain any deeming provision treating a foreign head office and its Pakistan branch as separate persons for service tax purposes. In the absence of such statutory fiction, it is legally impermissible to treat internal allocations as supplies between independent persons.

The charging provision under Section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011 presupposes the existence of a service provider and a service recipient who are separate persons. Likewise, reverse charge under Section 9(2) applies only where a resident person receives taxable services from a non-resident service provider. Both provisions necessarily require a transaction between two distinct persons. In the present case, that foundational requirement is absent. A person cannot, in law, render services to itself. Accordingly, no taxable supply arises.

---

### 2. Nature of the “Head Office Charges” – Internal Cost Allocation, Not Service Provision

The notice appears to proceed on the assumption that the “Head Office charges” represent management or business support services classifiable under CPC Code 83118 or similar categories. This assumption is factually incorrect.

The Agreed-Upon Procedures Report issued by RSM Hong Kong dated July 14, 2025, enclosed as Annexure “A,” confirms that the amounts recorded as “Head Office costs” represent allocation of general and administrative expenses incurred at the corporate level. These include corporate salaries, rent, legal and professional fees, travel, utilities, and other overheads.

The allocation is made strictly on the basis of the ratio of the Pakistan Branch’s turnover to the Company’s consolidated turnover. There is no markup, no profit element, no service-level agreement, and no defined deliverable. The arrangement is a mechanical apportionment of actual corporate overheads for internal accounting and financial reporting purposes.

A taxable service requires the existence of a discernible activity performed by one person for another in exchange for consideration. In the absence of a distinct provider, recipient, and service output, such internal cost allocations cannot be equated with provision of management consultancy or any other taxable service. In substance and in law, these are internal expense allocations within the same enterprise.

---

### 3. Charging Mechanism under Section 3 and Reverse Charge under Section 9 – Not Attracted

Section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011 levies tax only on taxable services provided or rendered in Sindh. Section 9(2) imposes reverse charge liability where a resident person receives taxable services from a non-resident service provider. Both provisions operate only where a taxable service is actually rendered between distinct persons.

In the instant case, no independent supply exists. The head office and branch are the same legal entity. Consequently, there is neither a provider nor a recipient in the statutory sense. Since no taxable service is rendered, the reverse charge mechanism is also not triggered.

---

### 4. Negative List Regime – No Dilution of the “Supply” Requirement

It is acknowledged that the Sindh Finance Act 2025 introduced a negative list regime, whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempted. However, this structural shift affects only the scope of taxable categories and does not dispense with the fundamental requirement of an actual supply of service.

Even under the negative list framework, the charging provision remains Section 3, which requires provision of a service for consideration. The threshold requirement of a supply between distinct persons remains intact. In the present case, since no service is rendered by one person to another, the negative list regime does not alter the legal position.

---

### 5. Harmonious Construction with Section 105 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

The true legal character of the arrangement becomes clearer when examined in light of Section 105 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“Ordinance”). Section 105 governs taxation of a non-resident carrying on business in Pakistan through a permanent establishment, including a branch.

For income tax purposes, Section 105 requires that profits attributable to the permanent establishment be computed as if it were a distinct and separate enterprise dealing independently with the head office. This “distinct entity” concept is a legal fiction strictly limited to profit attribution for income tax purposes. It does not create a separate legal personality for all statutory purposes.

Section 105 permits allocation of head office expenditures to the permanent establishment for computation of taxable profits, subject to prescribed limits. At the same time, it disallows deduction for compensation for services, including management services, performed by the head office for the permanent establishment. This clearly demonstrates that head office charges are treated as internal expense adjustments and not as genuine cross-border service transactions giving rise to income in the hands of the head office.

The Ordinance does not treat such allocations as income derived from Pakistan by the head office. Rather, they are recognized as part of the consolidated cost structure of the same enterprise for profit computation purposes. It would therefore be inconsistent to re-characterize the same internal allocation as a taxable supply under the SSTSA.

A harmonious interpretation of both statutes leads to the conclusion that internal profit attribution under Section 105 cannot be converted into a taxable service under Section 3 of the SSTSA, 2011.

---

### 6. Consideration and Reimbursement – No Taxable Event

Recent amendments clarifying that reimbursement of expenditure incurred for rendering taxable services forms part of consideration presuppose the existence of an underlying taxable service. Only where a service is actually rendered does reimbursement form part of its value.

In the present case, no independent service is rendered by one person to another. The allocation represents pure reimbursement of actual costs without markup and without an underlying supply. Therefore, the concept of consideration does not arise, and no taxable event is triggered.

---

### 7. Registration under Section 24 – Preconditions Not Fulfilled

Section 24 of the SSTSA, 2011 requires registration only where a person provides taxable services or is otherwise liable to pay tax under the Act. Since the Pakistan Branch neither provides taxable services in Sindh nor receives taxable services from an independent non-resident person within the meaning of Sections 3 and 9, the statutory precondition for registration is not satisfied.

In the absence of a taxable supply, compulsory registration cannot be imposed.

---

### Conclusion

In view of the foregoing legal and factual position, the “Head Office charges” represent internal allocation of corporate overheads within the same legal entity for purposes of profit attribution under Section 105 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. They do not constitute taxable services under the SSTSA, 2011. Consequently, registration under Section 24 is not applicable in the instant case.

Let’s slow this down and look at it like professionals who’ve seen amendment orders come and go.

However, this is where we must think carefully and not celebrate too early.

The key considerations before reversing the entire historical provision are:

First, is the factual matrix identical across all years? If the nature of inter-concession transfers and PCA accounting treatment has remained consistent, and the department’s reasoning in TY 2024 is principle-based (not year-specific), that strengthens the case for reversal.

Second, what is the status of prior years?  
• Are earlier amendment orders still under appeal?  
• Has any year attained finality against UEP?  
• Is there any litigation pending before CIR(A), ATIR, or higher forums?

If earlier years are still under active litigation, complete reversal may be slightly aggressive unless management is comfortable that the department’s current position reflects a settled view rather than a year-specific concession.

Third, is there any risk of departmental inconsistency? Unfortunately, tax jurisprudence in Pakistan has taught us that acceptance in one year does not legally bind the department in another year. The principle of consistency is persuasive, not absolute. That said, where the department has examined detailed documentation and explicitly concluded that the gain is notional, it becomes very difficult for them to take a contradictory position in adjacent years without fresh facts.

In my professional view, reversal is supportable provided:

• The department’s order clearly records acceptance on merits, not on technical grounds.  
• The reasoning is principle-based and not limited to minor documentation gaps.  
• No contrary binding appellate decision exists for earlier years.  
• Management is comfortable that the risk has moved from “probable” to at most “possible” or “remote.”

If these conditions are satisfied, retaining a provision would no longer reflect a faithful representation of risk. In fact, continuing to carry it may overstate liabilities.

In matters like this, prudence is good—but prudence should not fossilize into permanent pessimism once the risk profile has genuinely shifted.

Subject: Reversal of Provision – Gain/Loss on Inter-Concession Asset Transfers  

Dear Usman,  

Thank you for your email and for sharing the detailed background along with the historical assessment findings. We have carefully reviewed the factual position, the relevant extracts placed before the department in earlier years, and the specific findings recorded in Tax Years 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024.

At the outset, it is important to reiterate the legal and factual character of these transactions. The gain of Rs 709,574,611 arises from transfer of assets between concessions operated by the same legal entity. Under the Petroleum Concession Agreements and the Joint Operating Agreements, such transfers are required to be recorded at current replacement cost, subject to condition-based pricing (Conditions A to E). This is a contractual and accounting requirement rather than a commercial disposal to an external party. There is no third-party realization, no inflow of consideration, and no cessation of ownership at the enterprise level. The resulting gain or loss is therefore notional in nature.

Consistently, UEP has neutralized the accounting impact in its tax computation—excluding notional gains and adding back notional losses—so that taxable income reflects real income rather than book adjustments. The department, in multiple assessment proceedings, examined the issue specifically with reference to sections 68 and 75 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and Rule 5(c) of the Fifth Schedule. After reviewing supporting documentation, including policy extracts and operator approvals, the officers have repeatedly concluded that the explanation is verifiable and that no adverse inference is warranted. This acceptance is recorded for Tax Years 2020, 2021, 2022 and most recently Tax Year 2024.

The Tax Year 2024 amendment order under section 122(5A) is particularly significant because the department expressly acknowledged that the gain is notional in nature and accepted the adjustment made in the return. This is not a procedural relief but a substantive acceptance on merits following examination of documentation.

In light of the above, the risk profile that originally justified recognition of a provision has materially changed. Under the applicable accounting framework (IAS 37), a provision is appropriate only where an outflow is probable and there exists a present obligation. Given the repeated acceptance of the position by the assessing officers across multiple years, including the latest year under amendment proceedings, it would now be difficult to conclude that a probable outflow still exists in respect of this issue.

On that basis, reversal of the provision appears appropriate, provided that:  

• the factual matrix remains consistent across years;  
• there is no contrary binding appellate decision on record; and  
• management is comfortable that the likelihood of adverse treatment in open years has reduced from probable to, at most, possible or remote.  

As a matter of prudence and transparency, we would recommend appropriate disclosure in the notes to the financial statements explaining the background, the historical dispute, and the favorable findings recorded in recent assessment proceedings. This ensures clarity for auditors and stakeholders while aligning the balance sheet with the current risk assessment.

Strategically, the consistent departmental acceptance strengthens UEP’s position for all open years and, if required, may also be relied upon under the principle of consistency in any appellate proceedings.

Subject to review of the exact wording of the Tax Year 2024 order (to confirm that the acceptance is categorical and unconditional), we are of the view that reversal of the historical provision is technically supportable.

Please let us know if you would like us to review the draft accounting note or coordinate with the audit team to ensure alignment in treatment and disclosure.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

The gain of Rs 709,574,611 arises from transfer of assets between concessions operated by the same legal entity. These transfers are undertaken for operational efficiency and economies of scale and are governed by the Petroleum Concession Agreements and Joint Operating Agreements. The valuation mechanism, based on current replacement cost adjusted according to asset condition (Conditions A to E), is a contractual allocation framework rather than a commercial sale transaction. There is no disposal to a third party, no realization event in economic substance, and no inflow of consideration to the enterprise as a whole. The resulting gain or loss is therefore notional in nature and arises purely from PCA-mandated accounting treatment.

UEP has consistently neutralized this accounting impact in its tax computations by excluding notional gains and adding back notional losses so that taxable income reflects real income rather than internal book remeasurements. This treatment has been repeatedly examined by the tax authorities.
