Most importantly, in the amendment proceedings under section 122(5A) for Tax Year 2024, the department again scrutinized the same issue and expressly accepted that the gain was notional in nature and that the adjustment made in the return was justified. **Subject:** Response to Letter No. PQA/SST/ROYALTY-001 dated 23 February 2026 – Clarification on Applicability of Sindh Sales Tax on Royalty  

Dear Sir,

We refer to your above-captioned letter wherein it has been stated that the relationship between Port Qasim Authority (“PQA”) and Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited (“FAP”) has been viewed as a provision of “franchise service” and that Sindh Sales Tax (“SST”) is consequently chargeable on royalty under such classification.

With utmost respect, we consider it necessary to place on record certain critical statutory and legal clarifications.

---

### 1. No Amendment in the Definition of “Franchise” under SSTSA, 2011

At the outset, it is essential to clarify that **the definition of “franchise” as provided under section 2 of the SSTSA, 2011 has not undergone any amendment** through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 or otherwise.

The statutory ingredients of franchise — which typically require grant of representational rights, use of trade name or business system, operational control, marketing format, or associated intellectual property arrangements — remain exactly as they stood prior to the recent legislative changes.

Therefore, any assertion that the 2025 amendments have strengthened the classification of the PQA–Terminal relationship as franchise is, with respect, legally unsustainable. The franchise definition continues to stand in its original form, and its essential elements must independently be satisfied for such classification to apply.

---

### 2. Amendment Pertains to the Definition of “Services” — Not Franchise

The material amendment introduced through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 relates to the **definition of “services” under section 2(79) of SSTSA, 2011**, whereby the scope has been expanded to expressly include the *granting, assignment, transfer or allowing use of a right* as a taxable activity.

This enlargement of the taxable base is conceptually distinct from franchise.

In other words:

- Earlier, the scope of “services” did not explicitly include every form of granting of right.
- Post-amendment, the statutory net has widened.
- However, **the legislature did not amend the franchise definition**, nor did it provide that every grant of right shall automatically be treated as franchise.

The legal distinction is crucial. A broadened definition of “services” does not automatically convert all grant-of-right arrangements into franchise services. Franchise remains a specifically defined subset requiring fulfillment of defined statutory characteristics.

---

### 3. Nature of Relationship between PQA and Terminal Operators

The implementation agreement between PQA and FAP is fundamentally a concessionary arrangement granting operational rights over port infrastructure subject to regulatory conditions.

It does not involve:

- Grant of representational rights to operate under PQA’s trade name,
- Transfer of business format or marketing system,
- Continuous franchisor-type operational control over commercial strategy,
- Licensing of brand identity in the conventional franchise sense.

The relationship is infrastructural and concessionary in character, not representational or format-driven as contemplated under the franchise definition in SSTSA, 2011.

Accordingly, even independent of the 2025 amendments, the classification of this arrangement as franchise remains legally contestable and, in our considered view, unsustainable.

---

### 4. Tribunal Decision Does Not Attain Finality

We note your reference to the Appellate Tribunal SRB decision. With respect, the matter has not attained finality in constitutional terms.

Under the legal framework, orders of the Appellate Tribunal are subject to judicial scrutiny before the Honourable Sindh High Court under constitutional jurisdiction and, where applicable, before the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

Until the issue is examined and conclusively settled by an independent constitutional forum, the interpretational debate remains open. It would therefore be legally imprudent to treat the Tribunal’s view as determinative for all stakeholders, particularly when substantial questions of statutory interpretation remain unresolved.

---

### 5. Litigation Risk and Prejudice to Ongoing Proceedings

We respectfully submit that voluntary discharge of SST under the head of “franchise” may materially prejudice:

- Pending proceedings before SRB involving FAP,
- Similar disputes concerning other terminal operators,
- Broader stakeholder litigation involving the same legal question.

Such discharge may be construed as implicit acceptance of the franchise characterization, thereby weakening the defence strategy in ongoing and future litigation. The classification issue is not merely procedural; it goes to the root of the statutory interpretation of SSTSA, 2011.

---

### 6. Appropriate Classification in Light of Expanded Definition of “Services”

Without prejudice to the above legal position, it is acknowledged that the recent amendment to the definition of “services” under section 2 may independently bring certain grant-of-right arrangements within the expanded taxable scope.

However, if Sindh Sales Tax is to be charged post-amendment, it ought to be aligned with the correct statutory head — i.e., taxable services involving grant of right — and not under franchise, whose statutory elements remain unaltered.

The enlargement of the definition of services cannot be used to retroactively validate or reinforce a franchise classification where the definitional criteria are not satisfied.

---

### 7. Invoicing Mechanism under SSTSA, 2011

Under section 22 of SSTSA, 2011 read with the Sindh Sales Tax Rules, a registered service provider is required to issue a tax invoice in the prescribed manner.

However, proper invoicing presupposes clarity of classification. Implementing a payment-first and invoice-later model while classification remains legally disputed may create reconciliation and compliance complications, particularly where the applicable tax head is under challenge.

It would therefore be prudent to first resolve the correct classification in accordance with the Act before operationalizing the invoicing mechanism.

---

### 8. Conclusion and Request

In summary:

- The definition of “franchise” under SSTSA, 2011 remains unchanged.  
- The 2025 amendment pertains only to the expanded definition of “services.”  
- Grant of right does not automatically equate to franchise.  
- Tribunal findings have not attained constitutional finality.  
- Charging SST under franchise may materially prejudice ongoing litigation and stakeholder positions.

In light of the above, we respectfully request PQA to revisit the classification and not insist upon discharge of Sindh Sales Tax under the head of “franchise.” If tax is to be charged in view of the enlarged scope of services, it should be aligned with the appropriate statutory category consistent with the amended definition of services, and not franchise.

We remain available for a structured legal discussion to ensure that the matter is aligned with statutory interpretation while safeguarding the interests of all concerned stakeholders.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited  

---

**Subject: Response to Letter No. PQA/SST/ROYALTY-001 dated 23 February 2026 – Clarification on Applicability of Sindh Sales Tax on Royalty**

Dear Sir,

We refer to your above-captioned letter wherein it has been stated that the relationship between Port Qasim Authority (“PQA”) and Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited (“FAP”) stands classified as a “franchise” service and that Sindh Sales Tax is consequently chargeable on royalty under that head.

With utmost respect, we consider it necessary to place on record certain critical legal and factual clarifications.

At the outset, it is important to emphasize that **no amendment has been made in the statutory definition of “franchise”** under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“SSTSA, 2011”), either through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 or any subsequent amendment. The definition of franchise continues to remain exactly the same as it existed prior to the recent legislative changes.

The only material amendment introduced through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 pertains to the **definition of “services”**, which has been broadened to include, inter alia, the *granting of a right* as a taxable activity. This enlargement of the scope of “services” does not amend, dilute, or expand the statutory ingredients of a “franchise.” The two concepts remain legally distinct. Therefore, any willingness on part of terminal operators to discharge Sindh Sales Tax after the expansion of the definition of “services” is attributable solely to the widened scope of taxable services and **not** to any change in the definition of franchise.

The distinction is fundamental. The franchise definition under SSTSA requires specific elements — including representational rights, brand usage, system control, and operational integration — which, with due respect, are absent in the legal and commercial relationship between PQA and terminal operators. The relationship is one arising out of an implementation agreement granting operational rights over port infrastructure and is not in the nature of a franchise arrangement in the ordinary or statutory sense.

We note your reference to the decision of the Appellate Tribunal SRB. However, the matter has not attained finality. It is either sub judice or liable to be examined by an independent constitutional forum, including the Honourable Sindh High Court and potentially the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Tribunal findings, with respect, do not conclude the interpretational debate, particularly where substantial questions of law remain open. We are not privy to the precise legal submissions advanced before the Tribunal; however, based on our independent legal evaluation, the position that the relationship does not constitute franchise remains strongly tenable.

In this context, we respectfully submit that voluntary discharge of Sindh Sales Tax under the head of “franchise” would materially prejudice the legal position not only of FAP but also of other terminal operators. Such characterization may be construed as an implicit acceptance of the department’s stance and may adversely impact pending litigation before SRB and other forums. It could weaken the defence strategy in ongoing proceedings and distort the legal matrix affecting multiple stakeholders.

We fully acknowledge the recent enlargement of the definition of “services.” In view of that amendment, certain stakeholders, including terminal operators, have shown inclination to discharge Sindh Sales Tax on royalty under the broader taxable services framework. However, such discharge, if made, must be under an appropriate classification consistent with the amended definition of services — and not under the pre-existing and unchanged franchise definition.

We therefore respectfully request PQA to reconsider its position and not insist upon classification under “franchise.” If Sindh Sales Tax is to be charged in light of the expanded definition of services, it may be done under an appropriate service classification aligned with the concept of “granting of right,” rather than franchise.

Regarding invoicing mechanics, we agree that under SSTSA a service provider is obligated to issue a Sindh Sales Tax invoice. However, the statutory framework contemplates issuance contemporaneously with or prior to payment. A post-deposit invoicing model, as proposed, may create reconciliation and compliance complications, particularly where classification itself remains disputed. It would therefore be advisable to first settle the correct tax head and classification before implementing any procedural mechanism for charging and invoicing.

In summary:

- The definition of “franchise” remains unchanged before and after Sindh Finance Act, 2025.  
- The enlargement relates only to the definition of “services.”  
- Any discharge of tax, if at all, is attributable to the expanded scope of services and not franchise characterization.  
- Premature acceptance of franchise classification may materially prejudice pending litigation and stakeholder positions.  

We therefore request that this matter be revisited in the larger legal and commercial interest of all concerned stakeholders and aligned with the correct statutory interpretation.

We remain available for a detailed discussion to resolve the classification issue in a manner consistent with law and without compromising ongoing legal proceedings.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited

**Subject:** Response to Letter No. PQA/SST/ROYALTY-001 dated 23 February 2026 – Clarification on Applicability of Sindh Sales Tax on Royalty  

Dear Sir,  

We refer to your above-captioned letter wherein it has been stated that the relationship between Port Qasim Authority (“PQA”) and Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited (“FAP”) has been viewed as a provision of “franchise service” and that Sindh Sales Tax (“SST”) is consequently chargeable on royalty under such classification. With due respect, we consider it necessary to place on record certain statutory and legal clarifications to ensure that the matter is examined strictly in accordance with the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“SSTSA, 2011”).

At the outset, it is important to emphasize that there has been no amendment in the definition of “franchise” as contained in section 2 of the SSTSA, 2011. The statutory ingredients of franchise — which ordinarily require the grant of representational rights, use of trade name or business format, transfer of a business system, operational control or associated intellectual property elements — remain exactly as they existed prior to the Sindh Finance Act, 2025. Therefore, the recent amendments cannot be interpreted as having expanded or strengthened the franchise definition. The legal character and essential elements of franchise continue to stand unchanged, and any classification under this head must independently satisfy those statutory ingredients.

The material amendment introduced through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 pertains to the definition of “services” under section 2 of the SSTSA, 2011, whereby the scope of taxable services has been broadened to expressly include, inter alia, the granting, assignment, transfer or allowing the use of a right. This legislative enlargement has widened the taxable base; however, it does not amend, override or subsume the specific definition of franchise. A broadened definition of services does not automatically convert every grant-of-right arrangement into franchise service. Franchise remains a specifically defined subset requiring fulfillment of distinct statutory conditions, and the enlargement of the general definition of services cannot be conflated with the franchise concept.

The implementation agreement between PQA and FAP is fundamentally a concessionary and infrastructural arrangement granting operational rights over port facilities subject to regulatory oversight. It does not involve the grant of representational rights to operate under PQA’s trade name, nor does it entail transfer of a marketing system, business format, or franchise-type operational control as contemplated under the franchise definition in the SSTSA, 2011. The relationship is regulatory and concessionary in nature rather than representational or format-driven. Accordingly, even independent of the 2025 amendments, the classification of this arrangement as franchise remains legally contestable and, in our considered view, unsustainable.

We note your reference to the decision of the Appellate Tribunal SRB. With respect, such decision has not attained constitutional finality. Orders of the Tribunal remain subject to judicial scrutiny before the Honourable Sindh High Court and, where applicable, the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Substantial questions of statutory interpretation remain open for consideration by independent constitutional forums. Until such adjudication is concluded, it would be legally premature to treat the matter as conclusively settled, particularly where the interpretation materially affects multiple stakeholders and ongoing proceedings.

It is also respectfully submitted that voluntary discharge of SST under the head of franchise may materially prejudice not only FAP’s pending matters before SRB and other forums but also the broader litigation position of other terminal operators. Such discharge may be construed as implicit acceptance of the franchise characterization and could weaken the legal defence in ongoing and future proceedings. The classification issue goes to the root of statutory interpretation under SSTSA, 2011 and must therefore be approached with due caution.

Without prejudice to the foregoing legal position, we acknowledge that the enlargement of the definition of services under section 2 may independently bring certain grant-of-right arrangements within the expanded taxable scope prospectively. However, if Sindh Sales Tax is to be charged in view of that amendment, it must be aligned with the appropriate statutory classification reflecting grant of right under the widened definition of services, and not under franchise, whose statutory elements remain unchanged. The enlargement of services cannot be used to retrospectively validate or reinforce a franchise characterization where the definitional criteria are not satisfied.

Regarding invoicing, while section 22 of the SSTSA, 2011 read with the Sindh Sales Tax Rules requires issuance of a tax invoice by a registered service provider, proper invoicing presupposes clarity of classification and tax head. Implementing a payment-first and invoice-later model while the core classification remains disputed may create compliance and reconciliation complexities. It would therefore be prudent to first resolve the correct statutory characterization before operationalizing the invoicing mechanism.

In view of the above, we respectfully request PQA to revisit the matter and not insist upon discharge of Sindh Sales Tax under the head of franchise. If tax is to be charged pursuant to the expanded definition of services, it should be aligned with the appropriate statutory category consistent with the amended law, without prejudicing ongoing litigation or stakeholder positions. We remain available for further discussion to ensure that the matter is addressed in a manner consistent with the SSTSA, 2011 and the broader legal framework.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
Fauji Akbar Portia Marine Terminals Limited

Dear Zeeshan,  

I have carefully revisited the PwC advice dated 29 January 2026 fileciteturn0file0. Broadly, their technical analysis aligns with section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001; however, two areas require clearer articulation before KE proceeds with accepting bifurcation of invoices.

Firstly, the treatment of “goods” must be strictly confined to medicines supplied through OMI’s pharmacy in the true commercial sense. The opinion refers specifically to pharmacy sales, which is an important qualifier. The 5% withholding under section 153(1)(a) can only be supported where medicines are sold as standalone, off-the-shelf trading goods — separately identifiable, separately priced, and capable of independent sale through the pharmacy counter. A clear distinction must be maintained between such pharmacy sales and medicines administered during hospitalization as part of medical treatment. Medicines supplied in the course of inpatient care form an integral part of the healthcare service package. Even if itemised on the invoice, they remain embedded in the service component and should not automatically be carved out and treated as “goods.” Therefore, bifurcation should only be accepted where the pharmacy component genuinely represents an independent trading transaction. It would not be appropriate to treat all medicine line items as goods without examining the context of supply.

Secondly, the reimbursement discussion in the advice requires cautious application from KE’s standpoint. In law, reimbursement exists only where an expense is incurred specifically on behalf of KE, supported by third-party documentation, passed through at actual cost, and without any embedded profit element. Where OMI allocates doctors’ fees or other operational costs from its general revenue pool and includes such charges in the invoice, this does not qualify as reimbursement in the strict legal sense. Allocation of internal or pooled costs is not equivalent to a pass-through expense incurred on KE’s behalf. Unless there is a specific arrangement under which OMI incurs a cost exclusively for KE and merely recovers it without markup, such amounts remain consideration for services and would attract withholding accordingly. From a compliance perspective, reimbursement treatment should therefore not be assumed merely on the basis of invoice description.

Subject to these clarifications, the remaining analysis in the opinion appears technically sound. The distinction between 5% for genuine sale of goods and 15% for services is legally sustainable provided the factual matrix supports that classification. KE may consider accepting bifurcation only where pharmacy sales are clearly segregated and independently verifiable, while continuing to apply 15% on all hospitalization and treatment-related components, including medicines administered during care. In the absence of such clear demarcation, maintaining 15% on composite healthcare services remains the more conservative and defensible approach from a withholding perspective.

However, if medicines are merely incidental to hospital treatment and form part of an integrated healthcare package, FBR may argue that the dominant nature of the transaction is “services,” and therefore 15% should apply on the full amount. Second, the advice assumes that OMI qualifies as a seller of goods (not a manufacturer). That is correct in principle, but KE should obtain written confirmation from OMI that:
- the pharmacy sales are treated as trading sales in their books;
- no bundled pricing is involved; and  
- the bifurcation is not an artificial allocation introduced solely to reduce withholding exposure.

Third, consultants’ fee and reimbursement elements remain sensitive areas. Even though the opinion discusses reimbursement arguments, from KE’s perspective, unless the invoice clearly excludes pure pass-through amounts supported by third-party documentation, it is safer to treat amounts billed by OMI as consideration payable to OMI and apply withholding accordingly. Reimbursement defence usually creates litigation risk and should not be assumed lightly.

Fourth, consistency is important. If KE has historically deducted 15% on the entire invoice and now shifts to split rates, the change should be properly documented internally so that, in case of audit, it can be shown that the change was based on structured legal advice and revised invoice format.

If the billing structure genuinely reflects separate supply of goods and services, bifurcation is legally supportable. If not, the exposure would sit with the withholding agent.

In short, bifurcation may be accepted, subject to:
- clean invoice segregation,
- accounting consistency at OMI’s end,
- written confirmation from OMI on nature of supplies, and
- internal documentation at KE supporting rate application.

This keeps KE compliant while avoiding unnecessary over-withholding.

Dear Zeeshan,

I have revisited the PwC advice dated 29 January 2026 fileciteturn0file0 in light of your concerns. Overall, their technical position is reasonable, however two areas require clearer understanding before KE proceeds with bifurcation.

**1. “Goods” – Limited to Pharmacy Sales Only**

The advice repeatedly refers to supply of medicines through OMI’s *pharmacy*. This is an important qualifier. The 5% treatment under section 153(1)(a) can only be supported where medicines are sold “off the shelf” through the pharmacy as a trading activity.

There is a clear distinction between:

- Medicines purchased from the pharmacy counter (separately identifiable sale of goods); and  
- Medicines administered during hospitalization as part of medical treatment.

The latter forms part of an integrated healthcare service. If medicines are supplied as part of inpatient treatment and billed within hospitalization charges, they cannot automatically be carved out and treated as independent “goods.” In such cases, the dominant nature remains provision of services and 15% would apply.

Therefore, bifurcation should only be accepted where:
- Pharmacy sales are clearly segregated;
- They are independently priced and separately identifiable; and  
- They represent genuine trading transactions.

It would not be appropriate to treat every medicine line item as “goods” merely because it is a medicine. The context of supply matters.

**2. Reimbursement – Needs Reconsideration**

The reimbursement discussion in the advice needs careful application.

True reimbursement arises only where:
- An expense is incurred *specifically on behalf of KE*;  
- It is supported by third-party documentation;  
- No profit element is embedded; and  
- It is passed through on actual basis.

However, in OMI’s case, most doctors’ costs and related expenses arise from a general operational pool. If OMI allocates doctors’ fees or other costs from its overall revenue model and includes them in the invoice to KE, that is not reimbursement in the strict legal sense. It is consideration for services rendered by OMI.

A cost allocated from a general pool does not qualify as reimbursement. Reimbursement must be specific, identifiable, and incurred on behalf of KE under a clear arrangement. Otherwise, withholding exposure remains on the gross amount billed.

From KE’s perspective, it would not be advisable to assume reimbursement treatment unless:
- There is a specific arrangement;
- Supporting third-party invoices are available; and  
- The amount is clearly a pass-through item.

**3. Remaining Aspects**

Apart from the above two clarifications, the rest of the opinion appears technically sound. The rate distinction (5% for genuine sale of goods; 15% for services) is aligned with section 153 mechanics, subject to proper classification.

**Conclusion**

KE may consider accepting bifurcation, but strictly limited to:

- Genuine pharmacy “off-the-shelf” sales treated as goods (5%);  
- All hospitalization and treatment-related supplies, including medicines administered during treatment, treated as services (15%);  
- No automatic acceptance of reimbursement claims unless they meet strict pass-through criteria.

If these boundaries are clearly defined and documented, the position remains defensible. Otherwise, conservative application of 15% on composite healthcare services remains the safer route.

Dear Zeeshan,

I have reviewed the advice issued by A.F. Ferguson & Co. dated January 29, 2026 in respect of OMI’s healthcare revenue streams fileciteturn0file0 and set out below my understanding and practical implications from K-Electric’s perspective as a withholding agent.

**1. Current Position – Single Composite Bill (15% WHT)**  

At present, OMI is issuing a single consolidated invoice covering medicines, hospital services, diagnostics and consultants’ charges, and KE is deducting 15% withholding tax on the gross amount. From a conservative compliance standpoint, this approach is defensible because the dominant character of the transaction appears as “provision of healthcare services,” which falls under section 153(1)(b) (services) for corporate payers.  

However, this method may technically over-withhold where part of the invoice relates to sale of goods (i.e., medicines supplied through pharmacy), since sale of goods by a non-manufacturer corporate supplier generally attracts 5% under section 153(1)(a). In that sense, the current practice is conservative but not strictly aligned with the legal characterization of each revenue stream.

**2. Proposed Bifurcation – Goods vs Services**

PwC’s opinion clearly distinguishes between:

- Medicines, drugs, disposables, implants etc. – treated as *sale of goods* (5% WHT); and  
- Hospital services, diagnostics, room charges, etc. – treated as *services* (15% WHT) fileciteturn0file0  

On principle, this segregation is legally sound provided the following conditions are satisfied:

- The pharmacy sales are separately identified on the invoice.
- The pharmacy is part of OMI but clearly shown as sale of medicines (not bundled service).
- There is no artificial splitting merely to reduce withholding exposure.
- Supporting accounting classification and financial statements reflect this treatment consistently.

If these conditions are met, KE may apply:
- 5% on the goods portion; and  
- 15% on the services portion.

This would align more precisely with section 153 mechanics.

**3. Practical Risk Assessment**

While the bifurcation is technically correct, a few practical aspects require consideration:

- If historically KE has been deducting 15% on the entire bill, shifting to bifurcation may attract scrutiny only if the FBR views the supply as a composite service contract rather than distinct supply of goods and services.
- The key test would be whether medicines are independently sold (as pharmacy sales) or merely incidental to hospital treatment.
- If the invoice clearly segregates quantities, rates and GST/SST treatment separately, the legal footing becomes stronger.

From KE’s withholding perspective, the law does not require deduction at the higher rate where proper classification exists. However, any misclassification risk ultimately sits with the withholding agent.

**4. Sales Tax Angle (For Completeness)**  

Although your immediate query relates to income tax withholding, the opinion also touches upon sales tax treatment fileciteturn0file0. Medicines (if qualifying as drugs under the Drugs Act) are subject to a reduced 1% regime at manufacturer/importer level, and generally no further FST impact arises at hospital level. Hospital services are largely exempt under Sindh Sales Tax except room charges exceeding prescribed thresholds.  

This supports the conceptual distinction between goods and services at invoice level.

**5. My Overall Recommendation**

From a pure technical standpoint, bifurcation is legally sustainable if:

- Invoices are clearly split;
- Underlying accounting supports the split;
- There is no bundled pricing where goods cannot be independently identified; and
- A formal written clarification is obtained from OMI confirming the nature of each component.

However, from a risk-management lens, KE may consider the following approach:

- Seek a written confirmation/undertaking from OMI that the bifurcated components correctly reflect sale of goods and services under section 153.
- Ensure that goods portion represents actual pharmacy sale and not merely re-allocation of treatment cost.
- Maintain internal documentation to justify rate application in case of audit.

If OMI’s billing structure is robust and commercially defensible, there is no legal requirement to continue deducting 15% on the entire amount. Over-deduction merely for safety is not mandated under the Ordinance.

In summary, the bifurcation proposal is technically aligned with the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, subject to proper documentation and invoice integrity. The decision ultimately rests on KE’s appetite for strict legal compliance versus conservative over-withholding practice.

If required, I can also prepare a short internal note summarizing the withholding matrix for implementation by your taxation team.

parts: اس کو تھوڑا سا ریوائز کریں اور یہ دیکھیں کہ ان سپرلیلی چیزوں میں پرابلمس کو تو نہیں ہیں جو ایشوز اگر نہیں ہیں تو پھر ان کو چیزوں کو نا لسٹ دے دیں، اتنے ڈیٹیل میں نہیں ہمیں رسپانس دینا لیکن اگر کوئی ایفیفنی کوئی ان کے ایڈوائس میں کوئی ڈیفیکٹز ہیں یا کوئی کوئی چیز اوورلوک ہوئی ہے یا کوئی ایکسٹرا پریپوشن لینی ہے تو وہ ہائلائٹ کرنے

Zeeshan Sb,  

آپ نے بالکل درست نکتہ اٹھایا ہے — یہاں سیدھا “Section 22 allows depreciation to owner” والا سادہ جواب دینا مناسب نہیں ہوگا جب تک ہم پورا structure نہ سمجھ لیں۔ مسئلہ ownership سے زیادہ lease chain اور risk allocation کا ہے۔

Section 22 کا بنیادی اصول یہ ہے کہ depreciation اس شخص کو ملے گی جو depreciable asset کا owner ہو اور اسے اپنے business میں use کرے۔ لیکن اسی Ordinance میں leasing transactions کو ایک خاص انداز میں treat کیا گیا ہے، خاص طور پر finance lease scenarios میں، جہاں tax law عام commercial substance کو دیکھتا ہے نہ کہ صرف legal title۔

اب یہاں ambiguity یہ ہے:

Email میں لکھا ہے کہ “K-Solar (non-leasing company) being eligible to claim depreciation on their leased asset.”  

“Leased asset” کی اصطلاح خود دو مختلف scenarios create کر رہی ہے:

Scenario 1:  
K-Solar نے asset کسی leasing company سے lease پر لیا ہے (یعنی K-Solar lessee ہے)۔  
اس صورت میں:  
• Legal ownership leasing company کے پاس ہوگی۔  
• Leasing company کو depreciation ملے گی۔  
• K-Solar کو lease rentals deduction ملے گی بطور expense۔  
یہ classical structure ہے۔ یہاں K-Solar depreciation claim نہیں کر سکتی کیونکہ وہ owner نہیں ہے۔

Scenario 2:  
K-Solar asset کی owner ہے اور اس نے asset کسی third party کو lease پر دیا ہوا ہے۔  
اس صورت میں:  
• K-Solar legal owner ہے۔  
• Lease income وہ earn کر رہی ہے۔  
• Asset business purpose کے لیے use ہو رہا ہے (commercial exploitation through leasing)۔  
یہاں prima facie depreciation allowable ہو سکتی ہے — بشرطیکہ یہ finance arrangement disguised نہ ہو۔

Scenario 3 (جس کی آپ نے نشاندہی کی اور یہی اصل risk ہے):  
K-Solar نے asset کسی leasing company سے lease پر لیا، اور پھر وہی asset آگے کسی اور کو sub-lease کر دیا۔  

یہاں structure layered ہو جاتا ہے۔ اس صورت میں:

• Original leasing company depreciation claim کرے گی (because it is owner).  
• K-Solar lessee ہے — وہ lease rentals pay کرے گی اور expense claim کرے گی۔  
• اگر K-Solar sub-lease income earn کرے تو وہ business income ہو سکتی ہے۔  

لیکن یہاں K-Solar depreciation claim نہیں کر سکتی کیونکہ وہ legal owner نہیں ہے۔  

اگر وہ یہ کہے کہ چونکہ ہم income earn کر رہے ہیں اس asset سے اس لیے ہمیں depreciation بھی ملنی چاہیے، تو وہ double benefit کی طرف چلا جائے گا —  
یعنی:  
• Expense بھی claim ہو رہا ہے (lease rental as lessee)  
• Depreciation بھی claim ہو  
جبکہ ownership کسی اور کے پاس ہے۔  

Section 22 اس کو allow نہیں کرے گا کیونکہ شرط ownership کی ہے، صرف economic benefit کافی نہیں۔

اسی لیے context clear کرنا لازمی ہے، ورنہ ہم غلط premise پر advice دے دیں گے۔

میں suggest کروں گا کہ ہم پہلے K-Solar سے یہ factual clarifications لے لیں:

1. Asset کی legal ownership کس کے پاس ہے؟  
2. Asset کس نے capitalize کیا ہے اپنی books میں؟  
3. K-Solar lease rentals pay کر رہی ہے یا receive کر رہی ہے؟  
4. Lease agreement میں end-of-term ownership transfer clause ہے یا نہیں؟  
5. Asset sub-lease کیا گیا ہے یا نہیں؟  

یہ سوالات critical ہیں کیونکہ اگر K-Solar lessee ہے تو depreciation کا سوال ہی پیدا نہیں ہوتا۔  
اگر K-Solar lessor-owner ہے تو depreciation جائز ہو سکتی ہے۔  
اگر layered lease structure ہے تو مزید technical evaluation درکار ہوگا۔

اب میں ایک refined email draft تیار کر رہا ہوں جو ہم Zeeshan Sb کو بھیج سکتے ہیں clarification کے لیے:

---

Subject: Clarification Required – Depreciation Claim on Leased Asset (K-Solar)

Dear Zeeshan Sb,  

We have reviewed the query regarding depreciation claim by K-Solar (Private) Limited on a “leased asset.”  

Before forming a conclusive position under section 22 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, it is important to clarify the exact nature of the leasing arrangement. Depreciation is allowable only to the legal owner of a depreciable asset that is used in its business. Therefore, the tax treatment will depend entirely on the structure of the transaction.  

In order to advise accurately, could you please confirm the following:  

1. Whether K-Solar is the legal owner of the asset or has itself acquired the asset on lease from another leasing company?  
2. Whether K-Solar is paying lease rentals or receiving lease rentals in respect of the asset?  
3. Whether the asset has been capitalized in K-Solar’s fixed asset register?  
4. Whether the asset has been further sub-leased to another party?  
5. Whether the lease agreement contains any clause for transfer of ownership at the end of the lease term?  

If K-Solar is merely a lessee under a lease arrangement, depreciation would ordinarily be claimable by the legal owner (i.e., the leasing company), and K-Solar would be entitled to claim lease rentals as an expense.  

However, if K-Solar is the legal owner and is leasing out the asset as part of its business activity, depreciation may be admissible subject to satisfaction of the statutory conditions under section 22.  

Once we receive the above clarification, we will provide a definitive position aligned with the specific structure.  

Kind regards,  
Zuhair  

---

To: Zeeshan ur Rehman <zeeshanur.rehman@ke.com.pk>
Cc: Pervez Musani <pervez.musani@ke.com.pk>; Ahmed Arif <ahmed.arif@k-solar.com.pk>; Umer Jamal Khan <umer.jamal@ke.com.pk>
Subject: Advice require on depreciation Claim by Non-Leasing Company.

 

@Zeeshan ur Rehman as discussed in today meeting. Kindly take an advice from PwC regarding our company K-solar (the non-leasing company) being eligible to claim the depreciation on their leased asset?

Zeeshan Sb,  

I have critically re-examined the issue strictly in the context of section 22 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, keeping each condition and restriction of the provision in view rather than relying on a general “ownership equals depreciation” approach.

Section 22 allows depreciation to a person on depreciable assets that are:  

• owned by the person;  
• used in the person’s business; and  
• not otherwise restricted under the Ordinance.  

Now, let us dissect this carefully in the context of a non-leasing company giving an asset on lease.

First — Ownership  
Section 22 hinges on legal ownership. The Ordinance does not require the taxpayer to be a licensed leasing company. It only requires that the depreciable asset is owned by the person claiming depreciation. Therefore, regulatory status under SECP or NBFC Rules is irrelevant for income tax purposes.  

However, ownership must be real and not merely notional. If the lease agreement substantially transfers title or includes automatic transfer at the end without real residual risk, the department may argue that economic ownership has shifted. In such cases, mere legal title may not be sufficient if the arrangement is structured as a financing transaction.

Second — “Used in the Business” Requirement  
This is the more sensitive condition.

Section 22 requires that the asset must be used in the person’s business. The key question is:  
Is leasing out the asset part of K-Solar’s business activity?

If K-Solar is earning lease rentals and offering them to tax under the head “Income from Business”, then the asset is being used to generate business income. Leasing an asset for consideration is itself a business use. The law does not require physical use by the owner; commercial exploitation for income generation satisfies the “use” condition.

However, if the lease income is not characterized as business income, or if the asset is effectively deployed in the lessee’s independent project with risks entirely shifted, the department could argue that K-Solar is not “using” the asset in its own business but merely financing it.

Third — Partial Year Use and Timing  
Depreciation is allowable from the date the asset is put to use. If the asset has been capitalized but not yet leased or operationalized, depreciation would not be admissible for that dormant period.

Fourth — Finance Lease vs Operating Lease  
This is where the real risk lies.

If the arrangement is in substance a finance lease (for example:  
• lease term covers major economic life;  
• lessee bears insurance, maintenance, obsolescence risk;  
• bargain purchase option exists;  
• lease rentals recover full cost plus financing element),  

then the tax authorities may treat the transaction as a financing arrangement rather than business use of an asset.

In such a scenario, they could argue that:  
• The transaction is effectively a loan secured by asset;  
• The real income is finance income;  
• Depreciation should follow substance, not form.

Although the Ordinance does not expressly override legal ownership in section 22, litigation history shows that the department often challenges such arrangements under substance-over-form principles.

Fifth — No Restriction to “Leasing Companies”  
It is important to clarify: there is no provision in section 22 that restricts depreciation only to leasing companies. That concept comes from regulatory law, not tax law. Therefore, being a “non-leasing company” does not automatically disqualify depreciation.

Conclusion  

After applying each limb of section 22 critically:

Depreciation should be allowable to K-Solar provided that:  

1. K-Solar retains legal ownership of the asset;  
2. Lease income is offered to tax as business income;  
3. The asset is capitalized in its fixed asset register;  
4. The arrangement is not merely a disguised financing transaction;  
5. The asset is actually put to use for income generation.  

If these conditions are satisfied, section 22 supports the claim.

However, if the lease is structured in a manner where risks and rewards are substantially transferred and the economic substance is financing, the matter becomes disputable and requires deeper review of the agreement.

Before giving a final written position to the client, I would strongly recommend reviewing the lease agreement and confirming the tax treatment of lease rentals in the return.

This is one of those areas where the law looks simple on the surface but becomes fact-sensitive once you peel it layer by layer.

Zeeshan Sb,  

You are absolutely right to pause and examine the structure more carefully before giving a straight answer. Section 22 cannot be read in isolation from the commercial arrangement. The phrase “leased asset” in the email creates ambiguity, and depending on the structure, the tax result can be completely different.

Let us logically break this down in light of section 22 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

Section 22 allows depreciation only to the person who:  
• owns the depreciable asset; and  
• uses the asset in their business.

Ownership is the primary condition. The law does not grant depreciation merely because a person derives income from an asset. Legal ownership is critical.

Now the issue is: what exactly is the arrangement involving K-Solar?

There are three possible structures:

First possibility:  
K-Solar has acquired the asset on lease from a leasing company (i.e., K-Solar is the lessee).  

In this case:  
• The leasing company is the legal owner.  
• The leasing company claims depreciation.  
• K-Solar claims lease rentals as an expense.  

Here, K-Solar cannot claim depreciation because it does not own the asset. Section 22 would not permit it.

Second possibility:  
K-Solar owns the asset and has leased it to another party (i.e., K-Solar is the lessor).  

In this case:  
• K-Solar is the legal owner.  
• Lease income is being earned by K-Solar.  
• The asset is being commercially exploited in its business.  

Here, depreciation may be claimable under section 22, provided the asset is capitalized, lease income is offered to tax as business income, and ownership genuinely rests with K-Solar.

Third possibility (which is where complexity arises):  
K-Solar has taken the asset on lease from a leasing company and has further sub-leased it to another party.

In this layered structure:  
• The original leasing company remains the legal owner and claims depreciation.  
• K-Solar pays lease rentals (claims expense).  
• K-Solar earns sub-lease income.  

In such a case, K-Solar still cannot claim depreciation because ownership does not rest with it. Allowing depreciation in addition to lease rental expense would effectively result in a double tax benefit, which section 22 does not support.

Therefore, before issuing any formal advice, we must clarify the factual position.

I recommend sending the following clarification email:

Subject: Clarification Required – Depreciation Claim on Leased Asset (K-Solar)

Dear Zeeshan,  

We have reviewed the query regarding the eligibility of K-Solar (Private) Limited to claim depreciation on a leased asset.  

In order to advise conclusively under section 22 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, we require clarification on the exact structure of the leasing arrangement, as depreciation is allowable only to the legal owner of a depreciable asset used in its business.  

Kindly confirm the following:  

1. Is K-Solar the legal owner of the asset, or has it acquired the asset on lease from another leasing company?  
2. Is K-Solar paying lease rentals or receiving lease rentals in respect of the asset?  
3. Has the asset been capitalized in K-Solar’s fixed asset register?  
4. Has the asset been sub-leased to another party?  
5. Does the lease agreement contain a transfer-of-ownership clause at the end of the lease term?  

Once the above details are confirmed, we will provide a definitive and technically aligned position under section 22.

Kind regards,

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, depreciation is governed by section 22. The fundamental condition is not whether the taxpayer is a “leasing company” by status, but whether the taxpayer is the owner of the depreciable asset and the asset is used in the business for the purposes of deriving income. The law does not restrict depreciation only to companies licensed as leasing companies under SECP regulations. That distinction is relevant from a regulatory perspective, not from an income tax standpoint.

If K-Solar is the legal and beneficial owner of the asset, and the asset is leased out in the ordinary course of its business for earning lease rentals (which are taxable income), then the asset is being used for the purposes of business. In such circumstances, depreciation is generally allowable to the owner under section 22, subject to fulfillment of usual conditions—i.e., the asset must be depreciable property, capitalized in the books, and not otherwise restricted under any specific provision.

However, the tax treatment also depends on the nature of the lease arrangement. If the lease is structured as a finance lease in substance (where risks and rewards are substantially transferred and the lessee effectively becomes the economic owner), the accounting treatment under IFRS may differ. From a tax perspective, Pakistan’s tax law does not automatically follow IFRS classification; ownership and contractual rights remain key. We would need to examine whether the agreement transfers ownership at the end of the term, whether there is a bargain purchase option, and how risks and rewards are allocated. In a typical operating lease scenario, depreciation remains with the legal owner (i.e., the lessor).

In practice, we have seen non-banking and non-leasing entities (for example, energy project SPVs or equipment-holding companies) claiming depreciation on plant and machinery that is leased to group or third parties, provided lease income is offered to tax and the ownership position is clear. The tax authorities generally focus on substance—who owns the asset and who is deriving income from it.

– The lease agreement (to assess transfer of risks and ownership clauses);  
– Capitalization and recognition of the asset in K-Solar’s fixed asset register;  
– Treatment of lease income in the tax return; and  
– Any financing structure that may affect ownership characterization.

The fact that the asset has been sub-leased does not alter the original ownership structure. Unless ownership (legal or demonstrably beneficial in substance) has transferred to K-Solar under the primary lease agreement, depreciation cannot be claimed by it. Allowing depreciation in such circumstances would effectively result in duplication, particularly if the original lessor is already claiming depreciation on the same asset.

Therefore, based on the standard leasing model recognized under section 22, a non-leasing company that has acquired an asset under a lease arrangement cannot claim depreciation on that asset merely because it is using it or sub-leasing it. Zuhair, this is one of those deceptively simple questions that can go very wrong if we answer it in one line.

On a straight reading of section 22 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, depreciation is allowed to the person who “owns” the depreciable asset and uses it in deriving income from business. In a normal operating lease arrangement, the legal owner remains the lessor (typically a leasing company or bank), and the lessee merely claims lease rentals as revenue expenditure. In that situation, depreciation belongs to the lessor — not to the lessee.

However, the real answer depends entirely on the structure of the arrangement.

If K-Solar has taken the asset from a licensed leasing company under a finance lease, and the asset is legally owned by that leasing company, then depreciation would ordinarily be claimable by the leasing company. K-Solar, being the lessee, would claim lease rentals under section 20, subject to normal deductibility rules.

But if the so-called “lease” is in substance a hire purchase or financing arrangement where ownership (beneficial or legal) has effectively passed to K-Solar — or will pass at the end for a token consideration — then we must carefully examine whether K-Solar can be regarded as the owner for tax purposes. The Ordinance does not strictly define “ownership” as only legal title; courts in various contexts have recognized beneficial ownership where risks and rewards substantially vest with the user. That said, in Pakistan’s tax practice, in conventional finance leases routed through leasing companies, FBR’s position has consistently been that depreciation is for the lessor.

Another critical layer: you mentioned that this is “already a leased asset” and may have been further given to another party. If K-Solar itself is sub-leasing the asset, then the arrangement becomes more complex. In such a case:

- Who holds legal title?
- Is K-Solar capitalizing the asset in its books under IFRS 16?
- Is there any transfer of ownership clause?
- Is the original lessor claiming depreciation?
- Is there any double benefit risk?

We must avoid a situation where both parties claim depreciation on the same asset. That is something the department will immediately challenge.

So before giving a conclusive opinion, I would recommend formally obtaining:

1. The original lease agreement with the leasing company.  
2. Confirmation whether the lessor is claiming depreciation.  
3. Accounting treatment adopted by K-Solar (ROU asset vs capital asset).  
4. Details of any onward lease arrangement, if applicable.  

On first principles, if K-Solar is merely a lessee under a standard lease from a leasing company, depreciation should not be claimable by K-Solar. Lease rentals would be deductible instead.  

If, however, the transaction is structured in a manner where ownership vests with K-Solar and the leasing company is merely financing the acquisition, then the tax treatment may differ — but that conclusion must be grounded in the actual contractual terms, not accounting presentation alone.

Tax law does not follow labels. It follows substance — but only when the substance is demonstrable.

In matters involving leasing structures — especially in energy and infrastructure projects like this — documentation determines destiny.

**Subject: Master File and Local File – Transfer Pricing Documentation Requirements**

Dear Mr. Nabiel,

Thank you for your query regarding the template for Master File and Local File.

At the outset, we would like to clarify that there is no standard or prescribed template under the Income Tax Rules, 2002. The law does not provide a ready-made format; rather, it prescribes the mandatory contents that must be included in each document.

**Master File – Rule 27L**

The Master File is defined under Rule 27L of the Income Tax Rules, 2002. It provides a high-level overview of the multinational group’s global operations and transfer pricing policies. Broadly, the Master File must include:

- Organizational structure of the group (legal and ownership structure)
- Description of the group’s overall business and supply chain
- Details of intangibles owned, developed, and exploited by the group
- Group financing arrangements
- Consolidated financial statements
- Overall transfer pricing policies adopted by the group

Since the Master File reflects global group information, it is generally prepared and maintained at the group or parent level. The Pakistan entity typically obtains a copy for compliance purposes, where applicable.

**Local File – Rule 27N**

The Local File is prescribed under Rule 27N and is entity-specific. It must be maintained by the Pakistan entity where the prescribed threshold is met.

The Local File should contain, inter alia:

- Detailed description of the local entity’s business operations
- Nature, value, and terms of related party transactions (such as commission, royalty, and management fee)
- Copies of intercompany agreements
- Functional, Asset and Risk (FAR) analysis
- Selection and justification of the most appropriate transfer pricing method
- Benchmarking and economic analysis supporting arm’s length pricing
- Financial information with reconciliation to statutory accounts

In your case, where transactions involve commission, royalty, and management fee payable to UAE associated enterprises, the Local File becomes particularly important from an arm’s length and benefit test perspective.

Accordingly:

- The **Master File** is to be maintained at the group level in accordance with Rule 27L.
- The **Local File** must be prepared and maintained by the Pakistan entity under Rule 27N.

We can assist in structuring the Local File in line with statutory requirements and OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, and review the group Master File (once available) to ensure alignment with Pakistan compliance requirements.

Please let us know a convenient time to discuss scope and timelines.

Best regards,  
Zuhair

The Master File is defined under Rule 27L of the Income Tax Rules, 2002. It provides a high-level overview of the multinational group’s global operations and transfer pricing policies. Broadly, it should include:

- The legal and ownership structure of the group  
- Description of the group’s business operations and global supply chain  
- Details of intangibles and their ownership  
- Group financing arrangements  
- Consolidated financial statements  
- Overall transfer pricing policies adopted at group level  

Since the Master File relates to global group information, it is generally prepared and maintained at the parent or group level. The Pakistan entity typically obtains a copy for local compliance purposes, where applicable.

- Detailed description of the local entity’s business operations  
- Nature, value, and terms of related party transactions (including commission, royalty, and management fee)  
- Copies of intercompany agreements  
- Functional, Asset and Risk (FAR) analysis  
- Selection and justification of the most appropriate transfer pricing method  
- Benchmarking and economic analysis to support arm’s length pricing

This is a fairly standard request, but it signals something important.

When a client asks for a “template for Master File and Local File”, what they are really asking is not just for a format — they are asking for a defensible transfer pricing framework under Rule 27M and Rule 27N of the Income Tax Rules, 2002. In your case, since transactions are between Pakistan and UAE entities involving commission, royalty, and management fee, this will automatically fall within related party cross-border transactions, and therefore documentation becomes critical — especially in the current enforcement environment.

Now let me break this down practically, the way I would guide a client like Midas Safety Pakistan.

First, we should not simply send a generic template downloaded from the internet. The FBR expects substance. The Local File must reflect the actual business model, FAR analysis (Functions, Assets, Risks), benchmarking methodology, and justification of arm’s length pricing. The Master File must align with the global group structure and intercompany arrangements.

Second, before sending any template, it would be prudent to clarify:

- Are the Dubai entities part of a multinational group exceeding the consolidated revenue threshold prescribed under Rule 27N (i.e., PKR 1 billion for Local File and higher threshold for Master File applicability)?
- Has Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) been triggered at group level?
- Are these payments subject to withholding tax under section 152 and royalty under section 12/6 read with relevant DTAA (Pakistan-UAE)?
- Have any Advance Pricing Agreements (APA) or rulings been obtained?

In practical experience, management fee and royalty payments to UAE are frequently questioned by the department — especially on benefit test and duplication of services. So documentation must be structured carefully.

Section 34(5) mechanically provides that where a payable to a related party remains unpaid for more than three years, it becomes inadmissible in the year in which the three-year period lapses.

The law does not provide an explicit exception for regulatory delays.

Therefore, technically:

- If unpaid beyond three years, disallowance risk exists in FY 2026.

Do not add back in the return, but accept that in the event of scrutiny or proceedings under section 122(5A), the officer may apply section 34(5) and make an add-back.

**Subject: Technical Position – Adjustment of WHT on Early VPS Withdrawal under Section 149**

Dear [Name],  

We have independently reviewed the issue relating to adjustment of withholding tax deducted by a pension fund manager on early withdrawal of VPS against salary withholding under section 149 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”).

Set out below is a structured technical position for clarity.

---

### 1. Cautionary Technical View (Our Independent Assessment)

Clause (23A) of Part I of the Second Schedule provides that withdrawal before retirement age (or withdrawal exceeding 50% of accumulated balance) shall be chargeable to tax at the rate specified in section 12(6), and the pension fund manager is required to deduct tax at that rate at the time of payment.

Although the charge of tax ultimately flows from section 4 read with the relevant head-of-income provisions, clause (23A) establishes a specific taxation mechanism with a prescribed rate formula and a designated withholding agent.

Section 149, on the other hand, imposes an obligation on the employer to deduct tax on estimated income chargeable under the head “Salary.” The employer’s responsibility under section 149 is confined to computation of tax on salary income, after permissible adjustments as provided within that section.

The early VPS withdrawal is not salary income. It is a separately taxable receipt subject to its own withholding mechanism. In our view, the legislative scheme suggests that tax on such withdrawal is intended to be collected independently at source, with final reconciliation to occur through the employee’s annual return.

On this interpretation, employer-level adjustment of such withholding against salary tax under section 149 may not have been contemplated by the legislature. In practical enforcement terms, the tax authorities are likely to adopt a restrictive interpretation of section 149 and may contest such cross-adjustment in employer withholding proceedings (including potential exposure under section 161).

Accordingly, from a conservative compliance standpoint, the safer course would be to allow the employee to claim adjustment/refund in the annual return under section 168 rather than adjusting it at employer level.

---

### 2. Alternative View (Reflected in External Opinions)

An alternative interpretational view also exists.

Under section 168, tax deducted under the Ordinance is treated as adjustable unless specifically declared to be final tax. Clause (23A) does not designate the withholding as final tax. Furthermore, section 149 permits adjustment of tax withheld from the employee during the tax year.

On this reading, since the tax deducted by the pension fund manager is advance tax under the Ordinance and remains adjustable, there is no express statutory prohibition preventing its consideration while computing salary withholding under section 149.

It may also be argued that the Second Schedule does not create an independent charging provision; therefore, tax deducted under clause (23A) remains part of overall income tax liability of the employee and should be adjustable in principle.

On this interpretation, the employer may allow adjustment subject to appropriate documentation and safeguards, particularly ensuring that:

- The withdrawal is duly included in the employee’s taxable income;  
- Proper evidence of deduction by the pension fund manager is retained; and  
- The overall tax liability of the employee remains correctly computed.

---

### 3. Overall Position

The issue is interpretational in nature.

There is a legally arguable view supporting adjustment under section 149.  
There is also a defensible counter-view that the department may adopt, restricting employer-level adjustment on the basis that clause (23A) operates as a distinct withholding mechanism.

In the event of departmental challenge, the matter would likely require adjudication at appellate forums. The outcome of such proceedings cannot be predicted with certainty.

Accordingly, any decision to proceed with employer-level adjustment should be taken with awareness of potential scrutiny and litigation exposure.

We trust the above provides a balanced technical framework for consideration.

**Subject: Adjustment of WHT on Early VPS Withdrawal under Section 149**

Dear [Name],  

We have independently examined the issue relating to adjustment of withholding tax deducted by the pension fund manager on early withdrawal of VPS against salary withholding under section 149 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), and set out below our considered position.

Under clause (23A) of Part I of the Second Schedule, withdrawal before retirement age or withdrawal exceeding fifty percent of the accumulated balance is chargeable to tax at the rate specified in section 12(6), and the pension fund manager is required to deduct tax at that rate at the time of payment. Although the charge of tax itself flows from section 4 read with the relevant head-of-income provisions, the legislative scheme prescribes a specific taxation and withholding mechanism for such withdrawals. Section 149, on the other hand, places a statutory obligation on the employer to deduct tax on estimated income chargeable under the head “Salary.” The VPS withdrawal does not constitute salary income and is subject to its own designated withholding agent and rate formula. On a conservative reading of the statute, it may therefore be argued that the mechanism under clause (23A) is intended to operate independently, with final reconciliation of overall tax liability to take place through the employee’s annual return. On this basis, employer-level adjustment under section 149 may not have been specifically envisaged and could potentially be questioned by the tax authorities in withholding audits or proceedings under section 161.

At the same time, it is equally correct that clause (23A) does not create an independent charging provision, nor does it designate the withholding as final tax. Section 168 generally treats tax deducted under the Ordinance as adjustable unless expressly stated otherwise. Further, section 149 allows adjustment of tax withheld from the employee during the tax year. On this interpretational reading, it may be contended that tax deducted by the pension fund manager remains advance adjustable tax forming part of the employee’s overall income tax liability and, in principle, may be considered while determining net salary withholding. This represents a legally arguable view.

In light of the above, the issue is interpretational and capable of two views. While an adjustment under section 149 is not without legal support, it is also reasonable to expect that the tax department may adopt a stricter interpretation of the statutory framework and contest such treatment. In the event of challenge, the matter would likely require adjudication at appellate forums, and the outcome cannot be predicted with certainty at this stage.

Accordingly, any decision to proceed with employer-level adjustment should be taken with awareness of potential scrutiny and corresponding compliance exposure, and with appropriate internal documentation and safeguards in place.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

---

**Subject: Adjustment of WHT on Early VPS Withdrawal against Salary Withholding under Section 149**

Dear Adamjee,

Further to the recent discussions and the external opinions obtained in respect of adjustment of withholding tax deducted by the pension fund manager on early withdrawal of VPS against salary withholding under section 149 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), we have revisited the matter comprehensively.

As noted, two external advisors have taken the view that tax deducted on early withdrawal of pension — being deductible under clause (23A) read with section 12(6) — constitutes adjustable tax under section 168 of the Ordinance and may therefore be considered while computing salary withholding under section 149.

At the outset, it is important to appreciate the statutory structure. Clause (23A) provides that withdrawal before retirement age (or withdrawal exceeding 50%) shall be chargeable to tax at the rate specified in section 12(6), and the pension fund manager is required to deduct tax at source at that rate. The withholding mechanism is thus specifically embedded within the charging framework applicable to such withdrawal.

One interpretational view — which has been adopted in the external opinions — is that since section 168 treats tax deducted under the Ordinance as adjustable (unless expressly final), and section 149 allows adjustment of tax withheld from the employee during the tax year, there is no express statutory prohibition preventing the employer from factoring such withholding into its monthly salary tax computation. On this reasoning, the tax deducted by the pension fund manager is advance adjustable tax and may be considered in determining net salary withholding.

However, an alternative and more conservative view also merits consideration. Section 149 imposes a specific statutory obligation upon the employer to deduct tax on estimated income chargeable under the head “Salary”. The pension withdrawal in question is not salary income; it is a separately taxable receipt subject to its own charging and withholding provision. The fact that the legislature has prescribed a distinct rate mechanism and a separate withholding agent (i.e., the pension fund manager) indicates that tax on such withdrawal is intended to be collected independently at source, with final reconciliation occurring through the employee’s annual return.

From a practical enforcement perspective, tax authorities may take the position that employer-level adjustment of such withholding could potentially distort the computation of tax properly deductible on salary under section 149. In the absence of explicit statutory wording authorising cross-adjustment of this nature, the department is reasonably expected to adopt a stricter interpretation of section 149 and may contest such treatment in audit or proceedings under section 161.

Having said that, it is equally correct that the Second Schedule itself does not create an independent charging provision; the charge of tax flows from section 4 read with relevant head-of-income provisions. Therefore, a technical argument remains available that tax deducted by the pension fund manager is not final in nature and remains adjustable against overall tax liability of the employee.

In light of the above, the position may be summarised as follows:

- There exists a legally arguable view that WHT deducted on early VPS withdrawal is adjustable and may be factored into section 149 computations.  
- There also exists a material risk that the tax department may not accept such adjustment at employer level, on the basis that section 149 is confined to salary income estimation and that clause (23A) operates as a self-contained withholding mechanism.  
- In the event of challenge, the matter would become interpretational and may ultimately require adjudication at appellate forums; the outcome cannot be predicted with certainty at this stage.

Accordingly, if the Company elects to allow such adjustment, it may consider doing so subject to appropriate safeguards, including:

- Written employee declaration confirming inclusion of such withdrawal in taxable income in the annual return;  
- Proper documentation of tax deduction by the pension fund manager;  
- Internal payroll reconciliation ensuring no under-deduction arises on salary component itself.

Alternatively, the more conservative compliance approach would be to allow the employee to claim adjustment/refund at the time of filing the annual return under section 168, thereby eliminating employer-level exposure under section 149.

Given the competing interpretational views, our opinion is not that the adjustment is impermissible per se; rather, it is that the position is debatable and may attract departmental scrutiny. Any decision to proceed should therefore be taken with awareness of potential litigation exposure.

We remain available to discuss the practical implications and risk calibration based on quantum involved.

Regards,  
[Your Name]

---

2️⃣ **Reanda Haroon Zakaria Associates (16 July 2025)** – adopts a broader position that income tax is chargeable on total taxable income under section 4, and any tax deducted is to be treated as tax paid under section 168, hence adjustable, including WHT on early pension withdrawal against salary withholding under section 149 fileciteturn0file1.

---

### Core Legal Question

Can WHT deducted by a pension fund manager on early withdrawal (taxable under clause (23A) read with section 12(6)) be adjusted by the employer while computing monthly salary withholding under section 149?

This requires reading:

- Section 4 (charge on total taxable income)
- Section 11 (heads of income)
- Section 12(6) (tax rate mechanism for lump-sum receipts)
- Clause (23A) of Part I of Second Schedule
- Section 149 (salary withholding mechanism)
- Section 168 (adjustable vs final tax framework)

---

### Important Distinction: Nature of Tax Under Clause 23A

Clause (23A) clearly provides that withdrawal before retirement age (or beyond 50%) is:

- Chargeable to tax at the rate specified in section 12(6)
- Required to be deducted by pension fund manager at the time of payment

This is not a “separate head of income.” It is still part of taxable income, but it is subjected to a specific rate mechanism and mandatory withholding at source.

So the real issue becomes:

Is that withholding merely an advance adjustable tax under section 168?
Or does the specific charging/withholding mechanism prevent employer-level adjustment?

---

### Where the Debate Actually Lies

Section 149(1) allows employer to deduct tax on estimated salary income after adjusting:

- tax withheld from employee under other heads; and
- tax credits admissible under sections 61 and 63

The phrase “tax withheld from the employee under this Ordinance during the tax year” is broad. On literal reading, pension WHT falls within this language.

That is the foundation of both external opinions.

However.

Section 149 is a self-contained mechanism for computing withholding on *salary income*. The employer is responsible to ensure correct deduction based on estimated chargeable income under the head “Salary”.

Now here is the tension:

- Early pension withdrawal is not salary income.
- It is taxable under a specific charging and rate provision.
- The fund manager already deducted tax at source at the prescribed rate.
- Employer does not control that transaction.

If the employer reduces salary withholding because pension WHT exists, it risks:

- Under-deduction of salary tax if annual estimates change.
- Mismatch in reconciliation between IRIS salary withholding data and pension WHT data.
- Exposure under section 161 (failure to deduct correct salary tax).

From a pure legal interpretation standpoint, adjustment is arguable.
From a withholding risk management standpoint, it is aggressive.

---

### Practical Enforcement Reality

FBR system treats:

- Section 149 deductions separately (employer-based)
- Pension fund deductions separately (withholding agent-based)

During audit, officers normally evaluate employer compliance strictly on salary estimation basis. They rarely accept cross-adjustments that reduce monthly salary deductions unless the statute clearly mandates such adjustment.

And importantly:

Section 149 places primary responsibility on employer for correct salary withholding. If shortfall arises due to adjustment allowed internally, employer bears exposure — not the pension fund manager.

---

### My Technical Position

Legally defensible? Yes — based on literal reading of section 149 and section 168.

Conservative compliance position? No — because clause (23A) read with section 12(6) establishes a specific taxation mechanism that is intended to operate independently.

Where law creates a specific withholding mechanism tied to a specific rate (average of last three years), it indicates legislative intent that tax on that component is to be settled at source, subject to final annual reconciliation through return — not through employer salary adjustments.

---

### Most Balanced Approach

If Lucky Motor wishes to adopt adjustment:

- It should obtain written employee undertaking.
- It should ensure complete documentary evidence.
- It should reflect the adjustment transparently in payroll workings.
- It should maintain reconciliation for annual tax return filing.

Alternatively — and this is safer —

Allow employee to claim adjustment in annual return under section 168.
No employer-level exposure.
No 161 risk.
Cleaner compliance trail.

---

### Why the Earlier PwC View Was Conservative

The earlier internal view was driven by risk management under section 149 responsibility — not because the law expressly prohibits adjustment.

Adamjee’s point that it is “advance tax and adjustable” is legally supportable.
But employer risk allocation under section 149 changes the practical analysis.

---

### Strategic Recommendation

If this is material in amount and recurring, a short written clarification may be sought from FBR through a non-binding clarification route.

If immaterial, safer to leave adjustment to employee return stage.

---

Tax law often gives us two answers:

- the literal answer,
- and the defensible compliance answer.

The art of advisory lies in knowing which battlefield you are stepping into.

If you would like, I can now draft a revised response to Adamjee that:

• acknowledges both external opinions  
• explains the technical debate with section references  
• clarifies risk allocation under section 149  
• proposes a balanced way forward  

That will keep both legal integrity and client relationship intact.

Subject: Technical Position – Adjustment of WHT on Early VPS Withdrawal under Section 149  

Dear [Name],  

We have independently reviewed the question of whether withholding tax deducted by a pension fund manager on early withdrawal of VPS may be adjusted against salary withholding under section 149 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”).  

Clause (23A) of Part I of the Second Schedule provides that withdrawal before retirement age, or withdrawal exceeding 50% of accumulated balance, is chargeable to tax at the rate specified in section 12(6), and the pension fund manager is required to deduct tax at that rate at the time of payment. While the charge of tax ultimately flows from section 4 read with the relevant head-of-income provisions, the clause establishes a specific rate mechanism and designates a separate withholding agent for such withdrawals.  

Section 149, however, places a statutory obligation on the employer to deduct tax on estimated income chargeable under the head “Salary.” The VPS withdrawal is not salary income; it is a separately taxable receipt subject to its own withholding framework. On a conservative reading of the legislative scheme, it may therefore be argued that the tax deducted under clause (23A) is intended to operate independently, with final reconciliation occurring through the employee’s annual return. On this interpretation, employer-level adjustment under section 149 may not have been specifically contemplated and could potentially be challenged by the tax authorities, particularly in the context of employer withholding audits or proceedings under section 161.  

At the same time, an alternative interpretational view exists. Section 168 treats tax deducted under the Ordinance as adjustable unless expressly declared to be final tax. Clause (23A) does not designate the withholding as final. Further, section 149 permits adjustment of tax withheld from the employee during the tax year. On this reading, the tax deducted by the pension fund manager remains advance adjustable tax forming part of the employee’s overall liability and, in principle, may be considered while computing salary withholding. It may also be noted that the Second Schedule does not create an independent charging provision; the charge arises under section 4.  

In light of the above, the matter remains interpretational. A legally arguable view supports adjustment under section 149; however, there is also a reasonable likelihood that the tax department may adopt a stricter interpretation and contest such treatment. If challenged, the issue would require adjudication at appellate levels, and the ultimate outcome cannot be predicted with certainty.  

Any decision to allow employer-level adjustment should therefore be taken with due consideration of potential compliance exposure, along with appropriate documentation and internal safeguards.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]
