Upon review of both appeals against Order-in-Original No. 93 of 2018 dated March 2, 2018 fileciteturn0file0 and Order-in-Original No. 250 of 2019 dated April 1, 2019 fileciteturn0file1, it is evident that the dispute in both matters revolves around a single underlying issue: whether the Company can legally be characterised as having rendered taxable construction services under Tariff Heading 9824.0000 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011. The department has treated certain amounts (approximately Rs. 860 million in 2018 and Rs. 255 million in 2019) as consideration for services allegedly provided by the Company and, on that basis, imposed sales tax along with penalty and default surcharge. The Company’s consistent position is that no taxable service was rendered by it; the construction activity was undertaken by Sui Southern Gas Company Limited, an independently registered entity, and the amounts reflected in its accounts represent cost allocations or capital expenditures rather than consideration for services. Accordingly, the core question is one of legal characterisation — if the Company was not a service provider in law and did not receive consideration as such, the entire tax demand, together with penalty and surcharge, lacks foundation.

Recently, an assessment order under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2021 has been passed by the ACIR, whereby a tax demand has been created by recharacterising profit on debt as “income from other sources” and treating other receivables from SSGC as “other income,” both subjected to tax under section 39 of the Ordinance. The adjustments appear to have been made on the basis of the department’s position adopted in earlier tax years rather than an independent evaluation of the specific facts and legal position for the year under consideration. The order is being contested, and an appeal will be filed before the Commissioner (Appeals) challenging both the recharacterisation and the consequential tax demand.

One paragarph.

I have carefully reviewed both sets of Grounds of Appeal — against Order-in-Original No. 93 of 2018 dated March 2, 2018 fileciteturn0file0 and Order-in-Original No. 250 of 2019 dated April 1, 2019 fileciteturn0file1 — and when analyzed collectively, the underlying controversy in both matters is substantially identical.

At its core, the dispute is not about computation; it is about legal characterisation. In both orders, the Sindh Revenue Board has proceeded on the assumption that the Company rendered “construction services” falling under Tariff Heading 9824.0000 of the Second Schedule to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011. On this basis, specific amounts — approximately Rs. 860 million in the 2018 order and Rs. 255 million in the 2019 order — were treated as consideration for taxable services allegedly provided by the Company. Consequent to this characterisation, sales tax was demanded along with penalty under section 43 and default surcharge under section 44 of the Act.

The Company’s position in both appeals consistently challenges this fundamental assumption. It has been asserted that no taxable service was rendered by the Company at any stage. The construction activity in question — particularly relating to the branch pipeline — was carried out by Sui Southern Gas Company Limited (SSGC), an independently registered entity with SRB. The amounts recorded in the Company’s accounts do not represent consideration for services rendered; rather, they reflect cost allocations, reimbursements, or capital expenditures arising from the overall project structure. The department, therefore, has effectively reclassified a capital arrangement as a taxable service without establishing the essential elements required under the charging provisions, namely the existence of a service provider, a recipient, and identifiable consideration for a taxable service.

Accordingly, the central legal questions common to both appeals are whether the Company can, in law, be regarded as having rendered a taxable service within the meaning of sections 3 and 5 of the Sindh Act, and whether the impugned amounts can legally be construed as “consideration” for such service. If the Company did not provide a service and did not receive consideration in that capacity, the very foundation of the tax demand collapses. The consequential levy of penalty and default surcharge would also fail, as they are entirely dependent upon the sustainability of the principal tax liability.

From a management perspective, the significance of these appeals extends beyond the amounts involved for the respective years. The issue goes to the structural treatment of capital infrastructure arrangements and the legal identity of the service provider within the project framework. If the department’s interpretation were to be sustained, similar project-based or capital expenditure arrangements could potentially be exposed to sales tax demands in future periods. Conversely, if it is established that the Company was never a service provider in law, the tax exposure, along with the associated penalties and surcharge, would stand extinguished in its entirety.

I have carefully reviewed the Sindh Sales Tax Appeal in respect of Order-in-Original No. 1103 of 2024 dated May 20, 2024 fileciteturn1file0. When examined holistically, the dispute in this matter is fundamentally different in nature from the earlier characterisation cases and instead revolves around adjustment, discharge, and duplication of tax liability.

The core issue in this appeal is that the Deputy Commissioner has held that Sindh Sales Tax amounting to Rs. 168,952,892 is recoverable under section 23 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, without properly considering that the appellant had already deposited Rs. 110,856,547 into the Government Treasury through issuance of debit notes aggregating to Rs. 832,266,336 (relating to revised charges billed to Sui Southern Gas Company Limited for January and February 2017), along with a further payment in June 2018. The tabulated details on page 1 clearly show month-wise debit notes and the corresponding sales tax involved, aggregating to Rs. 110,856,547 fileciteturn1file0. Therefore, the appellant’s position is that the demand ignores tax already discharged.

A second key dimension of the dispute concerns input tax adjustment by SSGCL. The order alleges that SSGCL did not correspondingly reduce input tax; however, the appellant contends that SSGCL duly adjusted the input tax in its monthly return, particularly in June 2017, and that documentary evidence was available on record. Thus, the controversy also touches upon reconciliation between output tax declared by the appellant and input tax adjustments claimed by the customer.

Further, the imposition of default surcharge under section 44 and penalty under section 43 has been challenged on the ground that the appellant had already availed the facility under SRB Notification No. SRB-3-4/8/2019 dated May 18, 2019, whereby 15% default surcharge and 5% penalty (amounting to Rs. 1,519,530) were deposited. The grievance is that the department has imposed penal consequences without properly appreciating voluntary compliance and payments already made.

In summary, for management purposes, the underlying issue is not whether tax was chargeable in principle, but whether tax already deposited and adjustments already effected have been ignored, resulting in duplication of demand and unwarranted penal consequences. The case primarily revolves around reconciliation, evidentiary appreciation, and proper credit of payments made, rather than classification or taxability of the service itself.

I have critically reviewed both sets of Grounds of Appeal — the appeal against Order-in-Original No. 93 of 2018 dated March 2, 2018 fileciteturn0file0 and the appeal against Order-in-Original No. 250 of 2019 dated April 1, 2019 fileciteturn0file1 — and when examined together, the underlying dispute is conceptually the same in both cases.

From a management perspective, this is not a fragmented or technical dispute; it is fundamentally a characterisation issue.

In both orders, the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) has treated the Company as having provided “construction services” under Tariff Heading 9824.0000 of the Second Schedule to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011. On that basis, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that specific amounts (approximately Rs. 860 million in the 2018 order and Rs. 255 million in the 2019 order) represented consideration for taxable services rendered by the Company. Consequently, sales tax was demanded along with penalty under section 43 and default surcharge under section 44.

However, the Company’s consistent position in both appeals is that:

• No taxable service was rendered by the Company.  
• The Company did not receive consideration as a service provider.  
• The actual construction activity relating to the branch pipeline was carried out by Sui Southern Gas Company Limited (SSGC), which is itself a registered entity with SRB.  
• The amounts reflected in the Company’s accounts were either cost allocations, reimbursements, or capital expenditures — not consideration for construction services.

Therefore, the core legal questions underlying both cases are:

1. Whether the Company can legally be regarded as having rendered a “taxable service” within the meaning of sections 3 and 5 of the Sindh Act.  
2. Whether the amounts recorded can be treated as “consideration” for a service, as required under the charging provisions.  
3. Whether the same construction activity can be attributed to the Company when it was, in fact, performed by an independent, registered entity (SSGC).

In essence, this is a transaction characterisation dispute. The department has reclassified a capital/contractual arrangement as a taxable service without properly examining who actually rendered the service and who legally received consideration.

For management, the strategic significance is important. This is not merely about the quantum involved in these two years. If the department’s interpretation is upheld, similar capital infrastructure arrangements in the future could be exposed to sales tax demands, along with penalty and surcharge. Conversely, if it is established that no taxable service was rendered by the Company, the entire tax, penalty, and surcharge framework collapses.

In short, both appeals revolve around a single structural issue: whether the Company was ever a service provider in law. Everything else — tax, penalty, and surcharge — flows from that determination.

### Reliance on Lahore High Court Judgment – Penalty cannot be enforced through a “machinery approach” where there is no tax shortfall / revenue loss

In this regard, we respectfully place reliance on the recent judgment of the Honourable Lahore High Court, Rawalpindi Bench in **S.T.R. No. 07 of 2022 and connected references (Commissioner Inland Revenue vs. M/s D-Watson & another)**, decided on 03.07.2025, wherein the Court examined the scope of enforcement powers in the context of **POS integration defaults** and clarified a foundational principle that is directly relevant to the present proceedings: **where the statutory scheme is designed to recover tax shortfall, it cannot be expanded and used as a fallback to impose or recover stand-alone penalties for regulatory breaches that do not result in an ascertainable revenue deficit.** fileciteturn0file0L110-L138

The Honourable High Court held that the relevant “machinery” provision in the Sales Tax Act is tethered to **“tax not levied / short-levied / erroneously refunded”**, i.e., it is meant to protect the exchequer from **actual revenue loss**, and it cannot be stretched to become a blanket vehicle for imposing penalties for compliance-related breaches where **no quantifiable tax shortfall is established.** fileciteturn0file0L110-L131 The Court further emphasized the structural distinction between **tax liability** and **penal liability**, and held that enforcement must remain strictly within the four corners of the enabling provision and due process framework. fileciteturn0file0L143-L170

In such circumstances, the most severe penal consequences—such as sealing—become **disproportionate** and **legally vulnerable**, because the essential mischief (revenue leakage/evasion) is absent.

### Penal provisions must be strictly construed; if two interpretations exist, the one favourable to taxpayer prevails

The Lahore High Court also reaffirmed the settled principle of **strict construction of fiscal/penal provisions**, and relied upon the Supreme Court’s ruling in **Government of Punjab vs. Kunjah Textile Mills Ltd (2025 SCMR 239)**, holding that where more than one reasonable interpretation is possible, the one favourable to the taxpayer must be adopted. fileciteturn0file0L171-L179 In the present case, even assuming (for argument’s sake) that a printed POS number is treated as a prescribed formality, the facts clearly show that the transaction was **reported and traceable within SRB’s POS system**, hence the strict interpretation principle and proportionality both militate against invoking harsh penal measures.

Further, the Honourable High Court emphasized that any penalty carrying civil/quasi-criminal consequences must satisfy due process standards under **Articles 4 and 10A of the Constitution**, including clear notice, opportunity of hearing, and adjudication based on specific findings, including willful default supported by evidence. fileciteturn0file0L208-L241 In the instant case, the material on record (SRB portal evidence) itself negates any allegation of concealment, suppression, or intentional non-reporting; therefore, the jurisdictional and constitutional prerequisites for invoking penal proceedings—especially sealing—are not met.

ڈرافٹ ایک ای میل ڈرافٹ کریں جس کے اندر ہم اس کو اس ای میل میں کلائینٹ سے انکوائر کریں ریگارڈنگ جو ریسنٹلی سپر ٹیکس کا آرڈر پاس کیے ڈپارٹمنٹ نے اوور ٹیکس 22 جس کے اندر جو کمپٹیشن ایڈجسٹ اسپیشلی جو انہوں نے سبسڈی کو ٹیکس ایبل کر دیا ہے آن دا مس ایپلیکیشن آف سندھ ہائی کورٹ ججمنٹ کے اس میں انہوں نے سندھ ہائی کورٹ کا ججمنٹ جو تھا وہ منیمم ٹیکس آن ٹرن اوور تھا اس کو بنیاد بناتے ہوئے انہوں نے ایگزیمپشن ہماری 102 ای کے بھی انارڈینلی انکو کرتی ہے تو ایس پر ایور انڈرسٹینڈنگ اس پہ ہمیں اپیل فائل کرنی چاہیے تو اس میں آپ اپنا اپنے کنسرنز شو کریں کہ یا اپنا پوائنٹ آف ویو بتائیں کہ ہمیں اور اس کے اندر جو ہے ہماری ریفنڈ ایڈجسٹمنٹ 1.8 کے نہیں کی اور جو ایڈوانس ہولڈنگ شوڈ ہولڈنگ کو بھی کیٹر نہیں کیا تو اس ایک ای میل سے بنائیں جس کے اندر ہم یہ بتائیں اور یہ بولیں کہ یہ آرڈر پاس ہو گئے تو ہمیں جو ہے نہ کمشنر اپیلز میں اس کی اپیل فائل کرنی چاہیے

4.2 We respectfully reiterate that the scope of section 122(5A) of the Ordinance is not unbridled and cannot be invoked as a substitute for audit proceedings under section 177. The legislative scheme is clear: where the Department seeks to call for detailed information, explanations, or supporting evidence for verification purposes, the proper course is to initiate audit under section 177. In the absence of such initiation, resorting to section 122(5A) to embark upon a general verification exercise amounts to a fishing inquiry, which is impermissible in law. In this regard, reliance is placed on the decision of the Honourable Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue reported as 2010 PTD 111, wherein it was categorically held that amendments under section 122(5A) cannot be sustained on the basis of mere apprehensions or roving inquiries seeking information without definite and tangible material. The legal position was further clarified by FBR Circular No. 2 of 2021–22 dated July 1, 2021, which, while explaining the amendment introduced through the Finance Act, 2021, reaffirmed that section 122(5A) is not intended to be used as a parallel mechanism for conducting audit-like proceedings and must be exercised strictly within its defined statutory contours.

With reference to the notice issued under section 27(2) of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, whereby information has been sought on the premise that our client is engaged in “publishing, printing and reproduction services” falling under CPC 891, we respectfully submit the following factual and legal position for your kind consideration.

At the outset, it is important to clarify that the notice appears to proceed on two distinct assumptions: first, that the company is rendering publishing or printing services; and second, that it is receiving such services from other persons. Both aspects are addressed below in light of the applicable statutory and classification framework.

Under CPC Version 2.1, Division 89 covers “Other manufacturing services; publishing, printing and reproduction services; materials recovery services,” and Group 891 relates specifically to “Publishing, printing and reproduction services” fileciteturn2file3. The explanatory note to Group 891 clearly states that it includes situations involving the transfer of intangible inputs when outsourcing part or all of the production process, and expressly provides that the units rendering the service “do not own or retain usage rights to the intangible inputs” fileciteturn2file4. Further, subclass 89110 covers “Publishing, on a fee or contract basis,” and subclass 89121 covers printing services such as newspaper and book printing services, again in the context of services rendered on a fee or contract basis fileciteturn2file4. The defining feature of this group is therefore the rendering of publishing or printing functions for another person, without ownership of the underlying intellectual property.

In the present case, SMC is not engaged in publishing or printing services on a fee or contract basis for third parties. The company develops, owns and retains full intellectual property rights, including copyright and associated usage rights, in the books and content that it commercialises. Its business model is that of producing and selling books in its own name and for its own account. It does not undertake contract publishing, contract printing or reproduction of third-party content against consideration, nor does it publish material owned by others. The commercial substance of the activity is the exploitation of its own intellectual property through sale of finished books as goods. Since the essential condition under CPC 891 — namely, provision of services without ownership or retention of usage rights in the intangible inputs — is not met, the company’s activities do not fall within the ambit of Group 891.

As regards the second limb of the notice concerning services allegedly received from other persons, the company engages certain third-party vendors under toll manufacturing or job work arrangements. Under these arrangements, vendors carry out printing or related processing on content and materials owned by SMC. The intellectual property in the content remains vested in SMC at all times, and the vendors do not acquire any proprietary or usage rights in the books. Their role is confined to manufacturing or processing functions. Such arrangements do not alter the legal character of the company’s business, nor do they imply that SMC is rendering publishing services within the meaning of CPC 891. Vendor-wise details, including NTN and contact particulars, are being compiled and will be furnished separately for record and reconciliation purposes.

In view of the above, and based on the express language of CPC Group 891 and its explanatory notes, SMC is not engaged in “publishing, printing and reproduction services on a fee or contract basis.” The company’s principal activity is the sale of books as goods, supported by ownership and retention of intellectual property rights, which is legally and commercially distinct from the contract-based publishing or printing services contemplated under CPC 891. We trust that this clarifies the factual and legal position, and we remain available to provide any further clarification that may be required.

With reference to the notice issued under section 27(2) of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“the Act”), whereby information has been sought on the premise that our client is engaged in “publishing, printing and reproduction services” falling under CPC 891, we respectfully submit the following detailed factual and legal position for your kind consideration.

At the outset, it is important to clarify that the notice appears to seek information on two separate bases: firstly, on the assumption that SMC is rendering publishing or printing services; and secondly, that it is receiving such services from other persons. The company’s position on both aspects is explained below in light of the applicable classification framework under the CPC and the scheme of the Act.

Under CPC Version 2.1 (as updated 10.07.2025), Division 89 covers “Other manufacturing services; publishing, printing and reproduction services; materials recovery services,” and Group 891 specifically pertains to “Publishing, printing and reproduction services” fileciteturn2file3. The explanatory note to Group 891 expressly provides that the group includes situations involving the transfer of intangible inputs when outsourcing part or all of the production process, and clarifies that the units providing the service “do not own or retain usage rights to the intangible inputs” fileciteturn2file4. Subclass 89110 covers “Publishing, on a fee or contract basis,” and subclass 89121 covers “Printing services,” such as newspaper and book printing services, again explicitly in the context of services rendered on a fee or contract basis fileciteturn2file4. The consistent statutory theme across these subclasses is that the service provider performs publishing or printing functions for another person and does not own the underlying intellectual property.

**Subject: Response to Notice under Section 27(2) of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**

With reference to the notice issued under section 27(2) of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (“the Act”), whereby information has been sought on the premise that our client is engaged in “publishing, printing and reproduction services” falling under CPC 891, we respectfully submit the following factual and legal position for your kind consideration.

At the outset, it is important to clarify that the notice appears to proceed on two distinct assumptions:  

(i) that the company is rendering publishing/printing services; and  
(ii) that the company is receiving such services from other parties.

We address each limb separately below.

**1. Rendering of Publishing / Printing Services (CPC 891)**  

The classification under CPC 891 covers “publishing, printing and reproduction services, on a fee or contract basis.” A careful reading of the CPC explanatory notes makes it clear that this category generally applies where a person renders publishing or printing services to third parties, typically without owning or retaining intellectual property rights in the underlying content. In such arrangements, the publisher or printer merely performs a contractual function and does not hold copyright or proprietary rights in the content being published.

In the present case, SMC is not engaged in rendering publishing or printing services to third parties on a fee or contract basis. The company owns and retains full intellectual property rights, including copyright and usage rights, in the books and content being sold. The business model is that of sale of books as goods in its own name and for its own account.  

The company does not undertake contract publishing or contract printing for external customers. It does not print material owned by third parties against a service fee. Rather, it develops, owns, and commercially exploits its own intellectual property through sale of finished books.

Accordingly, the activity does not fall within the scope of CPC 891 and does not constitute a taxable service under section 3 read with section 8 of the Act. The assumption in the notice appears to be based on a general presumption associated with the word “publishing,” whereas the legal classification under the Act must be determined on the basis of substance and ownership of intellectual property.

In light of the above, no revenue arises from rendering publishing or printing services under CPC 891 during the period July 2025 to January 2026.

**2. Services Allegedly Received from Other Persons**

The notice further seeks details of publishing or printing services received from other persons during the relevant period.

In this regard, we respectfully submit that the company engages third-party vendors primarily under toll manufacturing arrangements. Under such arrangements, the vendors are engaged to perform printing or related processing on material/content owned by SMC. The intellectual property in the content remains with SMC at all times. The vendors do not publish content in their own capacity nor do they acquire any rights in the books or underlying material.

These arrangements are in the nature of tolling / job work, where processing is undertaken on goods owned by the principal. Such activity is distinct from publishing services rendered by an independent publisher. The vendors’ involvement is limited to manufacturing or processing functions and does not convert the company’s business into provision of publishing services.

To the extent applicable, the taxability of such toll manufacturing or job work arrangements is governed by the relevant federal and provincial tax framework, and not by any assumption that SMC is engaged in publishing services under CPC 891.

Vendor-wise details, along with NTN and contact particulars, will be furnished separately for record purposes; however, the mere receipt of toll manufacturing or job work services does not imply that SMC itself is engaged in rendering taxable publishing services.

**Conclusion**

In view of the foregoing:

- SMC is not engaged in rendering “publishing, printing and reproduction services” on a fee or contract basis under CPC 891.
- The company owns and retains intellectual property rights in the books and content sold by it.
- The primary activity is sale of books as goods in its own name and for its own account.
- Engagement of third-party printers under toll/job work arrangements does not alter the legal character of the company’s business.

We trust that the above clarifies the factual and legal position. The requested information, to the extent relevant, is being provided separately for record and reconciliation purposes.

Subject: Order-in-Appeal dated 27 February 2026 – Key Observations and Recommended Course of Action  

Dear [Client Name],  

We have reviewed the Order-in-Appeal passed by the Commissioner (Appeals-II), Sindh Revenue Board in Appeal No. 1304/2025, whereby the appeal filed by M/s Pakistan International Container Terminal Limited has been dismissed and the demand of Sindh Sales Tax amounting to Rs. 245,680,820 along with penalty and default surcharge has been upheld. fileciteturn0file0  

At the outset, a number of material defects appear in the order which, in our view, significantly affect the correctness and sustainability of the findings recorded by the appellate authority. The most fundamental defect relates to the observation made in the order regarding non-appearance of the appellant during the appellate proceedings. The order repeatedly records that neither the appellant nor its authorized representative appeared on the scheduled hearing dates and, on that basis, an adverse inference has been drawn and the matter has effectively been decided ex-parte. fileciteturn0file0 However, as also highlighted by EY, the authorized representatives had in fact attended the hearing. Therefore, the finding recorded in the order regarding complete non-appearance is factually incorrect and materially prejudicial to the appellant’s case. Such an incorrect recording of the proceedings constitutes a serious procedural defect and warrants rectification by the appellate authority itself.  

A second and equally significant concern is that the order does not adequately deal with the core factual controversy raised in the appeal. The principal dispute pertained to the characterization of certain revenues — particularly the cargo-related component — and whether such amounts constituted taxable services for the purposes of Sindh Sales Tax. This was a central factual ground raised in the memorandum of appeal; however, the order does not meaningfully examine or analyze this issue. Instead, the discussion largely revolves around legal propositions and presumptions arising from cross-matching of financial statements with SST returns. In effect, the most material factual ground raised by the appellant has not been properly adjudicated.  

In addition, as discussed during our earlier meeting, the memorandum of appeal originally filed appears to place comparatively greater reliance on legal arguments rather than fully articulating the factual matrix of the case. As a result, the appellate authority has largely confined its analysis to legal propositions while the underlying factual reconciliation — particularly regarding classification and reconciliation of the alleged short-declared turnover — has not been thoroughly examined in the order. This imbalance has likely contributed to the adverse outcome at the appellate stage.  

In light of the above deficiencies, we believe that two parallel courses of action should be considered. First, a miscellaneous/rectification application should be filed before the Commissioner (Appeals) highlighting the procedural and factual defects in the order, particularly the incorrect recording regarding non-appearance at the hearing and the failure to address the key factual ground relating to the nature and classification of the alleged taxable services. Since these defects go to the root of the appellate decision, the appellate authority should be requested to rectify the record and reconsider the matter.  

Secondly, in order to safeguard the client’s legal position and statutory timelines, an appeal should also be filed before the Appellate Tribunal SRB against the Order-in-Appeal. While preparing the Tribunal appeal, it would be advisable to place stronger emphasis on the factual aspects of the case, including the reconciliation of turnover and the specific treatment of cargo-related revenues which appear to have been overlooked in the present order.  

Furthermore, it would be important to evaluate the current recovery position in relation to this matter. We understand that approximately Rs. 400 million had previously been recovered by the department in connection with this dispute. It would therefore be necessary to determine how much of the demand of Rs. 245 million forming the subject matter of the present order has already been recovered and what portion, if any, remains outstanding. This assessment will allow us to evaluate the likelihood of further recovery proceedings and consider appropriate protective measures, if required.  

In summary, given the multiple factual and procedural infirmities in the appellate order, our preliminary view is that both remedial steps should be pursued simultaneously: (i) filing a rectification/miscellaneous application before the Commissioner (Appeals), and (ii) filing a substantive appeal before the Appellate Tribunal SRB with a stronger focus on the factual grounds of the case.  

We will be pleased to discuss the matter further and proceed with preparation of the necessary filings once we receive your confirmation and the updated position regarding recovery of the demand.  

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

Dear [Client Name],  

We have completed our preliminary review of the Order-in-Appeal passed by the Commissioner (Appeals-II), Sindh Revenue Board in Appeal No. 1304/2025 whereby the appeal filed by M/s Pakistan International Container Terminal Limited has been dismissed and the tax demand of Rs. 245,680,820 along with penalty and default surcharge has been upheld. fileciteturn0file0  

At the outset, the order appears to suffer from certain material factual and procedural deficiencies which, in our view, materially affect the validity of the findings recorded therein.  

Firstly, the order records that neither the appellant nor the authorized representative appeared during the appellate proceedings and, on that basis, the authority has drawn an adverse inference and proceeded to decide the matter essentially on an ex-parte basis. However, as also highlighted by EY, the hearing was in fact attended by the authorized representatives. The recording in the order that no one appeared from the appellant’s side is therefore factually incorrect and has clearly prejudiced the adjudication process. This incorrect recording of the hearing proceedings itself constitutes a significant procedural defect which ought to be brought to the attention of the appellate authority.  

Secondly, and more importantly, the order does not address the core factual controversy which formed the foundation of the alleged discrepancy. The entire dispute essentially arises from the reconciliation exercise carried out by the department between the audited financial statements and the SST returns, particularly in relation to cargo-related revenues. A substantial component of the amount identified through cross-matching relates to export-related cargo handling, which was treated differently in the appellant’s records because that portion represented royalty or export-related charges rather than taxable local services. However, the order does not examine or discuss this aspect at all. The export-related cargo component — which forms the principal basis of the alleged discrepancy — has not been analysed or adjudicated anywhere in the order. The omission to deal with this key factual ground significantly weakens the reasoning adopted by the appellate authority and, in our view, represents a fundamental gap in the adjudication.  

Additionally, as discussed during our earlier meeting, the memorandum of appeal originally filed appears to have placed comparatively greater reliance on legal arguments rather than fully articulating the factual matrix of the case. As a result, the order largely addresses legal propositions while the underlying factual reconciliation — particularly relating to the cargo and export-related component — has not been properly examined.  

In view of the above, we believe the matter requires immediate strategic action. As a first step, a miscellaneous/rectification application should be filed before the Commissioner (Appeals) highlighting the factual and procedural defects in the order. This would include the incorrect recording regarding non-appearance at the hearing and, more importantly, the failure to address the central factual issue relating to the export-related cargo component which forms the crux of the alleged discrepancy.  

At the same time, in order to safeguard the statutory timelines, an appeal should also be filed before the Appellate Tribunal SRB. While preparing the Tribunal appeal, it would be advisable to place stronger emphasis on the factual aspects of the case, particularly the classification and reconciliation of cargo-related revenues and the treatment of the export-related component which has not been examined in the present order.  

We would therefore recommend scheduling a meeting with the EY team at the earliest so that the factual position can be further consolidated and properly articulated. This would enable the miscellaneous application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to be filed in a more effective manner and also ensure that the appeal before the Tribunal is structured on stronger factual grounds.  

Separately, it would also be important to ascertain the precise recovery position in relation to this matter. We understand that approximately Rs. 400 million had earlier been recovered by the department in connection with this dispute. A bifurcation of that recovered amount would need to be obtained in order to determine how much of the present demand of Rs. 245 million has already been recovered. If the demand forming the subject matter of this order has already been substantially recovered, the risk of further recovery proceedings may not arise and consequently the need for immediate constitutional relief before the High Court may not be necessary.  

We would be pleased to discuss the matter further and coordinate with the EY team once we receive your confirmation.
